subject: history
description: History FET (Grades 10-12) consolidated bank. Topics keyed by atomic skill id (from data/history-skill-tree.json). Each pool = 20 items spread across CAPS Cognitive Levels: L1 30% (recall) / L2 40% (analyse/apply) / L3 30% (evaluate/argue). Input types: choice, true-false, cloze, sequence, image-match, sort-buckets, highlight-source, argument-builder, paragraph-template, source-comparison. Any question may carry optional 'source' block (text extract / image / map / cartoon with provenance). FET rule: no timer, 60% pass mark (12 of 20 correct). v1.1: Grade 10 fully authored (19 skills, 380 items); Grade 11 fully authored (15 skills, 300 items across 5 topics) pending head-of-ed review.

HIS.G10.T1.WIDER.A1.title: What 'civilisation' meant — and who decided
HIS.G10.T1.WIDER.A1.description: Concept of 'civilisation' as a label built on comparison and used to justify ranking, conquest and racism.
HIS.G10.T1.WIDER.A1.strand: T1 — Societies of the Wider World & Ancient Ethiopia
HIS.G10.T1.WIDER.A1.caps_topic: Societies of the Wider World in Ancient Times
HIS.G10.T1.WIDER.A1.recovery_strategy: 'Civilisation' is a LABEL applied by people in power, not a measurement. Test any claim with evidence: were there cities? Writing? Long-distance trade? Centralised government? If yes, the society was complex regardless of who labelled it 'uncivilised'.

questions.question: When 19th-century Europeans called a society 'civilised' or 'uncivilised', what were they actually doing?
options: Comparing it to their own society and ranking it
Counting how many cities it had
Naming the country it was in
questions.expected: Comparing it to their own society and ranking it
questions.memo: 'Civilisation' was never a neutral measurement. It was always a comparison made by people in power — usually placing themselves at the top.

questions.question: True or false: The label 'civilisation' meant the same thing to all people at all times in history.
questions.memo: The meaning changed depending on who was doing the labelling. Earlier Egyptians, Greeks, Chinese all defined 'civilisation' to centre themselves. Western scholarship later anointed Greek civilisation as supreme.

questions.question: Why did western scholarship claim Greek civilisation as 'supreme'?
options: To establish western civilisation as the inheritor of the ideal
Because Greece was the largest empire in history
Because Greek was the world's most common language
questions.expected: To establish western civilisation as the inheritor of the ideal
questions.memo: The claim 'Western civilisation is built on Greek civilisation' gave Europe a prestigious ancestry. Africans were prohibited from making similar claims about Egypt — even though Egypt is in Africa.

questions.question: The European view that Africa lacked civilisation came from _________ scholarship.
questions.memo: Pseudo-scientific racism in 19th-century European universities created the idea that African people were 'genetically inferior' — a claim without evidence used to justify colonialism.

questions.question: Pseudo-scientific theories of the 19th century claimed:
options: African people did not need education
questions.memo: 'Pseudo-' means 'fake'. These were not real science — they were dressed-up racism. Modern genetics has thoroughly refuted them.

questions.question: True or false: A 'Eurocentric framework' puts Europe at the centre and treats other places as less important.
questions.memo: 'Eurocentric' = treating Europe as the default. A Eurocentric history book might describe 1492 as the 'discovery' of the Americas — discovered by whom? People were already there.

questions.question: Sort each statement as a neutral observation or a value-loaded comparison.

items.text: The Aztec capital Tenochtitlán had a population of about 200,000 in 1500
Aztecs were savages who needed European Christianity
African kingdoms traded gold for North African salt
African societies were primitive and lagging behind
The Mali Empire used a written legal code
Africans were unable to appreciate complex culture

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: First test for spotting bias: does the statement describe what happened (neutral) or rank it (value-loaded)?

questions.question: European scholars said African societies were 'still in the dark ages'. What does this comparison assume?
options: That European progress is the standard everyone else must measure against
That African societies were physically darker
questions.expected: That European progress is the standard everyone else must measure against
questions.memo: 'Still in the dark ages' assumes a single road of progress with Europe ahead. African societies developed in their own ways — not behind on someone else's road.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to complete this explanation of how the label 'civilisation' worked.
questions.cloze_template: When Europeans called other societies '[1]', the label was always a [2]. The claim that someone is 'civilised' implies that others are '[3]' and therefore [4]. This is why the label was such a useful [5].
questions.memo: Comparison → ranking → assumed inferiority → justifies treating the 'uncivilised' badly. That is why the label was so politically useful.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show the author is making racist value-judgements, not stating facts.
questions.source_text: Africa was a continent without civilisation or significant historical achievements. Unable to appreciate the complexities of various cultures, Western thought concluded that the African continent was still in the dark ages, uncivilised and unresponsive to progress.
questions.task: Tap the phrases that reveal the author's racist value-judgements.

targets.phrase: without civilisation or significant historical achievements
targets.reason: Denies achievements that demonstrably existed (Aksum, Mali, Great Zimbabwe)

targets.phrase: Unable to appreciate
targets.reason: Assumes African inferiority before any evidence

targets.phrase: still in the dark ages
targets.reason: Eurocentric ranking on a single 'progress' scale

targets.phrase: uncivilised and unresponsive to progress

questions.expected: Three or more of the four target phrases identified
questions.memo: Each phrase is a value judgement dressed up as a description. Spotting them is the start of reading sources critically.

questions.question: Compare these two sources about Africa.

source_a.text: Mansa Musa, ruler of Mali, made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324. Records from Cairo state that he distributed so much gold that its price in Egyptian markets was depressed for over ten years.

source_b.text: Until the European explorers brought enlightenment, the African interior remained primitive and unknown, its peoples without organised states or written records.

statements.text: Mali had a powerful ruler in the 1300s
The African interior had no organised states before Europeans arrived
African gold flowed across the Sahara into Egypt and beyond
European explorers found peoples without written records
Both sources describe Africa's economic links to the wider world

questions.memo: Source A directly contradicts Source B. The contradiction shows that 19th-century European 'common knowledge' was wrong — and was wrong about things their own contemporary records could have corrected.

questions.question: Sort each statement as either a real feature of many precolonial African societies, or a myth invented by European scholars.

buckets.label: Was real in many precolonial African societies
Was a myth invented by European scholars

items.text: Long-distance trade routes
Africans 'lacked civilisation' before Europeans arrived
Written records (e.g. Timbuktu manuscripts)
African societies had no government
Centralised states with rulers and taxation
Africans were genetically less capable
Cities of tens of thousands of people
Africa was 'isolated from the outside world'

questions.memo: The myths persist because they are useful to those who benefit from believing them. The realities are well-documented in archaeology, written records and oral traditions.

questions.question: An Egyptian scholar of 500 BCE claims 'civilised people' come from Egypt. A Greek scholar of 400 BCE claims 'civilised people' come from Greece. What does this disagreement show about the label?
options: It is always shaped by who is using it
Only one of them can be right
The label is universal and timeless
questions.expected: It is always shaped by who is using it
questions.memo: The label travels with power. Whoever is dominant defines who is civilised — and almost always puts themselves at the top.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show the author is ranking societies rather than describing them.
questions.source_text: The Egyptians built the pyramids using sophisticated mathematics and engineering. However, this should be seen as an early step toward true civilisation, which would only later emerge in Greece and reach its fullest expression in modern Europe.
questions.task: Tap the words that smuggle a ranking into the description.

targets.phrase: early step toward true civilisation
true civilisation
targets.reason: Implies one true type — others are false

targets.phrase: fullest expression in modern Europe
targets.reason: Puts modern Europe at the top of the ranking

questions.expected: Two or more target phrases identified
questions.memo: The first sentence describes Egyptian achievements honestly. The second sentence quietly inserts a ranking that places modern Europe at the top. Spotting smuggled rankings is a core source-analysis skill.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The European label of civilisation was a political tool, not a scientific measurement.'
questions.thesis: The European label of 'civilisation' was a political tool, not a scientific measurement.

pool.text: Europeans applied the label to themselves and denied it to societies they planned to colonise
Kingdoms like Mali had cities, writing and government but were still called 'uncivilised' by European scholars
The label was used to justify slavery, land seizure and colonial rule
Greek philosophy is taught in many universities today
Modern Africans live in cities
European technology in the 19th century was more advanced than most African technology

questions.memo: The three strongest items together build the political-tool argument: the label moved with power, denied evidence in front of its users, and served colonial policy. e6 looks plausible but is a counter-argument — it might justify a 'technology-gap' claim, not a 'civilisation' ranking.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why 'civilisation' was a label, not a measurement.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why 'civilisation' was a label, not a measurement.

options.text: The label 'civilisation' was a political judgement, not a neutral measurement
Civilisation is a scientific category measured by city size
Only Greek societies were ever called civilised
European scholars called Mali and Aksum 'uncivilised' even though both had cities, trade routes and written records
Some European countries have museums about Africa
Ancient Greeks invented the word 'civilisation'
If the label had been a neutral measurement, societies with the same features would have received the same label — but European writers applied it based on power, not facts
It just shows that European scholars were sometimes mistaken
Greek scholars set the rules and Europeans followed them

questions.memo: A real argument has a clear claim, specific evidence and an explanation that links the two. Final paragraph: 'The label civilisation was a political judgement, not a neutral measurement. European scholars called Mali and Aksum uncivilised even though both had cities, trade routes and written records. If the label had been a neutral measurement, societies with the same features would have received the same label — but European writers applied it based on power, not facts.'

questions.question: Compare these two sources about Great Zimbabwe.

source_a.text: It would be quite unreasonable to imagine that the ruins were built by negroes. The lintels and stonework show too high a culture for the African race.

source_b.text: Examination of all the existing evidence, gathered from every quarter, still can produce not one single item that is not in accordance with the claim of Bantu origin and medieval date.

statements.text: The author attempts to use evidence to reach a conclusion
The author starts with a racist assumption rather than evidence
The author concludes that Africans built Great Zimbabwe
The author was writing before 1900
Both authors used the same research methods

questions.memo: Same site, opposite conclusions — because Mauch began with a racist conclusion ('too high a culture for the African race') and Caton-Thompson began with evidence. This is how prior beliefs shape what we 'see' in sources.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Western thought called Greek civilisation supreme but denied similar recognition to ancient Egypt — showing the label was racially selective.'
questions.thesis: Western thought called Greek civilisation supreme but denied similar recognition to ancient Egypt, showing the label 'civilisation' was racially selective.

pool.text: Ancient Egypt's achievements in mathematics, architecture and writing equal or exceed those of ancient Greece
Egypt is in Africa, while Greece is in Europe — and the denial of 'civilisation' tracks with this geography
Greek philosophy influenced Roman, then European, intellectual traditions — giving Europeans a motive to claim Greece as ancestor
Modern Egypt is a tourist destination
Greek statues are made of marble
Greek civilisation actually borrowed from earlier Egyptian thought (e.g. mathematics)

questions.memo: Three together build the racial-selectivity argument: Egypt deserves the label by the same criteria (e1), was denied it along racial geography (e2), and the denial served European identity-building (e3). e6 is true and interesting but works in a different direction — supports a 'borrowing' argument, not the racial-selectivity argument.

questions.question: Build a paragraph evaluating whether 'civilisation' is a useful word for historians today.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph evaluating whether 'civilisation' is a useful word for historians today.

options.text: Historians should be careful with the word 'civilisation' because it carries 200 years of ranking baggage
Historians should use 'civilisation' freely because it is a clear term
Historians should ban the word completely
The word has been used to deny achievement to African and Indigenous societies while crediting European ones
The word has Greek roots
School textbooks no longer use the word
Modern historians prefer specific descriptions — 'urban centre', 'centralised state', 'literate culture' — because these say what the society actually was without the ranking
Historians should always use older words to stay consistent with old textbooks
Specific descriptions are too long to use in school

questions.memo: A careful position recognises both the word's history and the alternatives now available.

questions.question: Compare these two sources, written 112 years apart, on what 'civilisation' means.

source_a.text: Civilisation is what European nations have. Other peoples lack it and must be taught.

source_b.text: Every long-lived community develops the things called marks of civilisation — cities, writing, law, art — but each in its own form.

statements.text: The author argues that civilisation looks different in different societies
The author treats civilisation as something only Europeans have
Both authors agree about what civilisation is
The author writes from a position of imperial power
The author lists 'cities, writing, law, art' as marks of civilisation

questions.memo: 112 years apart, opposite framings. The colonial governor weaponises the term to justify ruling others; the modern historian disarms it by recognising parallel forms across societies.

HIS.G10.T1.WIDER.A2.title: Ancient societies side by side
HIS.G10.T1.WIDER.A2.description: Comparing Egyptian, Greek, Indian, Chinese and Mesoamerican achievements on technology, trade, governance and learning.
HIS.G10.T1.WIDER.A2.strand: T1 — Societies of the Wider World & Ancient Ethiopia
HIS.G10.T1.WIDER.A2.caps_topic: Societies of the Wider World in Ancient Times
HIS.G10.T1.WIDER.A2.recovery_strategy: Anchor each society to 2 signature achievements: Egypt → pyramids + mathematics; Greece → philosophy + democracy; India → zero/decimal numerals; China → paper, printing, gunpowder, compass; Maya → calendar + astronomy; Aztec → urban planning (Tenochtitlán). Different strengths, not different rankings.

questions.question: Which ancient society built the pyramids of Giza?
questions.memo: Built around 2500 BCE on the west bank of the Nile, the pyramids served as tombs for pharaohs. Their construction required advanced mathematics, engineering and a large, organised workforce.

questions.question: Which ancient civilisation is widely credited with developing the concept of zero and the decimal number system used worldwide today?
questions.memo: Zero as a numeral (not just an absence) and the decimal place-value system spread from India via the Islamic world to medieval Europe. Try doing long division in Roman numerals to feel the difference.

questions.question: Which ancient civilisation built the famous Long Count calendar, used to track celestial movements with great precision?
questions.memo: The Maya Long Count calendar tracked dates with high precision. The famous '2012' date was simply a calendar cycle ending — not a doomsday.

questions.question: True or false: Ancient China invented paper, printing, gunpowder and the magnetic compass.
questions.memo: These 'Four Great Inventions' of China spread westward over centuries. Paper (Han dynasty), printing (Tang), gunpowder (Tang), compass (Han) — each reshaped life across Eurasia long before Europe's industrial era.

questions.question: Ancient Greek thinkers like Socrates, Plato and Aristotle developed the field of _________.
questions.memo: Greek philosophy explored ethics, politics, logic and the nature of reality, and shaped much of later European intellectual life.

questions.question: Which ancient city, the Aztec capital, had an estimated population of around 200,000 in 1500 — larger than most European cities of that time?
questions.memo: Built on an island in Lake Texcoco (under modern Mexico City), Tenochtitlán had causeways, aqueducts and chinampas (floating gardens). The Spanish destroyed it in 1521.

questions.question: Match each achievement to the society that produced it.

items.text: Pyramids and hieroglyphic writing
Socratic philosophy and Athenian democracy
Decimal number system and the concept of zero
Invention of paper and gunpowder
Long Count calendar and pyramidal temples in the Yucatán
Capital city of 200,000 with floating gardens (chinampas)
Mathematics used to build great stone monuments along the Nile
City-states with assemblies of male citizens

questions.memo: Each society had signature achievements. No single society led in everything — strengths developed in parallel.

questions.question: Greek democracy in Athens allowed which group to vote?
options: Male citizens of Athens only (not women, slaves or foreigners)
All adult residents including women and slaves
Only the king and his advisors
No one — Athens had a king
questions.expected: Male citizens of Athens only (not women, slaves or foreigners)
questions.memo: Athenian democracy was direct (citizens voted on laws), but the voting body was small. Women, slaves and metics (resident foreigners) were excluded — perhaps 10–20% of the population could vote.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to complete this comparison of ancient societies.
questions.cloze_template: Ancient Egypt developed advanced [1] used to build the pyramids. Ancient India formalised the concept of [2], which made arithmetic far easier. Ancient China invented [3], which transformed the spread of knowledge. The Maya tracked time with a precise [4]. None of these societies was 'ahead' of the others — they developed [5] strengths.
questions.memo: Side-by-side comparison shows different strengths, not different rankings — the heart of this skill.

questions.question: Tap the words and phrases that show the author is ranking, not describing.
questions.source_text: By 500 BCE, ancient Athens had pioneered the world's first true civilisation — democracy, philosophy and rational thought. While other societies remained primitive, the Greeks alone showed the way forward for human progress.
questions.task: Tap the loaded ranking language in this passage.

targets.phrase: the world's first true civilisation
targets.reason: Ranks Athens above all others; denies parallel achievements

targets.phrase: primitive
alone showed the way forward
targets.reason: Eurocentric ranking on a single 'progress' path

targets.phrase: the way forward for human progress
targets.reason: Assumes one path, with Greece (and later Europe) at its front

questions.expected: Three or more target phrases identified
questions.memo: Athens did pioneer specific things (philosophy, direct democracy in a city-state). The bias is in calling this 'first true' civilisation and dismissing parallel achievements in India, China, Egypt and the Americas.

questions.question: Sort each ancient achievement by the continent where it was produced.

items.text: Pyramids of Giza
Parthenon of Athens
Tenochtitlán
Great Wall of China
Library of Alexandria
Mayan temple cities (Tikal, Chichén Itzá)
Roman Colosseum
Indus Valley cities (Mohenjo-daro)

questions.memo: Major ancient achievements are spread across every continent. The Europe-only view of 'civilisation' deliberately ignored this geographic reality.

questions.question: Compare these two sources about ancient Egypt.

source_a.text: Ancient Egypt developed mathematics, monumental architecture and a complex bureaucracy supporting a population of around 3 million by 1500 BCE.

source_b.text: True civilisation began with the Greeks. Earlier peoples, including the Egyptians, lacked the rational mind that distinguishes civilised from primitive life.

statements.text: Egypt had millions of people supported by an organised state
Greeks were the first to be 'truly civilised'
Egyptians built mathematical knowledge
Earlier peoples lacked rational thought
Both sources praise Egyptian achievements

questions.memo: Same subject (Egypt), opposite framings. The 1894 source denies what the 2018 source documents. Choosing which framing to teach is itself a political act.

questions.question: A historian compares Greek democracy with Chinese imperial administration. What is the FAIREST comparison?
options: Each suited its own society — neither is universally 'better'
Greek democracy is always superior because it gave people a vote
Chinese administration is always superior because it lasted longer
They cannot be compared because they are too different
questions.expected: Each suited its own society — neither is universally 'better'
questions.memo: Greek democracy worked in small city-states with limited voter eligibility. Chinese administration kept a huge empire running for centuries with merit-based examinations. Both solved their society's challenges in ways suited to scale and context.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that, taken together, refute the claim that 'pre-1500 Africa had no learning or cities'.
questions.source_text: Travellers crossing the Sahara in the 14th century arrived at the West African city of Timbuktu. There they found a university with thousands of students, libraries stocked with manuscripts, scholars debating mathematics and astronomy, and a city more sophisticated than many European towns of the same period.
questions.task: Tap each phrase that contradicts a part of the 'dark continent' myth.

targets.phrase: city of Timbuktu
university with thousands of students
libraries stocked with manuscripts
scholars debating mathematics and astronomy
more sophisticated than many European towns
targets.reason: Direct counter-comparison to the Europe-first claim

questions.expected: Four or more target phrases identified
questions.memo: Each item refutes a different part of the 'dark continent' myth. Real evidence beats inherited assumptions.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The achievements of ancient civilisations should be compared side by side, not ranked on a single ladder.'
questions.thesis: The achievements of ancient civilisations should be compared side by side, not ranked on a single ladder.

pool.text: Egyptian mathematics, Indian numerals, Greek philosophy, Chinese inventions and Mayan astronomy each solved different problems — none is 'ahead' of the others
Ranking societies on a single scale always reflects the values of the ranker, not objective measurement
A society can be highly developed in one area (e.g. astronomy) and less so in another (e.g. metallurgy) — single-scale ranking hides this
Most ancient civilisations had ruling elites
Modern people enjoy travelling to ancient ruins
European thinkers in the 19th century always ranked Greece highest

questions.memo: The three strongest items together build the side-by-side case: parallel achievements (e1), the ranker-shapes-the-ranking principle (e2), and the multi-dimensional nature of development (e3).

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining what is wrong with calling ancient Greek civilisation 'the supreme civilisation'.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining what is wrong with calling ancient Greek civilisation 'the supreme civilisation'.

options.text: The 'supreme' label is a value judgement that ignores parallel achievements elsewhere
Greek civilisation was technically smaller than Chinese civilisation, so it cannot be supreme
Greek civilisation did not exist
Ancient Egypt, India, China and Mesoamerica all produced major scientific, philosophical and artistic achievements that Greek civilisation did not
Modern Greece has good food
Greek statues are made of marble
Calling one civilisation 'supreme' assumes a single ranking scale — but achievement happens in many areas, and different societies developed different strengths
Anything ancient is automatically supreme
Greek philosophy is the only thing that matters

questions.memo: A real argument has a clear claim, specific evidence and an explanation that links the two.

questions.question: Compare these two sources about pre-1500 long-distance travel.

source_a.text: Our treasure ships have crossed the seas to Africa and Arabia, exchanging gifts and trade with kings of many lands.
source_a.provenance: Chinese imperial decree, 1421, on the voyages of Admiral Zheng He

source_b.text: The world ends at the western edge of Europe. Beyond is only ocean, with monsters and the unknown.

statements.text: Long-distance maritime travel was achieved before 1500
European maps in 1490 showed accurate knowledge of the Indian Ocean
Chinese ships reached Africa decades before European exploration
Both authors agreed about what lay beyond Europe
The author claims the known world ends at Europe's edge

questions.memo: Zheng He's voyages (1405–1433) reached East Africa and the Persian Gulf with ships larger than anything Columbus would later command. Yet the 'discovery of the world' is usually credited to later European voyages — a clear example of which stories get told.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The idea that civilisation moved in a single line from Egypt → Greece → Rome → Europe ignores most of the world.'
questions.thesis: The idea that civilisation moved in a single line from Egypt → Greece → Rome → Europe ignores most of the world.

pool.text: The 'single line' story leaves out India, China and Mesoamerica entirely — yet each had advanced civilisations
Ancient Chinese inventions (paper, printing, gunpowder) reached Europe via Asia and the Islamic world, not via Greece or Rome
The line is drawn to give modern Europe a prestigious ancestor — it is identity-building, not history
Greek philosophy used the Greek alphabet
Roman roads were well built
Some modern European countries still teach Latin in schools

questions.memo: The three together build the case: massive geographic omissions (e1), evidence the actual flow of ideas wasn't single-line (e2), and the motive for the simplification (e3 — identity-building).

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why side-by-side comparison is fairer than single-scale ranking.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why side-by-side comparison is fairer than single-scale ranking.

options.text: Comparing civilisations side by side recognises that each developed different strengths suited to its environment and needs
All ancient civilisations were exactly the same
Comparison should be avoided altogether
Egyptian engineering, Indian mathematics, Chinese inventions and Mayan astronomy each excelled in different fields — no single society led in all of them
All ancient civilisations had pyramids
All ancient civilisations spoke Greek
A single ranking forces every society onto one ladder and rewards the values of whoever made the ladder. Side-by-side comparison lets each society's achievements stand on their own terms
Single rankings are too short to read
Comparisons should always say which is best

questions.memo: Side-by-side comparison is harder than ranking — it requires holding multiple frameworks at once. That difficulty is the point.

questions.question: Compare these two sources about the world in 1400 CE.

source_a.text: By 1400 CE, major centres of learning and trade existed in Timbuktu, Cairo, Baghdad, Delhi, Beijing and Tenochtitlán. None was clearly 'ahead' of the others — each was the centre of a regional system that knew little of the others.

source_b.text: By 1400 CE, Europe was poised on the edge of the Renaissance, the rebirth of true civilisation. The rest of the world remained in slumber.

statements.text: Multiple regional centres of learning existed by 1400
Europe was 'about to wake the rest of the world'
The non-European world was inactive in 1400
Both sources accurately describe global activity in 1400
Each region was the centre of its own system

questions.memo: 65 years apart, the same century, opposite framings. The 1950 textbook reflects mid-century Eurocentric history; the modern textbook treats regional centres as parallel rather than ranked.

HIS.G10.T1.WIDER.A3.title: The 'dark continent' myth and how it was disproven
HIS.G10.T1.WIDER.A3.description: How 19th-century European scholarship built the racist 'dark continent' myth, why it was politically useful, and the evidence that refutes it.
HIS.G10.T1.WIDER.A3.strand: T1 — Societies of the Wider World & Ancient Ethiopia
HIS.G10.T1.WIDER.A3.caps_topic: Societies of the Wider World in Ancient Times
HIS.G10.T1.WIDER.A3.recovery_strategy: The 'dark continent' label was invented during the 19th-century scramble for colonies. It served a purpose: if Africa had 'no history', Europeans could claim they were 'bringing' civilisation rather than seizing it. Counter-evidence already existed at the time — Aksum's stelae, Timbuktu's manuscripts, the ruins of Great Zimbabwe were known and deliberately dismissed.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'dark continent', used by 19th-century Europeans, refer to?
options: The false idea that Africa had no history, no states and no learning before Europeans arrived
A continent where most people wore dark clothes
questions.expected: The false idea that Africa had no history, no states and no learning before Europeans arrived
questions.memo: 'Dark' here meant 'unknown to us / without civilisation'. The label was not honest description — Europeans of the time knew about Aksum, Mali, Timbuktu and Great Zimbabwe and chose to ignore that knowledge.

questions.question: True or false: The 'dark continent' myth was a neutral description, not an active racist idea.
questions.memo: It was an active political tool used to justify the scramble for African colonies — claiming Europeans were 'bringing' civilisation rather than 'taking' land.

questions.question: The 'dark continent' myth helped justify European _________ of Africa.
questions.memo: If Africa was 'empty of history', then European conquest could be presented as 'discovery' or 'enlightenment' rather than what it was: invasion, land seizure and resource extraction.

questions.question: Which of the following is evidence that the 'dark continent' myth was false?
options: The libraries of Timbuktu held hundreds of thousands of manuscripts
questions.expected: The libraries of Timbuktu held hundreds of thousands of manuscripts
questions.memo: Hundreds of thousands of Timbuktu manuscripts (mathematics, astronomy, law, poetry, history) survive today, recently digitised. Their existence directly refutes 'Africa had no writing or scholarship'.

questions.question: Aksum (ancient Ethiopia) traded with which parts of the ancient world?
questions.memo: Aksum controlled Red Sea trade routes. Its connections to the wider world directly contradict the 'isolated dark continent' claim.

questions.question: True or false: Great Zimbabwe is an example of pre-1500 African architecture and statehood that the 'dark continent' myth tried to deny.
questions.memo: The stone-built city was occupied from around 1100 to 1450 CE. Its existence — known to European explorers from the 1870s onward — was deliberately misattributed to non-Africans for over 50 years.

questions.question: Sort each statement as real historical evidence or as a claim from the 'dark continent' myth.

buckets.label: A claim from the 'dark continent' myth

items.text: Timbuktu's manuscripts and university
'Africa had no writing before Europeans'
Stone walls and gold artefacts of Great Zimbabwe
'Africans were genetically incapable of building cities'
Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324
'Africa was empty of organised states'
Aksum's Roman coins and Red Sea trade routes
'Africans had no contact with the outside world'

questions.memo: The evidence side comes from real documents, ruins and trade records. The myth side comes from 19th-century European propaganda. Sorting them is the first step in critical reading.

questions.question: Why was the 'dark continent' myth politically useful for European colonisers?
options: It made conquest look like 'bringing civilisation' rather than seizing land
It made the climate seem cooler
It made African food look more interesting
It made European ships sail faster
questions.expected: It made conquest look like 'bringing civilisation' rather than seizing land
questions.memo: Naming work matters. 'Bringing civilisation' sounds like a gift. 'Seizing land' is theft. The myth made the second look like the first.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show the author is using the 'dark continent' myth as propaganda.
questions.source_text: Africa was a dark continent without history. The savage tribes wandering its interior had built nothing, written nothing and remembered nothing. It fell to the European nations to bring the light of civilisation to these benighted peoples.
questions.task: Tap the loaded propaganda language.

targets.phrase: without history

questions.question: Fill the blanks to complete a refutation of the 'dark continent' myth.

questions.memo: The refutation chain: name the three denials, point to three pieces of counter-evidence (Aksum, Timbuktu, Great Zimbabwe), then name what the myth actually was.

questions.question: Compare these two sources about West Africa.

source_a.text: The vast African interior remains unknown to civilisation. The natives we encountered have no government, no writing, and no memory of their past.

source_b.text: By 1300 CE, the Mali Empire spanned 1.3 million square kilometres, ruled by emperors with formal courts, served by a tax system, and famed for the scholarship centred on Timbuktu's universities.

Mali had a tax system and emperors

questions.memo: Source A and Source B describe the same continent, centuries apart in their writing dates. The contradiction is not because reality changed — it is because the explorer's report was wrong (or dishonest) about what was already there.

questions.question: Sort each piece of evidence by which part of the 'dark continent' myth it disproves.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show how racism (not evidence) shaped the early interpretation of Great Zimbabwe.
questions.source_text: Carl Mauch, who reached Great Zimbabwe in 1871, declared that it was 'impossible' that Africans could have built such structures. He attributed them to the ancient Phoenicians or to the biblical Queen of Sheba. For over 50 years, this view was the official position of European archaeology.

for over 50 years, this view was the official position

questions.expected: Two or more target phrases identified
questions.memo: Mauch's conclusion came BEFORE any analysis of the evidence. Anything-but-Africans was the operating rule. The 50-year institutional position shows the bias was not one person's mistake.

questions.question: Randall-MacIver (1905) and Caton-Thompson (1929) carried out scientific excavations at Great Zimbabwe. What did they conclude?

questions.memo: Proper archaeology found pottery, coins and dating evidence — all consistent with Shona origin and medieval African construction. The Rhodesian (and later apartheid SA) governments tried to suppress these findings because they undermined white-supremacist narratives.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The dark continent myth was a deliberate political tool, not an honest mistake.'
questions.thesis: The 'dark continent' myth was a deliberate political tool, not an honest mistake.

questions.memo: Together: evidence was available and ignored (e1), the myth's timing matches its political purpose (e2), and the anything-but-Africans pattern reveals motivation (e3). The three are mutually reinforcing.

questions.question: Compare these two sources about European involvement in Africa.

source_a.text: The civilised nations of Europe have a duty to bring light, government and Christianity to the dark continent.

source_b.text: European colonisation of Africa caused massive land dispossession, forced labour, the destruction of indigenous governments and the disruption of African societies that had functioned for centuries.

questions.memo: The pamphlet sells the colonial project; the textbook audits it. 135 years apart, the same continent, opposite framings. Which framing reaches more learners shapes what we collectively 'know'.

questions.thesis: Even after the 'dark continent' myth was refuted by archaeology, its influence has been hard to remove.

African economies vary widely today

questions.memo: Lingering myth shows up in textbook proportions (e1), everyday language (e2), and active suppression by interested governments (e3). Refuted ≠ removed.

questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why naming things accurately matters when describing African history.

questions.question: Compare these two sources about who built Great Zimbabwe.

source_a.text: The ruins at Great Zimbabwe were built by Phoenician or Arab visitors. The Bantu population of the area was incapable of such architectural achievement.

source_b.text: The Zimbabwe Bird, the soapstone carving recovered from Great Zimbabwe, appears on the national flag. The country's name itself — Zimbabwe — comes from the Shona phrase 'dzimba dzemabwe', 'houses of stone'.

HIS.G10.T1.ETHIOPIA.A1.title: Aksum: an African kingdom connected to the world
HIS.G10.T1.ETHIOPIA.A1.description: Aksum's location, trade networks, territorial extent and international connections from ancient times to ~600 CE.
HIS.G10.T1.ETHIOPIA.A1.strand: T1 — Societies of the Wider World & Ancient Ethiopia
HIS.G10.T1.ETHIOPIA.A1.recovery_strategy: Aksum was BIGGER than modern Ethiopia — including parts of Sudan, Eritrea, Djibouti, Somalia. It controlled the Red Sea, so trade ran in every direction: India and Arabia to the east, Rome and Greece to the north, Egypt and Nubia to the west. The Roman coins in Aksum's ruins are the receipt.

questions.question: The Kingdom of Aksum (ancient Ethiopia) was strategically located in:
options: The Horn of Africa, controlling Red Sea trade
West Africa, on the Atlantic coast
Central Africa, on the Congo River
Northern Europe, on the Baltic Sea
questions.expected: The Horn of Africa, controlling Red Sea trade
questions.memo: Aksum sat at the meeting point of Africa, Arabia and the Mediterranean. Its control of the Red Sea is what made it rich and powerful — trade had to flow through its hands.

questions.question: True or false: Ancient Ethiopia (Aksum) was smaller than modern Ethiopia.
questions.memo: Ancient Aksum was LARGER, including parts of present-day Sudan, Eritrea, Djibouti and Somalia. Borders shifted over centuries with trade, conquests and cultural exchange.

questions.question: Which of these goods did Aksum export to other parts of the ancient world?
questions.memo: These were the high-value, low-volume goods of ancient long-distance trade. Aksum sent them out via the Red Sea; in return came wine, olive oil, textiles and Roman pottery.

questions.question: Aksum controlled the _________ trade routes, connecting India, Arabia, and the Mediterranean.
questions.memo: Whoever controlled the Red Sea controlled the shortcut between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean. Aksum held that position for centuries.

questions.question: Aksum had trade and diplomatic ties with all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.memo: Aksum's connections — Egypt, Rome, Greece, Arabia and India — are documented through coins, texts and goods. Australia was not part of the ancient Mediterranean–Indian Ocean trade network.

questions.question: True or false: Roman coins have been recovered from Aksum's archaeological sites, providing physical evidence of trade between Aksum and Rome.
questions.memo: The coins are the receipt. They date from the 1st to the 4th centuries CE and prove sustained trade with the Roman Empire.

questions.question: Sort each item as something Aksum EXPORTED or IMPORTED.

items.text: Ivory
Gold
Wine
Olive oil
Ebony (dark hardwood)
Textiles (cloth and clothing)
Spices
Roman pottery

questions.memo: African exports were high-value raw materials. Imports were finished Mediterranean goods. This is the classic shape of long-distance pre-modern trade.

questions.question: Why was Aksum's control of the Red Sea so economically valuable?
options: It linked Africa to Arabia, India and the Mediterranean through one waterway
It was the only river Aksum had
It provided fresh water for farming
It was the source of African gold
questions.expected: It linked Africa to Arabia, India and the Mediterranean through one waterway
questions.memo: The Red Sea was the only sea-route shortcut from the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean before the Suez Canal. Controlling its African coast meant taxing or trading every passing ship.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to complete this picture of Aksum.
questions.cloze_template: Aksum was strategically located in the [1] of Africa, controlling the [2] Sea trade routes. Its exports included [3], gold and ebony, while its imports included [4] and olive oil. Trading partners reached as far as [5] in the east and [6] in the north.
questions.memo: Six geographic and economic facts in one paragraph: location, trade route, exports, imports, eastern reach, northern reach.

questions.question: Tap each phrase showing that Aksum was connected to the wider world, not isolated.
questions.source_text: The Axumite kingdom commanded the Red Sea, sending its merchant fleet to the Persian Gulf and the western coasts of India. Greek and Roman traders visited Aksum's ports. Egyptian and Arabian merchants knew the road to its inland capital. The wealth of three continents passed through its hands.
questions.task: Tap each phrase that proves Aksum was internationally connected.

targets.reason: Direct economic control of an international waterway

Egyptian and Arabian merchants knew the road to its inland capital
wealth of three continents passed through its hands

questions.expected: Four or more target phrases identified
questions.memo: Five different lines of evidence for the same conclusion: Aksum was a major node in global trade, not a backwater.

questions.question: Compare these two sources about Africa south of Egypt.

source_a.text: Roman coins, dating from the first to the fourth centuries CE, have been recovered from archaeological excavations at Axumite sites. The coins indicate sustained trade between Aksum and the Roman Empire.

source_b.text: Africa south of Egypt was, until the European explorations of the 1800s, a closed continent — isolated from Mediterranean civilisation and unknown to the literate world.

questions.memo: Source A presents physical evidence (coins). Source B makes a sweeping claim. The evidence refutes the claim — but the claim was widely taught for over a century.

questions.memo: Two independent kinds of evidence point to the same conclusion. Knowing how to sort sources by type is the start of source analysis.

questions.question: What does Aksum's wealth and international connections show about pre-1500 African history?
options: Many African kingdoms were active participants in global trade and diplomacy
Aksum was the only African kingdom that traded
questions.expected: Many African kingdoms were active participants in global trade and diplomacy
questions.memo: Aksum was one of several — Mali, Songhai, Great Zimbabwe and others were also actively trading. The pattern is regional, not one-off.

questions.question: Tap each fact that contradicts the claim that 'Africa was isolated from the wider world'.
questions.source_text: Located at the strategic crossroads of Africa, Arabia and the Mediterranean, Aksum was no isolated backwater. Its territorial extent, far larger than modern Ethiopia, included parts of present-day Sudan, Eritrea, Djibouti and Somalia. Its merchant fleet sailed the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. Its rulers sent diplomatic missions to Egypt, Nubia and Rome.

questions.memo: Four distinct lines of evidence — location, scale, trade, diplomacy — each refutes the isolation claim independently.

questions.thesis: The geographical extent of ancient Aksum disproves the idea that pre-colonial African states were small or weak.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining what evidence proves Aksum was connected to the Mediterranean.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining what evidence proves Aksum was connected to the Mediterranean.

options.text: Multiple lines of evidence — archaeological and written — prove that Aksum was deeply connected to the Mediterranean world
Aksum had no Mediterranean connections

These are just isolated finds that don't prove a real connection
The coins must have been planted there by modern archaeologists

questions.memo: Multiple independent evidence streams (coins, geography, texts) converge on the same conclusion. That convergence is what makes the case unfalsifiable.

questions.question: Compare these two sources about Aksum's standing in the ancient world.

source_b.text: Before the modern era, Africa produced no kingdom of significance comparable to those of Europe or Asia.

HIS.G10.T1.ETHIOPIA.A2.title: Religion, Portuguese contact and civil war
HIS.G10.T1.ETHIOPIA.A2.description: Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity, the arrival of Portuguese mercenaries and Jesuits, the Catholic conversion attempt, and the 1627–1632 civil war.
HIS.G10.T1.ETHIOPIA.A2.strand: T1 — Societies of the Wider World & Ancient Ethiopia
HIS.G10.T1.ETHIOPIA.A2.recovery_strategy: Ethiopia was ALREADY Christian (Orthodox) when the Portuguese arrived. The conflict was Christian-on-Christian: Catholics trying to convert Orthodox believers. The 5-year civil war (1627–1632) ended with the Jesuits defeated and expelled, but the country was left bitterly divided.

questions.question: What religion was practised in Ethiopia BEFORE the Portuguese arrived?
questions.memo: Ethiopia adopted Christianity in the 4th century CE under King Ezana of Aksum — over 1,000 years before the Portuguese arrived. By the time of contact, the Ethiopian Orthodox Church had a deep, distinctive tradition.

questions.question: True or false: The conflict between the Jesuits and Ethiopians was Christian-on-Christian, not Christian-on-non-Christian.
questions.memo: Both sides were Christian. The Jesuits were Roman Catholic; the Ethiopians were Orthodox. Each side considered the other heretical.

questions.question: Why did Ethiopia request Portuguese military aid in the early 16th century?
questions.memo: Ethiopia was a Christian state surrounded by Muslim neighbours, including the powerful Adal Sultanate. The 1540s wars against Adal forces nearly destroyed Ethiopia — hence the appeal for outside help.

questions.question: Portuguese mercenaries arrived under the command of _________ da Gama in the early 16th century.
questions.memo: Christopher da Gama, son of Vasco da Gama (who reached India in 1498), led mercenaries to help Ethiopia against the Adal Sultanate in the 1540s.

questions.question: What was the main goal of the Jesuit missionaries who arrived with the Portuguese?
options: To convert Ethiopian Orthodox Christians to Roman Catholicism
questions.expected: To convert Ethiopian Orthodox Christians to Roman Catholicism
questions.memo: The Jesuits saw Orthodox Christianity as 'heretical' — a divergence from the 'true' Roman Catholic faith that needed correcting. Their goal was conversion, not coexistence.

questions.question: True or false: The Ethiopian civil war (1627–1632) ended with the Jesuits defeated and expelled, and Orthodox Christianity restored as the state religion.
questions.memo: Five years of bitter conflict, but the outcome was clear: the Catholic emperor was overthrown, the Jesuits driven out, and Orthodox Christianity reinstated. The damage to social unity, however, lasted generations.

questions.question: Sort each motive as primarily religious or primarily political/strategic.

items.text: Jesuits wanted to convert Ethiopians to Roman Catholicism
Ethiopia needed Portuguese soldiers to fight Muslim invasions
Catholic missionaries believed Orthodox beliefs were heretical
Ethiopian emperors wanted European military allies against regional rivals
King Fasilides wanted to restore Orthodox Christianity as state religion
Ethiopia sent letters to Portugal asking for military aid
The Jesuits set up schools to teach Catholic doctrine
Fasilides built a fortified palace at Gondar to show royal power

questions.memo: Motives in history are often mixed (religion AND politics), but these examples lean clearly one way. Distinguishing the two is essential to analysing causation.

questions.question: The conflict between Jesuits and Ethiopian Orthodox Christians is sometimes described as 'a bizarre case of Christians wanting to convert Christians'. What does this phrase highlight?
options: Both sides were Christian, but considered each other heretical
Both sides worshipped the Greek gods
questions.expected: Both sides were Christian, but considered each other heretical
questions.memo: The phrase captures the absurdity. Catholic Europe assumed Africa needed Christianising — when Ethiopia had been Christian for over 1,000 years already.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to complete this summary of the Portuguese-Jesuit episode.

Portuguese mercenaries under [2] da Gama came in response to Ethiopia's request for help against [3] neighbours. With the soldiers came [4] missionaries who tried to convert Ethiopian Orthodox Christians to [5]. The 5-year civil war ended with the Jesuits [6] and the country bitterly [7].
questions.memo: Seven facts in one paragraph — the full arc of the episode from pre-existing Christianity, through military alliance, to religious conflict, to civil war, to expulsion and division.

questions.question: Tap each phrase showing the LASTING impact of the Jesuit episode on Ethiopia.
questions.source_text: The arrival of the Jesuits set in motion a devastating five-year civil war. The Roman Catholics demanded that Ethiopian Orthodox Christians abandon their ancient faith. The defeated Jesuits were eventually expelled, but Ethiopian society remained deeply divided over the religious question for generations.

abandon their ancient faith
remained deeply divided
for generations

questions.expected: Three or more target phrases identified
questions.memo: Wars end on dates; their consequences do not. The Jesuit episode left Ethiopia formally Orthodox again but socially scarred for generations.

questions.question: Compare these two sources about the Jesuit mission in Ethiopia.

source_a.text: The Jesuit mission attempted to overturn fifteen centuries of Ethiopian Orthodox tradition. Its failure preserved a uniquely African Christian heritage that continues today.

source_b.text: We brought the true Roman faith to the misguided Christians of Ethiopia. Their stubborn refusal of papal authority caused their own ruin.

questions.memo: Long before the 19th-century 'Scramble for Africa', Europeans had tried — and failed — to dominate Ethiopia religiously. The episode is a clear counterexample to the 'helpless Africa' narrative.

questions.question: Tap the phrases showing that ordinary Ethiopians played an active role in deciding their religious future.

The Ethiopian people rebelled. After five years of civil war, the rebels triumphed: the emperor was overthrown, the Jesuits expelled, and Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity restored as the state faith.

questions.question: Mali grew rich by controlling _________ trade routes.

We can't really know who started West African trade

questions.memo: Chronology refutes the introduced-by-outsiders story. The dates make it impossible.

questions.question: Compare these two sources about how African empires arose.

source_a.text: Archaeological and oral evidence shows that West African empires like Ghana, Mali and Songhai emerged from indigenous political and economic consolidation, building on trade networks that predated any contact with the Arab or Islamic world.

source_b.text: The Negro peoples of the West African interior had no capacity for state-building. Their political organisation was always borrowed from the more advanced peoples of the Mediterranean and Islamic worlds.

statements.text: West African empires emerged from indigenous consolidation
West Africans had no capacity for state-building
Political organisation was 'always borrowed' from more advanced peoples
Trade networks predated Arab contact
Both sources agree about who built the West African empires

questions.memo: The 19th-century text uses 'always borrowed' as a sweeping generalisation. The archaeology directly refutes it — but generalisations are stickier than evidence, which is why such narratives lasted so long.

HIS.G10.T2.MALI.A2.title: Mansa Musa and the spread of Islam
HIS.G10.T2.MALI.A2.description: Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca, the Cairo gold price collapse, and the gradual Islamisation of Mali's rulers and population.
HIS.G10.T2.MALI.A2.caps_topic: The rise and fall of the Mali Empire (case study)
HIS.G10.T2.MALI.A2.recovery_strategy: 1324 pilgrimage = Mansa Musa's gold so flooded Cairo that gold's price fell for years. Islam spread from the TOP (rulers) DOWN, slowly. questions.question: Who was Mansa Musa?
options: The most famous emperor of the Mali Empire
questions.expected: The most famous emperor of the Mali Empire
questions.memo: Mansa = 'emperor' or 'sultan' in the Mande language. Mansa Musa ruled Mali at its peak (1312–1337) and is often listed as one of the richest people in human history.

questions.question: In what year did Mansa Musa make his famous pilgrimage to Mecca?
questions.memo: 1324 — a date worth memorising. The pilgrimage took over a year, involved thousands of attendants, and put Mali on European maps for the first time.

questions.question: True or false: Mansa Musa distributed so much gold in Cairo that its price was depressed in Egyptian markets for years.
questions.memo: Contemporary Egyptian sources record the price of gold falling for a decade or more after the pilgrimage. The Mali king had — quite literally — too much gold.

questions.question: Mansa Musa travelled to _________ to perform the Islamic pilgrimage (Hajj).
questions.memo: Hajj to Mecca is one of the Five Pillars of Islam — required of all Muslims who can make the journey. Mansa Musa's pilgrimage demonstrated both his faith and his wealth.

questions.question: Mansa Musa brought back which famous figure to Mali after his pilgrimage?
questions.memo: Mansa Musa was so impressed by Cairo's architecture that he hired a famous Egyptian architect to come to Mali. Ishak-al Tuedjin went on to build the great mosques at Gao and Timbuktu.

questions.question: True or false: All Malians were Muslim from the time of Sundiata's founding of Mali.
questions.memo: Islam spread from the rulers down, slowly, over generations. Many ordinary Malians continued to practise indigenous African religions. Even Sundiata himself probably blended Islam with traditional beliefs.

questions.question: Sort each effect of Mansa Musa's pilgrimage by where it was felt.

items.text: Cairo's gold price depressed for over a decade
Architect Ishak-al Tuedjin recruited to build mosques
Mali appeared on European maps for the first time
Cairo merchants gained access to West African gold supply
Construction of great mosques at Gao and Timbuktu
Portuguese and Italian traders developed interest in Mali
The 'El Dorado' image of Africa took shape in European imagination
Islam's status as state religion strengthened among Mali's elite

questions.memo: One event — three continents felt the effects. That is how interconnected the 14th-century world was, and why dismissing African history as 'isolated' is so wrong.

questions.question: Why was Mansa Musa's pilgrimage politically significant beyond its religious purpose?
options: It advertised Mali's wealth and power to Egypt, North Africa, Portugal and the Italian merchant cities
It made Mali a European colony
questions.expected: It advertised Mali's wealth and power to Egypt, North Africa, Portugal and the Italian merchant cities
questions.memo: Mansa Musa used the pilgrimage as a diplomatic tour. Distributing gold, hosting feasts, recruiting talent — all signals to the wider world that Mali was a major power.

He returned to Mali with the architect [6], who built great mosques at Gao and Timbuktu. The pilgrimage advertised Mali's wealth to [7], North Africa and Europe.

source_b.text: African rulers of the medieval era possessed at most modest local wealth. Stories of vast African gold are travellers' tales and should be heavily discounted.

questions.question: Why did Mali appear on European maps for the first time AFTER Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage?

In many villages, traditional ceremonies, ancestor veneration and the role of local diviners continued well into and beyond the imperial period.

questions.question: Compare these two sources about Islam in West Africa.

source_a.text: Islam spread into the West African empires gradually and unevenly. The ruling dynasties adopted it from the late 13th century, but many rural populations continued indigenous practices for centuries afterwards, often blending the two traditions.

source_b.text: When Mansa Musa returned from his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1325, all of his subjects converted at once to the True Faith, and the worship of false gods was banished from Mali.

questions.memo: Source A is sober historical analysis. Source B is a religious-political idealisation that exaggerates the speed and completeness of conversion. Mass-conversion stories are usually political claims, not historical descriptions.

questions.thesis: Islam in Mali was adopted gradually and selectively, not imposed wholesale.

questions.memo: Four strong items each refute the 'whole country converted at once' story — by class (e1), by founder (e2), by rural practice (e3), by geographic distribution (e4).

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining how a single pilgrimage could reshape world economic perceptions.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining how a single pilgrimage could reshape world economic perceptions.

The pilgrimage changed nothing economically

Pilgrimages have no economic effect

questions.memo: An economic argument: perceptions of wealth → commercial attention → trade flows. The pilgrimage worked at the perception level, with real downstream effects.

questions.question: Compare these two sources about Africa's place in 14th-century world commerce.

source_a.text: The Egyptian historian al-Umari, writing in the 1340s, recorded that the Cairo gold market had not fully recovered from the visit of the Mali king Mansa Musa fifteen years earlier — testimony to the scale of West African wealth in the 14th century world economy.
source_a.provenance: Modern history citing al-Umari's contemporary account

source_b.text: Africa took no significant part in the world economy before the European voyages of the late 15th century opened the continent to international commerce.

European voyages 'opened' Africa to international commerce
Mali had significant wealth in the 14th-century world economy

questions.memo: A 1340s eyewitness account directly contradicts a 1965 textbook generalisation. The eyewitness has direct knowledge; the textbook has a political position. The mismatch shows how 20th-century historical writing erased much of pre-colonial African economic life.

HIS.G10.T2.MALI.A3.title: Timbuktu and Jenne: African centres of learning
HIS.G10.T2.MALI.A3.description: Why Timbuktu and Jenne became hubs of Islamic scholarship; the architecture and subjects taught; surviving manuscript evidence.
HIS.G10.T2.MALI.A3.caps_topic: The rise and fall of the Mali Empire (case study)
HIS.G10.T2.MALI.A3.recovery_strategy: Timbuktu had REAL universities (Sankoré, Djinguereber) teaching grammar, poetry, mathematics, medicine, astronomy alongside Islamic sciences. The manuscripts still exist — many were rescued and preserved during the 2012 jihadist occupation. Timbuktu was a destination scholars TRAVELLED TO, not just a stopover.

questions.question: By the 14th–15th centuries, Timbuktu was famous as:
options: A major centre of Islamic scholarship and learning
questions.expected: A major centre of Islamic scholarship and learning
questions.memo: Timbuktu had universities, libraries and thousands of students. It was Africa's intellectual capital for over 200 years.

questions.question: Which subjects were taught at Timbuktu's centres of learning?
options: Islamic sciences, grammar, poetry, mathematics, medicine and astronomy
questions.expected: Islamic sciences, grammar, poetry, mathematics, medicine and astronomy
questions.memo: Timbuktu's curriculum was broad — equivalent to a modern university with multiple faculties. Manuscripts on all these subjects survive today.

questions.question: True or false: Scholars travelled FROM many parts of the Islamic world TO study at Timbuktu.
questions.memo: Timbuktu was a DESTINATION for scholars — like Cairo, Damascus or Cordoba. Scholars came from North Africa, the Sahara fringes and beyond to teach and study there.

questions.question: The architect Mansa Musa brought back from Cairo to build mosques in Mali was called _________.
questions.memo: Ishak-al Tuedjin went on to build the great mosques of Gao and Timbuktu, and the royal audience chamber at Niani. His work survives in foundations and parts of the mihrab (prayer niche).

questions.question: Where did Ishak-al Tuedjin build great mosques after returning to Mali with Mansa Musa?
questions.memo: Gao on the Niger river and Timbuktu on the southern edge of the Sahara — both became architectural showpieces and learning centres of the Mali Empire.

questions.question: True or false: Hundreds of thousands of manuscripts from Timbuktu's libraries have survived to today.
questions.memo: Estimates range from 300,000 to 700,000 surviving manuscripts — many rescued from destruction during the 2012 jihadist occupation. Most are being digitised and studied today.

questions.question: Sort each subject as something HISTORICALLY taught at Timbuktu, or something that would NOT have been taught.

Astronomy and star-tracking

Quantum physics

questions.memo: Timbuktu's curriculum matched the medieval Islamic university model — broad and serious. The 'not taught' items are anachronistic (didn't exist yet).

questions.question: Why did Timbuktu (and Jenne) become major centres of learning?
options: Their position on trans-Saharan trade routes brought scholars, books and wealth together in one place
The Mali kings forced people to study
There was nothing else to do
questions.expected: Their position on trans-Saharan trade routes brought scholars, books and wealth together in one place
questions.memo: Trade brought wealth. Wealth funded libraries, schools and patronage. Position on trade routes brought scholars passing through. The three reinforced each other.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to complete the story of Timbuktu.

Subjects taught included Islamic sciences, grammar, [4], medicine and [5]. Scholars came from across the [6] world to study there. Hundreds of thousands of [7] from this period survive today.

Multiple scholars in Islamic sciences, grammar, poetry, mathematics, medicine and astronomy worked here, attracting students and teachers from across the Islamic world. The libraries contained tens of thousands of manuscripts on a wide range of subjects.

HIS.G10.T2.MALI.A4.title: Why Mali fell
HIS.G10.T2.MALI.A4.description: Decline of the Mali Empire: succession disputes, Tuareg raids, rise of Songhai, and the longer-term redirection of West African trade by the Atlantic slave trade.
HIS.G10.T2.MALI.A4.caps_topic: The rise and fall of the Mali Empire (case study)
HIS.G10.T2.MALI.A4.recovery_strategy: Mali fell for MANY reasons stacking up: succession fights at the top, Tuareg raids from the desert, Songhai rising to the east, and finally the Atlantic slave trade pulling trade and people toward the coast. No single cause did it. Songhai (not Europeans) directly absorbed Mali's core territory.

questions.question: When did the Mali Empire begin its long decline?
questions.memo: Mali peaked under Mansa Musa (early 1300s) and began its decline gradually from the late 1300s. The decline took over a century to complete.

questions.question: Who were the Tuareg, who raided the Mali Empire in its later years?
options: A nomadic people of the Sahara desert

HIS.G10.T3.ZIMBABWE.A1.title: The rise of Great Zimbabwe

questions.question: Around what date did Great Zimbabwe rise as a major kingdom?
questions.memo: Great Zimbabwe emerged around 1100 CE and was at its peak between roughly 1250 and 1450. It was abandoned before significant European contact in the region.

questions.question: Where is Great Zimbabwe located today?
options: Modern Ethiopia, in the Horn of Africa
questions.memo: The ruins are near the modern town of Masvingo in south-eastern Zimbabwe. The country took its name from the ruins after independence in 1980.

questions.question: True or false: Great Zimbabwe was unique — no other stone-walled kingdoms existed in southern Africa.
questions.memo: Great Zimbabwe was part of a REGIONAL pattern. Mapungubwe (older, in present-day Limpopo Province SA) and Thulamela (later) were stone-walled southern African kingdoms with similar trade and political features.

questions.question: Great Zimbabwe traded with the _________ Ocean coast.
questions.memo: Trade goods reached Great Zimbabwe via the East African coast — through Swahili-speaking ports like Sofala and Kilwa, which themselves traded across the Indian Ocean to Arabia, India, and China.

questions.question: What were Great Zimbabwe's main exports?
questions.memo: Gold from inland mines and elephant ivory were the two high-value goods that moved out via Sofala. In return came beads, cloth and porcelain from across the Indian Ocean world.

questions.question: True or false: Imported goods at Great Zimbabwe included glass beads from India and porcelain from China.
questions.memo: Excavations have recovered Indian glass beads, Chinese celadon porcelain and Persian pottery at Great Zimbabwe — direct material evidence of long-distance Indian Ocean trade.

questions.memo: Same shape as Mali's trade: raw materials out (gold, ivory, hides), finished goods in (beads, porcelain, cloth). Both empires made money from controlling the trade flow.

questions.question: Why was cattle wealth so important to Great Zimbabwe's elite?

Cattle were used as a weapon against enemies
Cattle were the only food source
Cattle had no role in society
questions.expected: Cattle were the basis of elite status, wealth, and political alliances through bride-wealth (lobola)
questions.memo: In southern African societies, large cattle herds = wealth + power + a tool for building alliances through marriage exchange. The elite at Great Zimbabwe owned the largest herds.

questions.question: What is the estimated peak population of Great Zimbabwe?
questions.memo: Estimates vary, but 10,000–20,000 is a widely accepted peak range. That's a substantial city by medieval standards — comparable to many European towns of the same period.

options: A large stone-walled compound for the ruling elite, probably with religious significance

questions.expected: A large stone-walled compound for the ruling elite, probably with religious significance
questions.memo: The Great Enclosure is the most famous part of the site: massive curved stone walls enclosing what was likely an elite residential and ceremonial space — possibly the royal women's quarters and initiation area.

questions.question: True or false: The stone walls at Great Zimbabwe had no military features such as battlements or arrow slits.
questions.memo: The walls were NOT designed for defence. No towers for archers, no battlements, no defensible gates. They marked SACRED and ELITE space, not military zones. Compare to medieval European castles which had all these features.

questions.question: Religious worship at Great Zimbabwe centred on _________.
questions.memo: Mwari (also called Musikavanhu) is the supreme creator god in Shona religion. Worship at Great Zimbabwe involved Mwari, mediums and ancestor veneration — practices that continue in the region today.

options: Older royal and religious area, built first
questions.expected: Older royal and religious area, built first
questions.memo: The Hill Complex sits above the rest of the site. It is the OLDEST part — probably the original royal and religious centre, with later building (including the Great Enclosure) spreading down into the valley.

questions.question: True or false: Great Zimbabwe had a centralised ruling elite distinct from the wider population.
questions.memo: Differences in housing quality, household goods, cattle consumption and access to imported luxuries all show a clear elite/commoner division. A city of 10,000–20,000 needs organised hierarchy to function.

questions.memo: A clear elite/commoner split was visible in housing, household goods, food remains and location within the site. This is what a complex pre-modern society looks like.

HIS.G10.T3.ZIMBABWE.A3.title: Who built it? The debate that won't die
HIS.G10.T3.ZIMBABWE.A3.description: Decline of Great Zimbabwe; the racist 19th-century interpretations (Carl Mauch); the scientific archaeology that proved African origin (Randall-MacIver 1905, Caton-Thompson 1929); apartheid-era suppression of these findings.
HIS.G10.T3.ZIMBABWE.A3.strand: T3 — Great Zimbabwe & Ethnic Fluidity / The Invention of 'Tribes'
HIS.G10.T3.ZIMBABWE.A3.caps_topic: Precolonial African Kingdoms and Empires in southern Africa (Great Zimbabwe)
HIS.G10.T3.ZIMBABWE.A3.recovery_strategy: The 'Phoenician / Arab / Queen of Sheba' theories were NOT honest mistakes — they were racist refusals to credit Africans with sophisticated stone architecture. Randall-MacIver (1905) and Caton-Thompson (1929) proved African origin with proper archaeology. The Rhodesian and apartheid governments later tried to suppress these findings to protect white-supremacist narratives.

questions.question: When was Great Zimbabwe abandoned?
questions.memo: Great Zimbabwe was abandoned around 1450 CE — before any significant European contact with the region. Trade routes shifted northward, the area's resources declined, and the population moved away gradually.

questions.question: Carl Mauch, the German explorer who reached Great Zimbabwe in 1871, claimed the ruins were built by:
options: Phoenicians or the biblical Queen of Sheba — anyone but Africans
questions.expected: Phoenicians or the biblical Queen of Sheba — anyone but Africans
questions.memo: Mauch declared it 'impossible' that Africans had built the ruins. He attributed them to ancient Phoenicians or to the biblical Queen of Sheba. The decision came BEFORE he examined any evidence.

questions.question: True or false: David Randall-MacIver (1905) proved that Great Zimbabwe was built by Africans.
questions.memo: Randall-MacIver conducted the first proper scientific excavation. Pottery, gold beads, and dating evidence all matched African (Shona) origin and a medieval (not ancient) date.

questions.question: Gertrude _________ -Thompson confirmed Great Zimbabwe's African origin in 1929.
questions.memo: Gertrude Caton-Thompson led an excavation in 1928–29. Her published report concluded that 'not one single item that is not in accordance with the claim of Bantu origin and medieval date' had been found.

questions.question: How did the Rhodesian and apartheid-era South African governments respond to the archaeology proving African origin?

They funded major new research projects

They had no opinion on the matter

questions.memo: White-minority governments in Rhodesia and apartheid SA needed the 'Africans couldn't have built it' story to support their own legitimacy. Suppressing the African-origin findings was a deliberate political choice.

questions.question: True or false: The 'Phoenician origin' theory about Great Zimbabwe was an honest scientific disagreement, not racism.
questions.memo: Mauch decided it was 'impossible' that Africans had built the ruins BEFORE examining the evidence. That's not science — that's racism dressed up as a conclusion. Mauch's contemporaries who looked at the actual evidence (Randall-MacIver) reached the African-origin conclusion easily.

HIS.G10.T3.TRIBES.A1.title: Precolonial African identities were fluid, not fixed

HIS.G10.T3.TRIBES.A1.strand: T3 — Great Zimbabwe & Ethnic Fluidity / The Invention of 'Tribes'
HIS.G10.T3.TRIBES.A1.caps_topic: Ethnic fluidity in the deep past and the colonial creation of 'tribes'
HIS.G10.T3.TRIBES.A1.recovery_strategy: Precolonial societies were MOBILE and MIXED. Refugees from wars/epidemics joined whichever strong ruler protected them (including women rulers). Marriage, trade and migration crossed group lines constantly. Internal divisions (royal vs commoner, insider vs outsider) often mattered MORE than 'tribal' belonging.

questions.question: Were precolonial African societies organised into fixed, separate 'tribes' that never mixed?
options: No — identities were fluid, overlapping, and mobile
Yes — fixed tribes had existed since time immemorial
Yes, but only in southern Africa
No — there were no group identities at all
questions.expected: No — identities were fluid, overlapping, and mobile
questions.memo: The 'fixed tribes since time immemorial' picture is a colonial myth. Precolonial Africans moved between groups through marriage, trade, refugee status and political alliance — and internal divisions (rank, royal vs commoner) often mattered more than 'tribe'.

questions.question: Which of these is true of precolonial Sotho-Tswana, Xhosa and Pedi societies?
options: They had overlapping identities and porous boundaries with neighbouring groups
They were completely isolated from each other
They had no internal divisions of rank or status
They were each a single fixed tribe with no internal variation
questions.expected: They had overlapping identities and porous boundaries with neighbouring groups
questions.memo: Sotho, Tswana and Pedi peoples often shared language varieties, intermarried, and absorbed each other's refugees. Xhosa polities included groups of Mfengu, Khoi and other origins. Boundaries were porous in practice.

questions.question: True or false: Marriage, trade and migration regularly crossed group lines in precolonial southern Africa.
questions.memo: Group lines were permeable. People intermarried across them, traded across them, and moved across them when seeking land or protection. The 'each tribe kept to its own' picture is a 19th-century European fiction.

questions.question: In precolonial African societies, distinctions of _________ (royal vs commoner) often mattered MORE than 'tribal' belonging.
questions.memo: Royal lineage, noble status, commoner birth, outsider status — these internal divisions structured precolonial life more than the supposed boundary between one 'tribe' and another. A royal of group X often had more in common with a royal of group Y than with a commoner of his own group.

questions.question: Who joined strong rulers as refugees in precolonial southern Africa?
options: People displaced by wars, epidemics or droughts — including following women rulers
Only people of the same tribe as the ruler
Only people from one specific village
questions.expected: People displaced by wars, epidemics or droughts — including following women rulers
questions.memo: Strong rulers attracted refugees from across the region. Queen Mantatisi of the Tlokwa, for example, led mixed groups absorbing Sotho, Tswana and other refugees during the Mfecane era. Origin mattered less than current protection.

questions.question: True or false: Women rulers existed in some precolonial African societies.
questions.memo: Queen Mantatisi of the Tlokwa, Modjadji the Rain Queen of the Balobedu, and several Xhosa chieftainesses are documented examples. The colonial picture of African societies as uniformly patriarchal-tribal hides this reality.

HIS.G10.T3.TRIBES.A2.title: How colonisers and missionaries invented 'tribes'
HIS.G10.T3.TRIBES.A2.description: How European colonial administrators turned fluid African identities into fixed 'tribes' for administrative control, and how Christian missionaries' language work reinforced this tribalisation.

HIS.G10.T3.TRIBES.A2.caps_topic: Ethnic fluidity in the deep past and the colonial creation of 'tribes'

Africans clustering in colonial towns was SURVIVAL strategy in a hostile environment, not proof of ancient tribalism.
