questions.memo: Colonial governance required categories. Each African had to be assigned a tribe, taxed accordingly, governed through 'tribal' authorities, and permitted to live only in his 'tribal' area. Without fixed tribes, indirect rule collapsed.

questions.question: True or false: Christian missionaries played a role in turning fluid African language groups into fixed 'tribes' by picking one dialect as the 'standard' written form.
questions.memo: When you write 'the' Xhosa Bible, you pick one dialect to be 'Xhosa'. Other dialects become 'wrong'. Speakers of those other dialects either conform to the standard or become a separate 'tribe'. The fluid language spectrum hardens into firm boundaries.

questions.question: True or false: Africans clustering by region or language in colonial towns was a survival strategy in a hostile environment — not proof that ancient tribalism had always existed.

questions.question: Tap each phrase showing how colonial administration created firm 'tribal' categories from fluid African life.
questions.source_text: The colonial administrative grid required clarity. Each African was to be assigned a 'tribe', taxed accordingly, governed through 'tribal' authorities, and permitted to live only in the area allocated to his 'tribe'. The fluid, overlapping identities of precolonial life did not fit. So colonial officials, with the help of missionaries who had reduced African languages to writing, drew firm lines: this group is Xhosa, that group is Sotho, the other group is Pedi. The lines were administrative inventions, not records of how Africans actually lived.

HIS.G10.T3.TRIBES.A3.title: Why tribalism still matters today
HIS.G10.T3.TRIBES.A3.description: How tribalism persists in modern South Africa, who benefits, and the difference between lived ethnic identity (healthy) and weaponised political tribalism (harmful).
HIS.G10.T3.TRIBES.A3.strand: T3 — Great Zimbabwe & Ethnic Fluidity / The Invention of 'Tribes'
HIS.G10.T3.TRIBES.A3.caps_topic: Ethnic fluidity in the deep past and the colonial creation of 'tribes'
HIS.G10.T3.TRIBES.A3.recovery_strategy: Modern tribalism in SA and Africa is a DIRECT inheritance of colonial design: borders, ID classifications, Bantustans, labour recruitment by 'tribe'. Politicians who mobilise tribally are using a colonial tool. Naming the colonial origin is the first step in dismantling its present-day power. Ethnic identity as lived experience is fine; weaponised tribalism is not.

questions.question: Why does tribalism persist in modern South Africa and across Africa?
options: Because it was embedded in colonial administration and post-colonial states inherited those structures
Because it is a natural and unchanging African feature
Because Africans deliberately invented it after independence
It does not persist — tribalism ended in 1994
questions.expected: Because it was embedded in colonial administration and post-colonial states inherited those structures
questions.memo: Colonial states built tribalism into pass laws, land allocation, labour recruitment and Bantustans. After independence, the institutional grooves remained. Removing the formal Bantustans in 1994 didn't erase the categories from political identity.

questions.question: Who sometimes finds tribalism useful in modern politics?
options: Politicians who use it for vote-mobilising or to shift blame onto other groups
questions.expected: Politicians who use it for vote-mobilising or to shift blame onto other groups
questions.memo: Tribalism is politically useful when you want to mobilise a 'we' against a 'them' without engaging on issues. It also lets ruling parties blame other groups for service-delivery failures rather than answering for them.

questions.question: True or false: Tribalism persists in modern South Africa partly because politicians find it electorally useful.
questions.memo: When a politician can deliver votes by mobilising 'their' tribe, the system rewards tribal mobilisation. Without that political reward, tribalism would have far less reach in modern public life.

questions.question: Understanding the _________ roots of modern tribalism is the first step in overcoming it.
questions.memo: If tribalism is 'ancient', it appears unchangeable. If it is named as a colonial inheritance, it appears as a political construction that can be undone by political work.

questions.question: Why does naming the colonial origin of 'tribes' matter for present-day politics?
options: It exposes weaponised tribalism as a colonial inheritance, not a natural feature of African life — making it easier to challenge
It makes the past more interesting but changes nothing
questions.expected: It exposes weaponised tribalism as a colonial inheritance, not a natural feature of African life — making it easier to challenge
questions.memo: 'Natural and ancient' things appear permanent. 'Constructed by politics' things can be unmade by politics. Naming the colonial origin shifts tribalism from the first category to the second.

questions.question: True or false: Ethnic identity as lived experience (e.g. speaking isiZulu at home) is the same thing as 'weaponised tribalism' in politics.
questions.memo: They are different things. Lived ethnic experience (language, food, culture) harms no one. Weaponised tribalism (politicians mobilising hatred, recruiting only along ethnic lines) causes real harm. Confusing the two is itself a problem.

Inter-group violence triggered by ethnic stereotyping

questions.memo: Lived items harm no one and are part of healthy belonging. Weaponised items cause damage — to political life, to social trust, sometimes to physical safety. Distinguishing the two is the foundation of a useful conversation.

questions.question: How does understanding the colonial origin of tribalism help in challenging it today?

questions.expected: It denaturalises tribalism — showing that what looks 'ancient and inevitable' is actually a relatively recent political construction
questions.memo: 'Denaturalise' = strip something of the appearance of being 'just how things are'. If tribalism is a colonial invention rather than ancient nature, it can be unmade — the same way it was made.

questions.memo: Five concepts: inheritance, mechanism, present-day actor, intervention point, distinction. Together they describe how tribalism persists and how to challenge it.

questions.question: Tap each phrase showing how modern tribalism inherits from apartheid administration.
questions.source_text: Modern South African tribalism is a colonial inheritance, not an ancient African feature. The Bantustans (homelands) of apartheid hardened the colonial 'tribes' into separate territories with their own pass laws, schooling and administrative offices. After 1994, the formal Bantustans were dissolved — but the deep grooves they cut into political identity, party recruitment and labour patterns have proved harder to remove. Politicians who today mobilise along tribal lines are working with tools the apartheid state gave them.

questions.question: Tap each phrase showing how to challenge tribalism without attacking ethnic identity.
questions.source_text: Combating tribalism does not mean stripping people of their ethnic identity. Speaking isiZulu, celebrating Heritage Day, preserving cultural traditions — these are part of healthy belonging. The work is to break the connection between ethnic identity and political weaponisation. That work starts with telling the truth about where modern tribalism came from: not from time immemorial, but from colonial administration and apartheid governance. What was created by politics can be unmade by politics.

HIS.G10.T4.ACHIEVE.A1.title: African science, mathematics and medicine
HIS.G10.T4.ACHIEVE.A1.description: African contributions to mathematics (Egypt, Ishango bone), medicine and surgery, metallurgy/iron-smelting, and astronomy (Kushite, Dogon).
HIS.G10.T4.ACHIEVE.A1.strand: T4 — Achievements of African People since Ancient Times
HIS.G10.T4.ACHIEVE.A1.caps_topic: Achievements of African People since Ancient Times
HIS.G10.T4.ACHIEVE.A1.recovery_strategy: Iron-smelting started IN AFRICA and spread out. Egyptian geometry was the foundation Greek mathematicians later built on. The Ishango bone (~20,000 years old) shows tally-marking long before similar tools elsewhere. Dogon = astronomy. Kushite = star calendar. African plant medicine still feeds modern pharmacology (e.g. quinine derivatives).

questions.question: Which African civilisation developed the advanced mathematics used to build the pyramids of Giza?
questions.memo: Ancient Egyptian mathematicians used geometry to lay out pyramid foundations with precision. Greek mathematicians (Pythagoras, Thales, Euclid) studied in Egypt and built on this earlier work.

questions.question: The Ishango bone, found in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, is evidence of early African:
questions.memo: The Ishango bone is approximately 20,000 years old. Its marks suggest counting, simple arithmetic and possibly lunar calendar tracking — among the oldest mathematical tools known anywhere in the world.

questions.question: True or false: Iron-smelting began in Africa and then spread to other parts of the world.
questions.memo: African iron-smelting dates back several thousand years and developed independently. The 'Iron Age came from outside Africa' story is wrong — the evidence runs the other way.

questions.question: The Dogon of _________ were renowned for their astronomical knowledge.
questions.memo: The Dogon, in Mali, have a long astronomical tradition with documented knowledge of stellar bodies including the Sirius star system. Their observations are part of a wider African astronomical heritage.

questions.question: The ancient Kushites of Sudan developed:
options: A calendar based on the study of the stars
questions.expected: A calendar based on the study of the stars
questions.memo: Kushite astronomy produced a working calendar based on celestial observation. The Kushites (centred on Meroë) were neighbours and partial heirs of Egyptian civilisation, and contributed their own scientific traditions.

questions.question: True or false: African plant-based medicinal knowledge has influenced modern pharmacology.
questions.memo: Many modern medicines began as African traditional remedies — quinine derivatives, certain antimalarials, and others. African herbal medicine remains an active source for pharmaceutical research today.

questions.memo: Four different African societies, four different scientific traditions. The pattern shows breadth — science wasn't 'an' African achievement, it was achievements plural across many regions.

questions.question: Tap each phrase showing the sophistication of ancient Egyptian medicine.
questions.source_text: The Edwin Smith Papyrus, dated to around 1600 BCE, contains 48 case studies of injuries and their treatments — including surgical interventions, splinting of fractures, and treatment of head and spinal wounds. Egyptian doctors specialised by body part — there were eye doctors, dental specialists, and gastrointestinal specialists — over a thousand years before similar specialisation appeared in Greek medicine.

questions.question: Ancient Egyptian architecture influenced which later European architectural traditions?
questions.memo: Greek temple design (columns, friezes, monumental stone) drew on earlier Egyptian models. Roman architecture inherited these and spread them across Europe. The European architectural lineage has Egyptian roots.

questions.question: What were Benin City (Nigeria) and Kumasi (capital of Asante) famous for?
options: Planned avenues, palaces, intersecting streets and gardens
questions.expected: Planned avenues, palaces, intersecting streets and gardens
questions.memo: Benin City had a planned grid of streets, palaces, gardens and a famous earthen wall system. Kumasi was a major Asante capital with similar urban features. Both predate or rival many European cities in urban planning.

questions.question: True or false: The Russian poet Alexander Pushkin (1799–1837) had African ancestry.
questions.memo: Pushkin's maternal great-grandfather, Abram Petrovich Gannibal, was an African brought to Russia as a child and rose to become a military engineer under Peter the Great. Pushkin's African ancestry is well documented and celebrated.

questions.question: African art deeply influenced the European art movement called _________ (associated with Pablo Picasso).
questions.memo: Picasso's encounter with African masks (especially during a visit to the Trocadéro ethnographic museum in 1907) shaped his cubist work — most famously visible in 'Les Demoiselles d'Avignon'. Cubism owes a major creative debt to African art.

questions.question: Jazz music originated from:
options: African musical traditions carried by enslaved people to the Americas, blended with European harmony and instrumentation
An invention of a single American musician
Indigenous American music with no African input
questions.expected: African musical traditions carried by enslaved people to the Americas, blended with European harmony and instrumentation
questions.memo: Jazz is a creation of the African diaspora. Rhythms, call-and-response, polyrhythm, blue notes — all carry African musical heritage. Blended with European instruments and harmonic frameworks in the Americas, the result was jazz.

questions.question: True or false: People of African descent have made major contributions to global sport, including athletics, football, cricket, basketball and boxing.
questions.memo: African and African-diaspora athletes have dominated or shaped many global sporting codes. Their contributions are part of the continent's wider cultural reach.

[4], a music born of African diaspora rhythmic traditions, reshaped global popular music. Cities like [5] (Nigeria) had planned streets and palaces before many European cities. African and African-diaspora athletes have shaped global [6].
questions.memo: Six contributions across architecture, art, literature, music, urban planning and sport. The reach is genuinely global.

questions.question: Tap each phrase showing how African art reshaped European modernism.
questions.source_text: In 1907, Pablo Picasso visited the Trocadéro ethnographic museum in Paris and encountered a major collection of African masks and sculptures. The forms he saw there — geometric stylisation, emotional intensity, bold abstraction — directly shaped his work on 'Les Demoiselles d'Avignon' and the cubist movement that followed. African aesthetic principles entered the heart of European modernism through this and similar contacts. Yet for decades, art history textbooks credited cubism as a purely European invention.
questions.task: Tap each phrase showing African influence on cubism and modernism.

targets.phrase: encountered a major collection of African masks and sculptures
geometric stylisation, emotional intensity, bold abstraction
directly shaped his work on 'Les Demoiselles d'Avignon' and the cubist movement
African aesthetic principles entered the heart of European modernism
art history textbooks credited cubism as a purely European invention

questions.expected: Four or more target phrases identified
questions.memo: Five claims tracing the African → cubism → modernism chain. The point is not only that the influence happened, but that it was deliberately written out of standard art history.

questions.question: Compare these two views of the origins of cubism.

source_a.text: Picasso's cubist breakthrough in 'Les Demoiselles d'Avignon' (1907) drew directly on African mask traditions he encountered at the Trocadéro ethnographic museum. The geometric stylisation that defines cubism has African roots that are now widely acknowledged in art history.

source_b.text: Cubism is a purely European invention, the brilliant insight of Picasso and Braque working in Paris. It owes nothing of significance to influences from outside the European tradition.

statements.text: Cubism drew directly on African mask traditions
Cubism is 'a purely European invention'
Cubism's African roots are now widely acknowledged in art history
Cubism owes 'nothing of significance' to outside influences
Both sources agree about cubism's origins

questions.memo: Picasso himself acknowledged the African influence on his work. The 'purely European' framing required ignoring the artist's own statements and the visible evidence in the paintings themselves.

questions.question: Sort each item as ORIGINATING in Africa or as a non-African tradition INFLUENCED BY African contributions.

Asante royal regalia and court culture

questions.memo: African contributions move in both directions — originals (built in Africa) and influences (carried out from Africa into other cultures). Both kinds of contribution count.

questions.question: What does Pushkin's African ancestry — and his role as a founding figure of Russian literature — illustrate?
options: African influence reached into European cultural traditions in unexpected ways, including the foundation of Russian literature
Russian literature has nothing to do with Africa
Pushkin was the only African in Europe
African ancestry was never mentioned by Pushkin himself
questions.expected: African influence reached into European cultural traditions in unexpected ways, including the foundation of Russian literature
questions.memo: Pushkin was openly proud of his African ancestry and wrote about it. Russian literature's founding figure was partly of African descent — a fact that complicates any simple 'Africa vs Europe' cultural division.

questions.question: Tap each phrase showing the sophistication of West African urban planning at Benin City.
questions.source_text: By the 17th century, Benin City — the capital of the Kingdom of Benin in modern Nigeria — was an urban centre of perhaps 80,000 inhabitants, organised on a planned grid of intersecting streets. The royal palace covered an area of several square kilometres. The city was surrounded by a system of earthen walls and moats — together some of the largest pre-modern earthworks in the world. European visitors of the period described Benin as 'larger and finer than any town in Europe of our own time'.

questions.memo: Five concrete features of Benin City as a major pre-modern city — and a 17th-century European visitor's own admission that it surpassed European cities. The 'no African cities' myth cannot survive these specifics.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why African cultural contributions are often hidden in standard accounts.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why African cultural contributions are often hidden in standard accounts.

options.text: African cultural contributions to Europe and the wider world are often hidden in standard accounts because acknowledging them would undermine narratives of European cultural superiority
African cultural contributions are hidden because they don't really exist
African contributions are equally credited everywhere

African art is colourful
European art is famous

It doesn't matter where contributions come from
Modern researchers exaggerate African cultural influence

questions.memo: Telling whose contributions count is itself a political act. The hidden contribution problem is a feature of how cultural histories have been written, not a feature of what actually happened.

questions.question: Compare these two views of Benin City.

source_a.text: Benin City in the 17th century was a planned urban centre of perhaps 80,000 inhabitants, with a royal palace covering several square kilometres and a surrounding system of earthen walls and moats that ranks among the largest pre-modern earthworks anywhere.

source_b.text: Before British colonisation, the peoples of the West African forests lived in small, unorganised settlements without urban planning, monumental architecture, or significant scale.

statements.text: Benin City had perhaps 80,000 inhabitants in the 17th century
West African forest peoples lived 'in small, unorganised settlements'
Benin City's earthworks rank among the largest pre-modern in the world
Pre-colonial West Africa had no urban planning or monumental architecture
Both sources agree about Benin City's scale

questions.memo: The British colonial framing was published exactly during the years (1897) when Britain destroyed Benin City and looted the Benin Bronzes. The 'no urban planning' claim served the political need to justify the destruction.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'African-diaspora music has been the foundation of modern global popular music.'
questions.thesis: African-diaspora music has been the foundation of modern global popular music.

questions.memo: Four strong items trace the African-diaspora musical chain through four eras: foundational genres (e1), rock origins (e2), hip-hop dominance (e3), persistent musical principles (e4).

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why jazz is considered an African contribution.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why jazz is considered an African contribution to world culture.

options.text: Jazz is rightly considered an African contribution because its core elements — polyrhythm, call-and-response, blue notes, improvisation — came from African musical traditions carried by enslaved people to the Americas
Jazz has nothing to do with Africa
Jazz was invented entirely in Europe

Polyrhythm, call-and-response, blue notes and improvisation — the defining features of jazz — are documented elements of West African musical tradition. African-American musicians blended these with European harmony and instrumentation to create jazz
Jazz is popular at festivals
Some jazz musicians are famous

Recognising jazz as an African contribution doesn't deny European harmonic influence — it correctly identifies whose musical traditions provided the rhythmic and vocal foundation. Through jazz, African musical heritage entered the centre of global popular music
African contribution to jazz is too small to mention
Music has no cultural lineage

questions.memo: Lineage argument for music: identify the elements, identify their origins, identify the blending. Crediting both halves (African + European) is the honest move.

questions.question: Compare these two views of African influence on European modernism.

source_a.text: Picasso's own statements, the visible aesthetic features of cubist works, and the chronology of his visits to the Trocadéro African collection all confirm that African masks were a major influence on the cubist breakthrough.

source_b.text: Cubism was the spontaneous brilliance of European modernist genius. Suggestions of 'African influence' are politically motivated revisionism that diminishes Picasso's own creative achievement.

statements.text: Picasso's own statements confirm African influence on cubism
Suggestions of African influence are 'politically motivated revisionism'
Cubism was the 'spontaneous brilliance of European modernist genius' with no outside influence
The chronology of Picasso's Trocadéro visits and the aesthetic features of his works support African influence on cubism
Both sources see African influence on cubism as well-documented

questions.memo: The 1980s defensive piece accuses honest scholarship of being 'politically motivated' — a classic projection move. Acknowledging influence doesn't diminish the artist; it credits a wider creative ecology.

HIS.G10.T4.ACHIEVE.A3.title: Ubuntu: an African philosophy for the world
HIS.G10.T4.ACHIEVE.A3.description: The philosophy of ubuntu/botho ('umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu' — 'I am because you are'); its emphasis on shared humanity and community; its challenge to individualism and greed; its modern relevance including the post-1994 SA constitution.
HIS.G10.T4.ACHIEVE.A3.strand: T4 — Achievements of African People since Ancient Times
HIS.G10.T4.ACHIEVE.A3.caps_topic: Achievements of African People since Ancient Times
HIS.G10.T4.ACHIEVE.A3.recovery_strategy: Ubuntu is a CLAIM about what makes us human: we become human THROUGH others. That's a serious philosophical position, not a politeness rule. It DIRECTLY challenges individualism, greed, and 'every-person-for-themselves' thinking. The post-1994 SA constitution invokes ubuntu in its founding values for exactly this reason.

questions.question: The Nguni saying 'umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu' translates roughly as:
options: 'A person is a person through other people' / 'I am because you are'
questions.expected: 'A person is a person through other people' / 'I am because you are'
questions.memo: This is the core ubuntu claim: our personhood is constituted through our relationships with others. We become fully human together — not alone.

questions.question: What does the philosophy of ubuntu directly challenge?
options: Individualism, greed, unhealthy competition and excessive self-enrichment
questions.expected: Individualism, greed, unhealthy competition and excessive self-enrichment
questions.memo: Ubuntu takes a position. Its insistence that personhood is shared puts it directly against the 'every-person-for-themselves' worldview that treats greed and unlimited self-enrichment as natural.

questions.question: True or false: Ubuntu emphasises shared humanity, community and our connection to a wider universe.
questions.memo: Ubuntu's positive content: we belong to each other, to our communities, and to the wider world. The negative side of the same coin: the 'individual standing alone' picture of human life is a mistake.

questions.question: Complete the Nguni proverb: 'umuntu ngumuntu _________'.
questions.memo: 'Ngabantu' = 'through people'. The proverb is one of the most-quoted summary statements of ubuntu, found in Zulu and (with small variations) across other Nguni languages.

questions.question: Where is ubuntu invoked as a founding value in modern South Africa?
options: The post-1994 democratic constitution's founding values
questions.expected: The post-1994 democratic constitution's founding values
questions.memo: The 1996 South African Constitution's preamble and Bill of Rights invoke ubuntu as a foundational moral commitment of the new democratic order. It is named explicitly in major Constitutional Court rulings.

questions.question: True or false: Ubuntu is just a polite way of telling people to be nice to each other.
questions.memo: Reducing ubuntu to 'be nice' empties it of its actual content. Ubuntu is a philosophical claim about what makes us human — and a direct challenge to individualist and greed-based worldviews. That is much more than politeness.

questions.question: Sort each value as ALIGNED WITH UBUNTU or as OPPOSED TO UBUNTU.

items.text: Shared humanity and community
Greed and excessive self-enrichment
Mutual responsibility and care
'Every person for themselves' individualism
Recognising the dignity of every person
Treating other people as obstacles to defeat
Connection to the wider universe and to ancestors
Unlimited competition with no concern for others' wellbeing

questions.memo: Ubuntu is not neutral on what kind of life is worth living. Its alignment with community, mutual care, dignity and connection — and its opposition to greed, hyper-individualism and indifferent competition — is its substantive claim.

questions.question: Why is ubuntu more than just a politeness rule?
options: It makes a substantive philosophical claim about what makes us human — that personhood is constituted through relationships
It is a politeness rule and nothing more
It is just a saying, with no real content
It is a recipe for cooking traditional food
questions.expected: It makes a substantive philosophical claim about what makes us human — that personhood is constituted through relationships
questions.memo: Saying 'we are persons through other persons' is a CLAIM about the nature of human personhood. It is on the same conceptual level as Descartes' 'I think, therefore I am' — a real philosophical position with implications for ethics, politics, and law.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to summarise ubuntu philosophy.
questions.cloze_template: The philosophy of [1] (botho in Sesotho) is captured in the Nguni saying 'umuntu ngumuntu [2]' — 'I am because you are'. It emphasises [3] humanity, community, and our connection to a wider universe. Ubuntu directly challenges [4], greed and unhealthy competition. In modern South Africa, ubuntu is invoked as a founding value in the post-1994 democratic [5].
questions.memo: Five elements: the philosophy's name, its core saying, its central value, what it challenges, where it appears institutionally in modern SA.

questions.question: Tap each phrase showing ubuntu as a substantive philosophical claim, not just politeness.
questions.source_text: Ubuntu is not merely a rule of social courtesy. It is a substantive philosophical claim about the nature of human personhood: that we become fully human through our relationships with other humans, and that no person stands fully formed outside their community. From this claim flow ethical commitments: to shared responsibility, to mutual care, to the dignity of every person. Ubuntu also implies a challenge to ways of life built around individual self-maximisation at the expense of others.
questions.task: Tap each phrase showing ubuntu's substantive philosophical content.

targets.phrase: not merely a rule of social courtesy
substantive philosophical claim about the nature of human personhood
we become fully human through our relationships with other humans
From this claim flow ethical commitments
challenge to ways of life built around individual self-maximisation at the expense of others

questions.expected: Four or more target phrases identified
questions.memo: Five claims showing ubuntu has the structure of a philosophy: makes a metaphysical claim, generates ethics, and stands in opposition to alternative worldviews. That's the same shape as any serious philosophical tradition.

questions.question: Compare these two views of ubuntu.

source_a.text: Ubuntu is a substantive philosophical tradition with significant implications for ethics, law and politics. It claims that personhood is constituted relationally — that we become fully human through and with others — and that this generates duties of mutual care and dignity. The post-1994 South African Constitution invokes ubuntu in this serious sense.

source_b.text: Ubuntu is essentially the African version of 'be nice to others'. It is a useful slogan for tourism and political speeches, but has no real philosophical content.

statements.text: Ubuntu has significant implications for ethics, law and politics
Ubuntu is essentially 'the African version of be nice to others'
Personhood is constituted relationally — through and with others
Ubuntu has 'no real philosophical content'
Both sources take ubuntu equally seriously as a philosophical tradition

questions.memo: The dismissive view ('just be nice') still appears in some commentary, but it doesn't survive contact with the actual philosophical literature on ubuntu or with the Constitutional Court's serious use of the concept.

questions.question: Sort each life choice as COMPATIBLE with ubuntu or as IN TENSION WITH ubuntu.

items.text: Sharing food and resources with neighbours in need
Pursuing unlimited personal wealth regardless of community impact
Caring for elderly relatives within an extended family
Treating community members as competitors to defeat
Volunteering time to support a community project
Excluding others from opportunities to maximise personal gain
Restorative justice — repairing harm rather than only punishing
'I owe nothing to anyone — my success is mine alone'

questions.memo: Ubuntu is not just a feeling — it generates specific guidance on how to live. Sorting concrete choices by ubuntu-alignment shows the philosophy at work.

questions.question: How does ubuntu connect to environmental responsibility?
options: Ubuntu's claim that we are part of a wider universe extends moral concern beyond humans to the natural world we depend on
Ubuntu encourages exploiting nature for personal gain
Ubuntu is purely about human individuals
questions.expected: Ubuntu's claim that we are part of a wider universe extends moral concern beyond humans to the natural world we depend on
questions.memo: If 'I am because you are' extends beyond immediate humans to the wider web of life and the spirit world (as many ubuntu traditions hold), then exploiting ecosystems is exploiting that wider 'you' — and is in tension with ubuntu.

questions.question: Tap each phrase showing the role of ubuntu in the post-1994 South African constitutional order.
questions.source_text: The post-1994 South African Constitution invokes ubuntu in its founding values. The Constitutional Court has cited ubuntu directly in major rulings — including the landmark decision abolishing the death penalty (S v Makwanyane, 1995), where ubuntu's emphasis on shared humanity was central to the reasoning. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission drew on ubuntu's emphasis on community and restoration rather than only retribution. Ubuntu became a serious constitutional and moral concept in the new democratic state, not merely a slogan.
questions.task: Tap each phrase showing ubuntu's serious constitutional and judicial role.

targets.phrase: Constitution invokes ubuntu in its founding values
Constitutional Court has cited ubuntu directly in major rulings
landmark decision abolishing the death penalty (S v Makwanyane, 1995)
Truth and Reconciliation Commission drew on ubuntu's emphasis on community and restoration
serious constitutional and moral concept in the new democratic state, not merely a slogan

questions.expected: Four or more target phrases identified
questions.memo: Five concrete institutional uses of ubuntu — constitution, court ruling, named case, TRC, status as serious concept. The 'just a slogan' framing cannot survive this list.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Ubuntu is a serious philosophical tradition, not a marketing slogan.'
questions.thesis: Ubuntu is a serious philosophical tradition, not a marketing slogan.

pool.text: Ubuntu makes a substantive metaphysical claim about the nature of human personhood — that we are constituted through and with others
Ubuntu generates concrete ethical commitments (mutual care, shared responsibility, dignity of every person) and concrete prohibitions (greed, hyper-individualism)
The post-1994 South African Constitution and the Constitutional Court have invoked ubuntu in major rulings — including the landmark S v Makwanyane case abolishing the death penalty
Ubuntu has been the subject of substantial scholarly philosophical work across African and global philosophy departments
Ubuntu is an Nguni word
South Africa has eleven official languages

questions.memo: Four strong items: metaphysical claim (e1), ethical implications (e2), constitutional uptake (e3), academic philosophical engagement (e4). Each is independent evidence of ubuntu's serious status.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why ubuntu challenges greed and excessive self-enrichment.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why ubuntu challenges greed and excessive self-enrichment.

options.text: Ubuntu directly challenges greed and excessive self-enrichment because it claims that our personhood is constituted through our relationships with others — making the 'I owe nothing to anyone' worldview philosophically incoherent
Ubuntu has no view on greed or self-enrichment
Ubuntu encourages unlimited personal wealth

If 'I am because you are' is true, then I cannot be a full person while ignoring or harming the community that constitutes me. Greed and excessive self-enrichment, which treat others as means or obstacles, contradict this foundational claim
Greed is generally seen as bad
Many cultures have proverbs about sharing

This challenge is not just a feeling — it is a philosophical consequence of ubuntu's core claim. That is why ubuntu can guide concrete decisions about wealth distribution, public service, and how communities should be organised
Ubuntu has nothing to say about money or wealth
Greed is fine as long as it doesn't hurt anyone

questions.memo: From the metaphysical claim ('we are persons through others') flows a concrete ethical position ('greed is incoherent'). This is what serious philosophy looks like — not just sentiment.

questions.question: Compare these two views of ubuntu's role in post-1994 South Africa.

source_a.text: Ubuntu was a serious moral foundation for the post-1994 constitutional settlement and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. The Constitutional Court has cited it as part of its reasoning in landmark cases, including S v Makwanyane (1995) abolishing the death penalty.

source_b.text: Ubuntu in modern South Africa is mostly tourist marketing and political slogan — invoked at speeches, ignored in practice, of no real institutional consequence.

statements.text: Ubuntu was a serious moral foundation for the post-1994 settlement
Ubuntu is 'mostly tourist marketing and political slogan'
The Constitutional Court has cited ubuntu in landmark cases including S v Makwanyane
Ubuntu has 'no real institutional consequence'
Both sources see ubuntu's constitutional role in the same way

questions.memo: Both views exist in modern South African discourse. The institutional record (Constitution, TRC, named Constitutional Court rulings) supports the serious-foundation view. The cynical framing has rhetorical appeal but doesn't engage with the actual record.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Ubuntu has global relevance — its insights matter beyond Africa.'
questions.thesis: Ubuntu has global relevance — its insights matter beyond Africa.

pool.text: Ubuntu's challenge to hyper-individualism and greed speaks directly to global problems including extreme economic inequality and environmental destruction driven by short-term self-maximisation
Ubuntu's emphasis on shared humanity offers a moral basis for global cooperation on issues — like climate change or pandemic response — that require coordinated action across communities
Ubuntu has been engaged seriously by philosophers, theologians and political theorists outside Africa as a substantive contribution to global ethical thought

Ubuntu's relational picture of personhood is consonant with, and adds to, parallel insights in other philosophical traditions (Confucian, communitarian, feminist) — making it a partner in a broader global conversation
Ubuntu is an African concept
Africa has many philosophical traditions

questions.memo: Four strong items: relevance to global problems (e1), basis for global cooperation (e2), engagement by global scholarship (e3), conversation with other traditions (e4). The case for global relevance is multi-dimensional.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining ubuntu's potential role in modern public life.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining ubuntu's potential role in modern public life.

options.text: Ubuntu offers a substantive moral framework for modern public life — one that prioritises shared humanity, mutual care, and limits on greed
Ubuntu has no application to modern public life
Ubuntu is only relevant to private personal conduct

The post-1994 South African Constitution and Constitutional Court have already drawn on ubuntu in concrete legal decisions, including the landmark S v Makwanyane case. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission applied ubuntu's restorative emphasis to processing apartheid-era harm
Ubuntu is mentioned at sporting events
Heritage Day is a public holiday

When a philosophical tradition is taken seriously enough to shape constitutional law and major institutions, it has clearly demonstrated its capacity for application to public life — and its ongoing implications for how we organise modern society are substantial
Philosophy is irrelevant to public life
Modern public life should be guided only by individualist values

questions.memo: Demonstrated application argument: ubuntu has ALREADY shaped major modern institutions in SA — that is concrete evidence of its capacity to do so further.

questions.question: Compare these two assessments of ubuntu's significance.

source_a.text: Ubuntu represents one of Africa's substantial philosophical contributions to global thought. Its relational view of personhood, its insistence on shared humanity, and its critique of hyper-individualism offer a serious counterpoint to dominant Western liberal philosophies — and have been engaged as such by philosophers worldwide.

source_b.text: African societies produced practical customs and folk wisdom, but never developed philosophy properly so called. The systematic philosophical traditions of the world are confined to ancient Greece, India, China and modern Europe.

statements.text: Ubuntu is a substantial African philosophical contribution to global thought
African societies 'never developed philosophy properly so called'
Ubuntu offers a serious counterpoint to dominant Western liberal philosophies
Systematic philosophical traditions are 'confined to ancient Greece, India, China and modern Europe'
Both sources recognise ubuntu as serious philosophy

questions.memo: The mid-20th-century European claim — that 'real' philosophy excludes Africa — was a circular bias: define philosophy in a way that excludes African traditions, then 'discover' that Africa has no philosophy. Modern global philosophy departments have largely abandoned this exclusion.

HIS.G11.T1.IBERIA.A1.title: Why Europe set sail — and what 'the Atlantic World' was
HIS.G11.T1.IBERIA.A1.description: What drove Spanish and Portuguese expansion, the role of monarchy and Church, push vs pull factors, and the meaning of 'the Atlantic World'.
HIS.G11.T1.IBERIA.A1.strand: T1 — The Atlantic World (Spanish & Portuguese; Dutch & English)
HIS.G11.T1.IBERIA.A1.caps_topic: The Atlantic World: Europe comes into contact with the wider world during the 15th to 18th centuries (Spanish and Portuguese)
HIS.G11.T1.IBERIA.A1.recovery_strategy: Europeans sailed for RICHES and were PUSHED by hardship at home (poverty, land shortage, religious war) as much as pulled by gold abroad. Monarchies and the Church bankrolled and blessed the voyages. 'The Atlantic World' is one connected system — Europe + west Africa + the Americas + the islands — tied together by a triangular trade where the most valuable 'cargo' was enslaved people.

questions.question: What was the main reason Spanish and Portuguese explorers set out across the oceans from the 1400s?
options: To gain wealth through trade in goods like gold, silver and sugar
To map the shape of the whole Earth for science
To make friends with distant kingdoms
To find a cooler place to live
questions.expected: To gain wealth through trade in goods like gold, silver and sugar
questions.memo: The driving force was wealth. Trade in gold, silver, sugar and — most profitably — enslaved people promised riches that explorers, merchants and monarchs all wanted a share of.

questions.question: True or false: Improvements in shipbuilding and navigation (like the caravel) gave the Spanish and Portuguese a head-start in long ocean voyages.
questions.memo: Better ships (the caravel could sail against the wind), the compass and improved maps made long Atlantic voyages possible. Technology gave Iberia its early lead.

questions.question: Early Spanish and Portuguese voyages were funded and blessed by the monarchy and the _________ Church.
questions.memo: Spain and Portugal were Catholic powers. Their kings and queens, together with the Catholic Church, paid for voyages and declared them a holy mission to spread Christianity.

questions.question: In the study of why people migrate, a 'push factor' is:
options: Something bad at home that drives people to leave
An attractive reward that pulls people to a new place
questions.expected: Something bad at home that drives people to leave
questions.memo: Push factors push you OUT of home — poverty, land shortage, religious conflict. Pull factors pull you TOWARD somewhere new — riches, land, opportunity.

questions.question: True or false: 'The Atlantic World' means only the countries of western Europe.
questions.memo: The Atlantic World is the whole connected system around the Atlantic Ocean — western Europe, west Africa, the Americas and the Caribbean, and the Atlantic islands — not just Europe.

questions.question: In the triangular trade of the Atlantic World, the most valuable 'cargo' carried from Africa was enslaved _________.
questions.memo: The triangular trade moved goods between three regions, but the cargo at its centre — and the source of the greatest profit — was enslaved African people.

questions.question: Sort each reason as a 'push' factor (driving Europeans to leave home) or a 'pull' factor (attracting them abroad).

buckets.label: Push — drove them to leave Europe

items.text: Poverty and land shortage at home
Gold and silver in the Americas
Religious conflict and persecution in Europe
Profits from the sugar trade
Few opportunities for poor and lower-class Europeans
The chance to gain land and status overseas

questions.memo: Push = the bad things at home (poverty, no land, religious war). Pull = the rewards abroad (gold, sugar profit, land). Most explorers were driven by both at once.

questions.question: Why did Spanish and Portuguese monarchies and the Catholic Church support the voyages of exploration?
options: They expected a share of the wealth and a chance to spread Catholic Christianity and power
They wanted explorers to take holidays abroad
They were forced to by other European countries
They wanted to reduce trade and stay isolated
questions.expected: They expected a share of the wealth and a chance to spread Catholic Christianity and power
questions.memo: Monarchs wanted the riches and the prestige; the Church wanted to spread Catholicism. Backing the voyages served both — money and souls.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to complete this explanation of the Atlantic World.
questions.cloze_template: 'The Atlantic World' refers to the regions connected around the [1] Ocean from the 1400s to the 1800s: western Europe, west [2], the Americas and the [3]. These regions were linked by a [4] trade, in which goods and enslaved [5] were exchanged across the ocean.
questions.memo: Four regions (Europe, west Africa, the Americas, the Caribbean and islands) linked by a triangular trade — with enslaved people at the centre — make up the Atlantic World.

questions.question: Compare these two explanations of why Europeans sailed.

source_a.text: Our brave explorers ventured forth out of pure curiosity and a noble desire to discover unknown lands for the good of all mankind.

source_b.text: Younger sons with no land to inherit, merchants chasing profit, and the poor with little to lose all had powerful reasons to seek fortune across the sea.

Hardship and the hunt for profit drove people to leave Europe
The poor and landless had strong reasons to take the risk
Exploration was done for the good of all mankind
Both sources agree on why Europeans sailed

questions.memo: Source A is a flattering 'noble curiosity' story. Source B points to the real push and pull: hardship at home and profit abroad. The two disagree about motive.

The Americas
Inland China
Japan

questions.memo: The Atlantic World is defined by the Atlantic Ocean: Europe, west Africa, the Americas and the Caribbean. East Asian lands like China and Japan belonged to different trade systems.

questions.question: Tap the words that show this writer is describing trade for PROFIT, not exploration for curiosity.
questions.source_text: The Crown invested heavily in these voyages because the returns were enormous: cargoes of silver and sugar sold at a vast profit, and the trade in enslaved labour promised riches greater still.
questions.task: Tap the phrases that reveal a profit motive.

targets.phrase: the returns were enormous
targets.reason: Frames the voyage as an investment for gain

targets.phrase: sold at a vast profit
promised riches greater still
targets.reason: Shows the goal was wealth, not discovery

questions.memo: Every phrase here is about money — returns, profit, riches. The 'noble explorer' image hides a hard commercial calculation.

questions.question: 'Mercantile trade' (mercantilism) in this period mainly meant:
options: Trading goods to build up the wealth and power of one's own country
Giving goods away freely to other nations
A type of map used at sea
questions.expected: Trading goods to build up the wealth and power of one's own country
questions.memo: Mercantilism = trading to enrich your own nation. Colonies existed to supply raw materials and profit to the mother country, not to benefit the colonised.

questions.question: Place these steps of early European expansion in the order they generally happened — earliest first.

items.text: Advances in shipbuilding and navigation (the caravel, the compass)
Monarchies and the Church agree to fund voyages
Explorers cross the Atlantic seeking trade and riches
Colonies and trade networks are established overseas

questions.memo: First the technology made voyages possible, then royal and Church backing paid for them, then the voyages happened, then colonies and trade followed.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Europeans sailed mainly for profit and were pushed by hardship at home — not mainly out of curiosity.'
questions.thesis: Europeans sailed mainly for profit and were pushed by hardship at home, not mainly out of curiosity.

pool.text: Monarchies and merchants invested in voyages expecting large financial returns
Poverty, land shortage and religious conflict gave ordinary Europeans strong reasons to leave
The most profitable trade — in enslaved people, silver and sugar — drove the whole system
Some sailors enjoyed seeing new places
Maps from this period are now displayed in museums
A few explorers genuinely were curious about the world's geography

questions.memo: The three strong items show profit (e1, e3) and push factors (e2) drove expansion. e6 is a real counter-point — curiosity existed — but it was not the main engine.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining what 'the Atlantic World' was.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining what 'the Atlantic World' was.

options.text: The Atlantic World was one connected system of regions around the Atlantic Ocean
The Atlantic World was just another name for western Europe
The Atlantic World was a single country
Western Europe, west Africa, the Americas and the Caribbean were tied together by a triangular trade
The Atlantic Ocean is very large
Europeans built many ships
Goods, people, ideas and diseases all moved between these regions, so events in one shaped the others
The regions had nothing to do with one another
Only Europe mattered in this system

questions.memo: Claim (one connected system) + evidence (four regions, triangular trade) + explanation (people, goods and ideas moved between them) makes a complete answer.

questions.question: Compare how these two sources explain Europe's voyages.

source_a.text: We sail in the name of God to carry the true faith to heathen peoples and save their souls from darkness.

source_b.text: The spices, gold and human cargo brought back by these fleets made the Crown and its merchants wealthy beyond measure.

statements.text: The voyage is justified as a religious, soul-saving mission
The voyage is described in terms of wealth and profit
Enslaved people ('human cargo') are part of what made the trade profitable
Both sources describe exactly the same motive
The voyage is presented as carrying 'the true faith'

questions.memo: The same expansion was sold two ways: as a holy mission (A) and as a money-making business (B). Both motives were real and worked together.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The monarchy and the Church were essential to European expansion — explorers could not have done it alone.'
questions.thesis: The monarchy and the Church were essential to European expansion; explorers could not have done it alone.

pool.text: Voyages were extremely expensive and needed the Crown's money and ships
The Church declared the voyages a holy mission, giving them moral authority
Royal charters gave explorers the legal right to claim land and trade
Some explorers were brave sailors
Ships were made of wood
A handful of voyages were privately funded by merchants alone

questions.memo: Money (e1), moral authority (e2) and legal right (e3) all came from Crown and Church. e6 is a fair counter — some private funding existed — but the system depended on royal and Church backing.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why the Atlantic World should be studied as one connected system, not as separate continents.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why the Atlantic World should be studied as one connected system.

options.text: The regions of the Atlantic World affected one another, so they must be studied together
Each continent's history is completely separate
Only Europe's history matters in this period
Sugar grown by enslaved Africans in the Americas was sold in Europe, whose ships had carried the enslaved from Africa
The Atlantic Ocean has strong currents
Europe has many countries
A change in one region — a war, a demand for sugar, a slave revolt — rippled across the whole Atlantic system
The regions never traded with one another
Each region developed in total isolation

questions.memo: Connected system (claim) + the sugar-slavery chain linking three regions (evidence) + ripple effects across the Atlantic (explanation) shows why it must be studied as one whole.

questions.question: Compare these two views on whether Europeans were 'pushed' or 'pulled' into expansion.

source_a.text: It was the lure of gold, spices and new riches that drew adventurers irresistibly across the sea.

source_b.text: Crowded, poor and torn by religious war, Europe pushed out those who could find no future at home.
source_b.provenance: Social history of early modern Europe, 2012

statements.text: This source stresses the attraction of riches abroad (a pull factor)
This source stresses hardship in Europe driving people out (a push factor)
This source mentions religious war as a cause
This source mentions gold and spices
Both sources together show expansion had both push and pull causes

questions.memo: Source A captures the pull (riches abroad); Source B captures the push (hardship at home). Read together, they show expansion had both kinds of cause.

HIS.G11.T1.IBERIA.A2.title: The Spanish conquest of the Americas
HIS.G11.T1.IBERIA.A2.description: Columbus, Cortés and Pizarro; the roles of guns, Indigenous allies and disease; the Church's justification; the decimation and genocide of Indigenous peoples.
HIS.G11.T1.IBERIA.A2.strand: T1 — The Atlantic World (Spanish & Portuguese; Dutch & English)
HIS.G11.T1.IBERIA.A2.caps_topic: The Atlantic World: Europe comes into contact with the wider world during the 15th to 18th centuries (Spanish and Portuguese)
HIS.G11.T1.IBERIA.A2.recovery_strategy: Guns mattered, but DISEASE and ALLIES mattered more. Smallpox killed huge numbers of Indigenous people before battles even began, and peoples crushed by the Aztecs and Incas often joined the Spanish. The Church declared the conquest holy. The result was not settlement — it was invasion, mass death and genocide of the original populations.

questions.question: Who invaded the island of Hispaniola from 1492, beginning Spanish conquest in the Americas?
questions.memo: Columbus landed in the Caribbean in 1492 and began the Spanish invasion of Hispaniola — the start of the conquest of the Americas.

questions.question: Hernán Cortés led the Spanish invasion of which empire in Mexico?
questions.memo: Cortés attacked the Aztec Empire in Mexico. Pizarro, separately, attacked the Inca Empire in Peru.

questions.question: Francisco Pizarro invaded the _________ Empire in Peru.
questions.memo: The Pizarros invaded the Inca Empire in Peru. Cortés = Aztec (Mexico); Pizarro = Inca (Peru).

questions.question: True or false: A major reason small Spanish forces could defeat huge empires was that Old World diseases like smallpox killed enormous numbers of Indigenous people.
questions.memo: Indigenous Americans had no immunity to smallpox and other Old World diseases. Epidemics killed millions, often before battles, fatally weakening the Aztec and Inca empires.

questions.question: The Catholic Church helped justify the conquest by presenting it as a mission to:
options: End all warfare in the Americas
questions.memo: The Church framed conquest as saving souls by converting Indigenous people to Catholicism — giving a religious cover to invasion and seizure of land.

questions.question: True or false: The arrival of the Spanish in the Americas was a peaceful settlement that benefited the local people.
questions.memo: It was an invasion, not peaceful settlement. War, enslavement, land seizure and disease decimated Indigenous populations — a genocide, not a benefit.

questions.question: Sort each factor by how it helped the Spanish defeat much larger empires.

items.text: Guns, steel swords and horses
Smallpox epidemics that killed millions
Peoples conquered by the Aztecs joining the Spanish
Cannon that frightened and outranged defenders
No immunity among Indigenous people to Old World illness
Local groups hoping to overthrow their Inca or Aztec overlords

questions.memo: Three forces combined: superior weapons, devastating disease, and Indigenous allies who hated their overlords. No single one explains the conquest.

questions.question: Why did some Indigenous groups fight ALONGSIDE the Spanish against the Aztecs?
options: They had been conquered and oppressed by the Aztecs and hoped to break free
They wanted to learn the Spanish language
questions.expected: They had been conquered and oppressed by the Aztecs and hoped to break free
questions.memo: The Aztec Empire ruled many peoples by force. Some of those peoples allied with the Spanish, hoping to throw off Aztec domination — only to fall under Spanish rule instead.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to explain how a small Spanish force defeated the Aztec Empire.
questions.cloze_template: The Spanish had [1] and horses the Aztecs had never faced, but even more deadly was [2], which killed huge numbers before battle. The Spanish were also joined by Indigenous [3] who resented Aztec rule. The result was not settlement but [4] of the original population.
questions.memo: Guns + disease + allies = conquest, and the outcome for Indigenous people was mass death, not benefit.

questions.question: Place these events of Spanish conquest in chronological order — earliest first.

items.text: Columbus invades Hispaniola (from 1492)
Cortés invades the Aztec Empire in Mexico (1519–1521)
Pizarro invades the Inca Empire in Peru (1530s)

questions.memo: Columbus (1492) opened the Caribbean; Cortés took Mexico in the 1520s; Pizarro took Peru in the 1530s.

questions.question: Tap the words that reveal the Spanish writer is justifying conquest rather than simply describing it.
questions.source_text: By God's grace we subdued these savage idolaters and brought them the gift of the true faith, taking lawful possession of lands the heathens had wasted.
questions.task: Tap the phrases that justify the invasion.

targets.phrase: savage idolaters
targets.reason: Dehumanises Indigenous people to excuse conquest

targets.phrase: the gift of the true faith
targets.reason: Frames invasion as a generous religious mission

targets.phrase: lawful possession
targets.reason: Claims a right to take land that was not theirs

targets.phrase: lands the heathens had wasted
targets.reason: Pretends the land was empty or misused to justify seizure

questions.memo: Each phrase turns a violent seizure into a holy gift. Naming Indigenous people 'savages' and their land 'wasted' was how invasion was made to sound righteous.

questions.question: Compare these two accounts of the Spanish conquest.

source_a.text: The Spaniards entered the villages and spared neither children nor the old; the people died in numbers beyond counting.
source_a.provenance: Bartolomé de las Casas, Spanish friar, 1542

source_b.text: Our captains won glorious victories, planting the Cross and the royal banner over the conquered lands.
source_b.provenance: Spanish conquistador's report to the King, 16th century

statements.text: The conquest is described as mass killing of ordinary people
The conquest is celebrated as glorious victory
The author writes to impress the King
The author condemns the cruelty he witnessed
Both sources describe the conquest as gentle and peaceful

questions.memo: Las Casas, a critic, recorded the slaughter; the conquistador, reporting to his king, dressed it as glory. Who is writing, and for whom, shapes what gets said.

questions.question: The word 'decimated', used for Indigenous populations after conquest, means they were:
options: Reduced to a small fraction of their former numbers
questions.expected: Reduced to a small fraction of their former numbers
questions.memo: Through war, enslavement and above all disease, Indigenous populations collapsed — in many regions by 90% within a century. That scale of loss is why historians speak of genocide.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or a MYTH about the Spanish conquest.

items.text: Disease killed more Indigenous people than Spanish weapons did
A few hundred Spaniards beat huge empires by courage alone
Indigenous allies were crucial to the Spanish victories
The conquest was a peaceful, agreed settlement
The Church framed the conquest as a holy mission
The Americas were almost empty before the Spanish arrived

questions.memo: The 'brave few against the many' story is a myth: disease and allies, not courage alone, decided it — and the Americas were densely populated before the catastrophe.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Disease and Indigenous allies, more than Spanish bravery, explain the conquest of the Americas.'
questions.thesis: Disease and Indigenous allies, more than Spanish bravery, explain the conquest of the Americas.

pool.text: Smallpox and other diseases killed a huge share of the Indigenous population, often before battle
Peoples oppressed by the Aztecs and Incas joined the Spanish in large numbers
Empires already weakened by epidemics could not resist effectively
The Spanish wore metal armour
Spanish ships were large
Spanish guns and horses did give them a battlefield advantage

questions.memo: Disease (e1, e3) and allies (e2) are the strongest explanations. e6 is a genuine counter — weapons mattered — but they alone could not have toppled empires of millions.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why the conquest of the Americas is described as genocide, not settlement.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why the conquest is described as genocide, not settlement.

options.text: The conquest destroyed Indigenous societies on a massive scale, which is why it is called genocide
The conquest was a peaceful exchange of cultures
The conquest left Indigenous populations unchanged
War, enslavement and disease reduced some Indigenous populations by around 90% within a century
The Spanish built some churches
Spanish became a common language
A loss of life and culture on that scale, caused by invasion, is what the word genocide describes — not a settlement that people chose
It was simply bad luck that diseases spread
Indigenous people invited the Spanish to rule them

questions.memo: Claim (mass destruction = genocide) + evidence (≈90% population loss) + explanation (invasion-caused loss on that scale is genocide) makes the case clearly.

questions.question: Compare these two explanations of why the Spanish won so quickly.

source_a.text: It was the unshakeable courage and superior faith of the Spanish soldier that overcame the heathen hordes.

source_b.text: Epidemic disease had already emptied the cities, and tens of thousands of Indigenous allies marched with Cortés against the Aztec capital.

statements.text: Victory is explained by Spanish courage and faith
Victory is explained by disease and Indigenous allies
Tens of thousands of Indigenous people fought alongside Cortés
The Indigenous people are dismissed as 'heathen hordes'
Both sources give the same explanation

questions.memo: The old patriotic story credits Spanish courage; modern history credits disease and allies. The second is supported by evidence; the first is national myth.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The Catholic Church gave the Spanish conquest its moral cover.'
questions.thesis: The Catholic Church gave the Spanish conquest its moral cover.

pool.text: Conquest was officially declared a mission to convert Indigenous people and save their souls
Royal charters blessed by the Church gave the Spanish a 'right' to seize land
Labelling Indigenous people 'heathens' made their conquest seem justified
Spanish priests wore robes
Churches were built from stone
Some friars, like Las Casas, condemned the cruelty of the conquest

questions.memo: The Church supplied the justification: a holy mission (e1), a 'right' to the land (e2), and the 'heathen' label (e3). e6 is a real counter — not all churchmen agreed — but the institution still provided the cover.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why 'a few brave Spaniards beat millions' is a misleading way to describe the conquest.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why 'a few brave Spaniards beat millions' is misleading.

options.text: The 'brave few' story hides the real reasons the Spanish won
The 'brave few' story is the most accurate account
The Spanish had no advantages at all
Disease had already killed millions, and tens of thousands of Indigenous allies fought with the Spanish
Spanish soldiers came from Spain
The conquest happened a long time ago
Crediting courage alone erases the role of epidemics and of the Indigenous peoples who shaped the outcome
Bravery is the only thing that ever wins wars
Indigenous people played no part in events

questions.memo: The myth (claim) is corrected by disease and allies (evidence), and crediting bravery alone erases the real causes (explanation).

questions.question: Compare these two views on who shaped the outcome of the conquest.

source_a.text: The history of the conquest is the story of a handful of extraordinary European men.

source_b.text: Without the Tlaxcalans and other Indigenous allies, and without the smallpox that ran ahead of the Spanish, Cortés would have achieved nothing.

statements.text: The outcome is credited to a few European men
The outcome is credited to Indigenous allies and disease
Indigenous people are treated as central to events
Indigenous people are left out of the story
Both sources agree on who shaped the conquest

questions.memo: Source A is a 'great men' story that erases Indigenous people; Source B puts allies and disease at the centre. The shift shows how history is rewritten as we ask better questions.

HIS.G11.T1.IBERIA.A3.title: A new racial order, disease and resistance
HIS.G11.T1.IBERIA.A3.description: Portuguese reach into the Americas, Africa and the East; the Atlantic slave trade; disease; the racialised class structure; and Indigenous and enslaved resistance.
HIS.G11.T1.IBERIA.A3.strand: T1 — The Atlantic World (Spanish & Portuguese; Dutch & English)
HIS.G11.T1.IBERIA.A3.caps_topic: The Atlantic World: Europe comes into contact with the wider world during the 15th to 18th centuries (Spanish and Portuguese)
HIS.G11.T1.IBERIA.A3.recovery_strategy: The colonial order was RACIALISED: Europeans on top, then mestizos/mulattoes with limited mobility, then Indigenous people and enslaved Africans at the bottom — birth and race, not just money, fixed your place. Portugal opened the Atlantic slave trade and reached Brazil, Africa and the East. Disease devastated the Americas. And the colonised never simply accepted it — resistance was constant.

questions.question: Which country opened large-scale European slave trading along the African coast and colonised Brazil?
questions.memo: Portugal led the early Atlantic slave trade and colonised Brazil, while reaching Africa and the East. Spain focused on conquering the Americas.

questions.question: True or false: In the new colonial society, a person's place was fixed mainly by race, not only by wealth.
questions.memo: The colonial order was racialised. Europeans sat at the top, then mixed-race mestizos and mulattoes, then Indigenous people and enslaved Africans — race, not just money, decided your rank.

questions.question: In the Spanish colonies, people of mixed European and Indigenous descent were called _________.
questions.memo: Mestizos (European + Indigenous) and mulattoes (European + African) sat in the middle of the racial order, with only limited room to rise.

questions.question: Which of these did European colonisers bring that devastated Indigenous populations?
options: New diseases such as smallpox and measles
questions.expected: New diseases such as smallpox and measles
questions.memo: Old World diseases — smallpox, measles, influenza — spread among people with no immunity, killing huge numbers. Disease was the deadliest force of the whole encounter.

questions.question: True or false: Indigenous people and enslaved Africans simply accepted Spanish and Portuguese rule without resisting.
questions.memo: Resistance was constant — armed revolts, escapes, runaway communities, and the daily refusal to cooperate. The colonised were never just passive victims.

questions.question: The trade that forcibly carried enslaved Africans across the ocean to the Americas is called the _________ slave trade.
questions.memo: The Atlantic (or transatlantic) slave trade shipped enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to work in the Americas — the human heart of the Atlantic World system.

questions.question: Sort each group by its usual place in the colonial racial order.

items.text: Europeans born in Spain or Portugal
Mestizos and mulattoes (people of mixed descent)
Indigenous people
Enslaved Africans
Colonial governors and landowners from Europe
Free people of part-European, part-African descent

questions.memo: Europeans on top; mixed-race people in the middle with limited mobility; Indigenous people and enslaved Africans at the bottom. Race fixed the structure.

questions.question: Why is it wrong to say the colonial class system was based on wealth alone?
options: Because race set limits no amount of money could fully overcome
Because everyone in the colonies was equally rich
Because there were no rich people in the colonies
Because wealth did not exist yet
questions.expected: Because race set limits no amount of money could fully overcome
questions.memo: A wealthy person of African or Indigenous descent still ranked below poorer Europeans. Race, not just money, fixed a person's place — that is what 'racialised' means.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to describe the new colonial society.
questions.cloze_template: The colonies developed a [1] class structure. [2] Europeans held the top positions, while [3] people and enslaved [4] were placed at the bottom. A person's race, more than their [5], decided their place.
questions.memo: A racialised order: Europeans on top, Indigenous people and enslaved Africans at the bottom, with race outweighing wealth.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show enslaved and Indigenous people actively RESISTING colonial rule.
questions.source_text: Reports from the colony complained that the enslaved would flee into the forests to form free communities, that whole villages refused to pay tribute, and that workers broke their tools and burned the cane fields.
questions.task: Tap the phrases that describe acts of resistance.

targets.phrase: flee into the forests to form free communities
refused to pay tribute
targets.reason: Open refusal to obey colonial demands

targets.phrase: broke their tools and burned the cane fields

questions.memo: Fleeing to form free communities, refusing tribute, breaking tools and burning fields — all are resistance. The colonised fought back in many ways.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on life in the colonies.

source_a.text: Through hard work, a man of any background may in time rise to wealth and respect in these new lands.

source_b.text: However rich an Indigenous or African family became, the law and custom kept them beneath the poorest Spaniard.

statements.text: The colonies are described as a place where anyone can rise
Race set limits that wealth could not overcome
The source is advertising the colonies to attract settlers
Even wealthy non-Europeans ranked below poor Europeans
Both sources describe an equal society

questions.memo: The pamphlet (A) sells a dream of open opportunity; the historian (B) shows race fixed people's place. Advertising and reality told different stories.

questions.question: Communities formed by people who escaped slavery and lived free in remote areas were known as:
questions.memo: Escaped enslaved people formed free 'maroon' communities in forests and mountains, sometimes resisting recapture for generations — proof that resistance was real and organised.

questions.question: Sort each item as something the Portuguese DID in their expansion, or something they did NOT do.

buckets.label: The Portuguese did not do this

items.text: Colonised Brazil
Built early slave-trading posts on the African coast
Reached trade routes to the East (India and beyond)
Ended the slave trade in the 1500s
Gave colonised peoples equal rights
Carried enslaved Africans across the Atlantic

questions.memo: Portugal colonised Brazil, opened African slave-trading posts, reached the East and carried enslaved Africans across the Atlantic. It did not end slavery or grant equality.

questions.question: Why did some poor Europeans and mixed-race people gain limited upward mobility in the colonies?
options: The racial order placed them above Indigenous people and enslaved Africans, giving them room to rise
Because race did not matter in the colonies
Because they were given noble titles
Because they owned the largest plantations
questions.expected: The racial order placed them above Indigenous people and enslaved Africans, giving them room to rise
questions.memo: The racialised order gave poorer Europeans and mestizos/mulattoes a rung to climb because others were placed beneath them. Mobility existed, but the ceiling and the floor were set by race.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The colonial order was racialised — race, not just wealth, fixed a person's place.'
questions.thesis: The colonial order was racialised: race, not just wealth, fixed a person's place.

pool.text: Europeans held the top positions regardless of individual ability
Wealthy people of Indigenous or African descent still ranked below poor Europeans
Laws and customs assigned rights and limits according to racial category
The colonies had hot weather
Some colonists owned cattle
A few exceptional individuals did manage to rise above their racial category

questions.memo: Europeans on top by race (e1), wealth not enough to escape it (e2), and law fixing it (e3). e6 is a fair counter — rare exceptions existed — but they prove the rule was about race.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why disease was the deadliest part of the European arrival in the Americas.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why disease was the deadliest part of the European arrival.

options.text: Imported disease killed more Indigenous people than any weapon
Disease had no real effect on the Americas
Indigenous people were immune to European diseases
Indigenous people had no immunity to smallpox, measles and influenza, and died in their millions
The Spanish brought horses
Europeans built ships
With no prior exposure, whole populations collapsed within decades, breaking the societies that might have resisted
Disease only affected a few individuals
The diseases were harmless

questions.memo: Claim (disease was deadliest) + evidence (no immunity, millions dead) + explanation (population collapse broke resistance) makes a strong paragraph.

questions.question: Compare these two sources about resistance to colonial rule.

source_a.text: The natives, being simple and content, gladly accepted the rule and religion of their new masters.

source_b.text: Court records are full of runaway slaves, burned plantations and armed revolts that the authorities could never fully suppress.

statements.text: The colonised are described as content and obedient
The colonised are shown resisting through escape and revolt
The evidence comes from court and archive records
The source claims the natives 'gladly accepted' their masters
Both sources agree the colonised resisted constantly

questions.memo: Officials liked to claim everyone was content (A); the archives reveal constant resistance (B). The records contradict the comfortable official story.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Indigenous people and enslaved Africans actively resisted colonial rule.'
questions.thesis: Indigenous people and enslaved Africans actively resisted colonial rule.

pool.text: Escaped enslaved people formed free maroon communities that defended themselves for generations
There were repeated armed revolts and uprisings across the colonies
Everyday resistance — sabotage, refusing tribute, escape — was constant
The colonies were far from Europe
Sugar was grown in the colonies
Many revolts were eventually crushed by colonial forces

questions.memo: Maroon communities (e1), armed revolts (e2) and everyday resistance (e3) prove the colonised fought back. e6 is a real counter — many revolts failed — but failure does not mean there was no resistance.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why the colonial order is described as 'racialised'.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why the colonial order is described as 'racialised'.

options.text: The colonial order ranked people by race, making race the basis of power
The colonial order treated everyone equally
The colonial order had no rich or poor
Europeans held power at the top while Indigenous people and enslaved Africans were fixed at the bottom by race
The colonies grew sugar and tobacco
Spanish was widely spoken
Because race, not effort or wealth, decided rank, the inequality was built into the system itself
Because anyone could become wealthy and powerful
Because race played no part in colonial life

questions.memo: Claim (ranked by race) + evidence (Europeans on top, others fixed at the bottom) + explanation (race not effort decided rank) explains 'racialised'.

questions.question: Compare these two views on the legacy of Spanish and Portuguese colonisation.

source_a.text: The Iberians brought language, religion and civilisation to peoples who had little of their own.

source_b.text: Colonisation left a lasting legacy of population collapse, racial hierarchy and dispossession across South America and Africa.

statements.text: Colonisation is presented as a gift of civilisation
Colonisation is presented as leaving harm and inequality
Population collapse and racial hierarchy are named as legacies
