The colonised are said to have had 'little of their own'
Both sources judge colonisation the same way

questions.memo: The old textbook (A) frames colonisation as a gift; modern history (B) records its lasting damage. The 'gift of civilisation' story ignores the human cost.

HIS.G11.T1.DUTCHENG.A1.title: The Dutch and English challenge Iberia
HIS.G11.T1.DUTCHENG.A1.description: How Holland and Britain imitated and overtook Spain and Portugal through navigation, piracy and royal backing; the Cape refreshment station; New Amsterdam becoming New York.
HIS.G11.T1.DUTCHENG.A1.strand: T1 — The Atlantic World (Spanish & Portuguese; Dutch & English)
HIS.G11.T1.DUTCHENG.A1.caps_topic: The Atlantic World: Europe comes into contact with the wider world during the 16th to 19th centuries (Dutch and English)
HIS.G11.T1.DUTCHENG.A1.recovery_strategy: The Dutch and English COPIED the Spanish and Portuguese — same ships, same navigation — and at first got ahead partly by PIRACY, robbing Iberian treasure ships. Then they overtook them. Track the takeovers: the English took New Amsterdam from the Dutch and renamed it New York, and the English later took the Cape from the Dutch.

questions.question: How did the Dutch and English first build their sea power in the 1500s and 1600s?
options: By copying Spanish and Portuguese ships and navigation
By inventing the first ocean-going ships
questions.expected: By copying Spanish and Portuguese ships and navigation
questions.memo: The Dutch and English were latecomers. They imitated Spanish and Portuguese shipbuilding and navigation, then overtook them — they did not start from scratch.

questions.question: True or false: Dutch and English sailors often attacked and robbed Spanish and Portuguese treasure ships (piracy).
questions.memo: Piracy and privateering — robbing Iberian treasure ships — was an early way the Dutch and English gained wealth at Spain's and Portugal's expense.

questions.question: The Dutch set up a refreshment station in 1652 at the _________ of Good Hope.
questions.memo: The Dutch East India Company set up a refreshment station at the Cape of Good Hope to resupply ships sailing to and from the East.

questions.question: The Dutch town of New Amsterdam in North America was renamed _________ after the English took it.
questions.memo: The English seized New Amsterdam from the Dutch and renamed it New York. Remember: English took it FROM the Dutch, not the other way round.

questions.question: True or false: The Dutch and English were the first Europeans ever to sail the oceans.
questions.memo: The Spanish and Portuguese sailed the oceans first. The Dutch and English came later, copied them, and then overtook them.

questions.question: Like the Iberians, Dutch and English voyages were also backed by their _________.
questions.memo: Royal backing mattered everywhere: Dutch and English monarchies (and trading companies they chartered) funded and protected the voyages, just as Spain and Portugal had.

questions.question: Sort each event by who took territory FROM whom.

buckets.label: English took it from the Dutch
Dutch held or settled it first

items.text: New Amsterdam, renamed New York
The refreshment station at the Cape of Good Hope (1652)
The Cape Colony, later taken by Britain
The mid-Atlantic colony first settled by the Dutch

questions.memo: The Dutch settled the Cape and New Amsterdam first; the English later took BOTH from them. The direction of takeover runs Dutch → English.

questions.question: Why did the Dutch and English get into mercantile trade in goods like timber, sugar and enslaved Africans?
options: To build national wealth and compete with Spain and Portugal
To give the goods away to other nations
Because their monarchs banned all trade
Because they had no ships of their own
questions.expected: To build national wealth and compete with Spain and Portugal
questions.memo: Mercantile trade was about national wealth and power. The Dutch and English chased the same profitable goods — timber, sugar, enslaved people — to compete with the Iberian powers.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to describe how the Dutch and English rose to power.
questions.cloze_template: The Dutch and English [1] the navigation and shipbuilding of Spain and Portugal. At first they gained wealth partly through [2], robbing Iberian ships. With backing from their [3], they then took over key sites — the English seized [4] from the Dutch and renamed it New York, and later took the [5] as well.
questions.memo: Copied the Iberians, used piracy, won royal backing, then took New Amsterdam (→ New York) and the Cape from the Dutch.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on how the Dutch and English built their power.

source_a.text: The English and Dutch were bold innovators who single-handedly opened the oceans to trade.

source_b.text: They learned their seamanship from Iberian rivals and grew rich partly by plundering Spanish and Portuguese ships.

statements.text: The Dutch and English opened the oceans single-handedly
They learned from the Spanish and Portuguese
They grew rich partly through piracy
They are called bold innovators who acted alone
Both sources fully agree

questions.memo: The patriotic story (A) makes them lone pioneers; the modern account (B) shows they copied the Iberians and used piracy. Evidence supports B.

questions.question: What was the main purpose of the Dutch refreshment station at the Cape?
options: To resupply passing ships with food and water on the route to the East
To mine gold in the interior
To convert the Khoisan to Catholicism
questions.expected: To resupply passing ships with food and water on the route to the East
questions.memo: The Cape station existed to give passing Dutch ships fresh food and water on the long voyage between Europe and the East — not as a colony at first, though it grew into one.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show this writer is justifying piracy as something noble.
questions.source_text: Our gallant sea-captains, serving God and the Queen, relieved the Spanish of their ill-gotten treasure and won glory for the nation.
questions.task: Tap the phrases that dress up piracy as honourable.

targets.phrase: gallant sea-captains
serving God and the Queen
targets.reason: Claims a holy and patriotic motive for robbery

targets.phrase: relieved the Spanish of their ill-gotten treasure
targets.reason: Excuses theft by calling the victims' wealth 'ill-gotten'

targets.phrase: won glory for the nation

questions.memo: The same act — robbing ships — is dressed as holy, patriotic and glorious. Naming the loot 'ill-gotten' shifts the blame onto the victims.

questions.question: Place these events in chronological order — earliest first.

items.text: Dutch set up the Cape refreshment station (1652)
English seize New Amsterdam and rename it New York (1664)
Britain takes control of the Cape Colony (around 1800)

questions.memo: Cape station 1652 → New York taken 1664 → Britain takes the Cape around 1800. The English steadily displaced the Dutch over 150 years.

questions.question: What does it tell us that the Dutch and English fought one another as well as the Spanish?
options: European powers competed fiercely for trade and territory, not just against non-Europeans
Europe had no interest in the colonies
Trade was shared equally between nations
questions.expected: European powers competed fiercely for trade and territory, not just against non-Europeans
questions.memo: The Atlantic World was a scene of constant European rivalry. The Dutch and English fought each other for colonies and trade — competition drove the whole system.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The Dutch and English succeeded by imitating the Iberians, not by inventing something new.'
questions.thesis: The Dutch and English succeeded by imitating the Iberians, not by inventing something new.

pool.text: They copied Spanish and Portuguese ship designs and navigation methods
They entered the same trades — sugar, timber, enslaved people — that the Iberians had opened
They first gained wealth by raiding Iberian ships rather than finding new routes
Dutch windmills were famous
English is spoken in many countries today
The Dutch did make real improvements to ship and financial design

questions.memo: Copied designs (e1), entered Iberian trades (e2), raided rather than pioneered (e3). e6 is a fair counter — they refined things — but the foundation was imitation.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining how the English displaced the Dutch in the Atlantic World.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining how the English displaced the Dutch.

options.text: The English steadily took over key Dutch possessions in the Atlantic World
The Dutch took over all English possessions
The Dutch and English never competed
The English seized New Amsterdam (renaming it New York) and later took the Cape Colony from the Dutch
The Dutch built windmills
The English liked tea
Control of these ports gave Britain command of major trade routes the Dutch had pioneered
The takeovers made no difference to trade
The Dutch were happy to give everything away

questions.memo: Claim (English displaced the Dutch) + evidence (New York and the Cape) + explanation (control of trade routes) tells the story.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on the Dutch arrival at the Cape.

source_a.text: A small station was established merely to grow vegetables and supply fresh water to our ships bound for the Indies.

source_b.text: From that small station grew a settler colony that pushed the Khoisan off their grazing land within a generation.

statements.text: The Cape was meant only as a supply station for passing ships
The station grew into a settler colony that dispossessed the Khoisan
The Khoisan lost their grazing land
The original purpose was vegetables and fresh water
Both sources describe the Cape the same way

questions.memo: The Company's plan (A) was a modest supply station; the outcome (B) was a settler colony that dispossessed the Khoisan. Intentions and consequences differed sharply.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'European rivalry, not cooperation, shaped the Atlantic World.'
questions.thesis: European rivalry, not cooperation, shaped the Atlantic World.

pool.text: The English and Dutch repeatedly fought one another over colonies and trade routes
Dutch and English wealth was built partly by raiding Spanish and Portuguese ships
Control of ports like New York and the Cape passed by conquest from one power to another
Europe is a continent
Ships used sails
European powers sometimes signed treaties to divide territory

questions.memo: Wars between powers (e1), piracy (e2) and conquest of ports (e3) show rivalry drove events. e6 is a fair counter — treaties happened — but they usually followed conflict.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why it is misleading to call the Dutch and English the 'first' great sea powers.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why calling the Dutch and English the 'first' great sea powers is misleading.

options.text: The Dutch and English built on Iberian foundations, so they were not the first
The Dutch and English invented ocean sailing
No European power sailed before 1600
Spain and Portugal had already crossed the oceans and built empires when the Dutch and English began copying them
The English liked sailing
The Dutch built canals
Calling them 'first' erases the Iberian pioneers whose ships, routes and methods they adopted
Being first is the only thing that matters in history
The Iberians never sailed anywhere

questions.memo: Claim (not first, built on Iberia) + evidence (Spain and Portugal went before) + explanation ('first' erases the pioneers) makes the point.

questions.question: Compare these two views of Dutch and English piracy against Spain.

source_a.text: These daring captains were heroes who broke the cruel Spanish monopoly and enriched their homelands.

source_b.text: They were state-backed pirates whose plunder of treasure fleets funded the rise of rival empires.

statements.text: The captains are praised as heroes
The captains are called state-backed pirates
Their plunder is said to have funded rival empires
They are said to have broken a 'cruel Spanish monopoly'
Both sources praise the captains as honourable heroes

questions.memo: One nation's hero is another's pirate. The schoolbook (A) celebrates; the historian (B) names the plunder plainly. Both describe the same acts.

HIS.G11.T1.DUTCHENG.A2.title: Slavery as the engine of Dutch and British wealth
HIS.G11.T1.DUTCHENG.A2.description: Enslaved labour and the accumulation of capital; 12 million Africans; the slave ship and the Middle Passage; plantation crops; the difference between indentured servitude and chattel slavery.
HIS.G11.T1.DUTCHENG.A2.strand: T1 — The Atlantic World (Spanish & Portuguese; Dutch & English)
HIS.G11.T1.DUTCHENG.A2.caps_topic: The Atlantic World: Europe comes into contact with the wider world during the 16th to 19th centuries (Dutch and English)
HIS.G11.T1.DUTCHENG.A2.recovery_strategy: Slavery was the ENGINE, not a sideshow: at least 12 million Africans were shipped across the Atlantic, and the profits built Dutch and British capital. Indenture vs slavery: an indentured servant was unfree for a FIXED term and then freed; an enslaved African was unfree for LIFE, the status was INHERITED by their children, and it was fixed by RACE.

questions.question: Roughly how many enslaved Africans were carried across the Atlantic between the 16th and 19th centuries?
questions.memo: At least 12 million Africans were forcibly carried across the Atlantic — one of the largest forced movements of people in history.

questions.question: The brutal ocean crossing that carried enslaved Africans to the Americas was called the _________ Passage.
questions.memo: The 'Middle Passage' was the middle leg of the triangular trade — the horrific voyage carrying enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to the Americas.

questions.question: True or false: Profits from slavery and the slave trade helped build up Dutch and British wealth (capital).
questions.memo: Slavery was an engine of capital accumulation. Sugar, tobacco and cotton grown by enslaved people, and the trade itself, generated profits that enriched Holland and Britain.

questions.question: Which crops were mainly grown on the plantations using enslaved labour?
questions.memo: Sugar, cotton and tobacco were the great plantation crops of the Caribbean and the southern British colonies, all worked by enslaved Africans.

questions.question: True or false: An indentured servant was enslaved for life, and so were their children.
questions.memo: That describes chattel slavery, not indenture. An indentured servant was unfree for a fixed term, then freed; their children were born free.

questions.question: The slave _________ — the vessel that carried captives across the Atlantic — sits at the centre of Atlantic history.
questions.memo: The slave ship is at the heart of Atlantic history: it links capture in Africa to labour in the Americas, and its conditions defined the Middle Passage.

questions.question: Sort each feature as belonging to INDENTURED SERVITUDE or to CHATTEL SLAVERY.

items.text: Unfree for a fixed number of years, then released
Unfree for life
The status passed to one's children
Entered into by a contract, often to pay for passage
Fixed by race
The person could not be bought and sold as property forever

questions.memo: Indenture: fixed term, by contract, children born free. Slavery: for life, inherited, fixed by race, treated as property. The difference is fundamental.

questions.question: Why is it accurate to call slavery the 'engine' of the plantation economy rather than a minor part of it?
options: The plantations could not have produced their profitable crops without enslaved labour
Slavery affected only a handful of people
Enslaved people did only light work
questions.expected: The plantations could not have produced their profitable crops without enslaved labour
questions.memo: Sugar, cotton and tobacco profits depended entirely on enslaved labour. Remove slavery and the whole plantation economy collapses — that is why it was the engine.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to compare indenture and slavery.
questions.cloze_template: An indentured servant was unfree for a [1] term and was then freed, and their children were born [2]. An enslaved African was unfree for [3], the condition was [4] by their children, and it was fixed by [5].
questions.memo: Indenture = fixed term, children free. Slavery = for life, inherited, fixed by race. That is the crucial distinction.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that reveal the inhuman treatment of enslaved people aboard the slave ship.
questions.source_text: The captives were packed below decks with no room to sit upright, chained in pairs for the whole voyage, while those who sickened were thrown overboard to save provisions.
questions.task: Tap the phrases showing they were treated as cargo, not people.

targets.phrase: packed below decks with no room to sit upright
targets.reason: Treated as cargo to be crammed in

targets.phrase: chained in pairs for the whole voyage
targets.reason: Held in chains throughout the crossing

targets.phrase: thrown overboard to save provisions
targets.reason: Lives treated as less valuable than supplies

questions.memo: Each phrase shows people treated as cargo: packed, chained, and discarded to save supplies. This was the reality of the Middle Passage.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on the role of slavery in European wealth.

source_a.text: The fortunes of our great merchant families were built on sugar, and that sugar was built on the labour of the enslaved.

source_b.text: Slavery was an unfortunate but small affair, with little bearing on the prosperity of European nations.

statements.text: Slavery was central to European merchant wealth
Slavery was a small affair with little economic effect
Merchant fortunes are linked directly to enslaved labour
Both sources weigh slavery's importance the same way
Slavery is described as having 'little bearing' on prosperity

questions.memo: Source A makes slavery central to European wealth; Source B downplays it. Modern evidence backs A — the profits were enormous and foundational.

questions.question: Why did European traders increasingly turn to enslaved AFRICANS rather than enslaving Native Americans or relying only on European servants?
options: Native Americans died from disease or resisted, and indentured servants were freed after their term
Africans worked for free by choice
There were no Native Americans left anywhere
questions.expected: Native Americans died from disease or resisted, and indentured servants were freed after their term
questions.memo: Native Americans died in huge numbers from disease or escaped; indentured servants had to be freed. Enslaved Africans, held for life and unable to blend in, became the labour force planters fixed on.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or a MYTH about Atlantic slavery.

items.text: At least 12 million Africans were carried across the Atlantic
Slavery had little effect on European economies
Enslaved status was inherited by one's children
Indentured servants and enslaved Africans were treated identically
Plantation crops like sugar depended on enslaved labour
Most enslaved people were freed after a few years

questions.memo: True: 12 million, inherited status, sugar depended on it. Myths: that it was economically minor, the same as indenture, or temporary.

questions.question: What does describing the slave trade as a 'triangular' trade tell us?
options: Goods went to Africa, enslaved people to the Americas, and plantation produce back to Europe
Ships only ever sailed in straight lines
The trade lasted only three years
questions.expected: Goods went to Africa, enslaved people to the Americas, and plantation produce back to Europe
questions.memo: The triangle: European goods → Africa; enslaved Africans → the Americas (the Middle Passage); sugar, cotton and tobacco → Europe. Each leg made a profit.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Slavery was the engine of Dutch and British wealth, not a minor side activity.'
questions.thesis: Slavery was the engine of Dutch and British wealth, not a minor side activity.

pool.text: At least 12 million Africans were trafficked, generating profit at every stage of the trade
The profitable plantation crops (sugar, cotton, tobacco) depended entirely on enslaved labour
Merchant fortunes, ports and industries grew on slavery's profits
The Atlantic Ocean is salty
Sugar is sweet
Some merchants traded in goods other than enslaved people too

questions.memo: Scale and profit (e1), crops dependent on it (e2), fortunes built on it (e3). e6 is a fair counter — other trades existed — but slavery powered the whole system.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining the difference between indentured servitude and chattel slavery.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining the difference between indentured servitude and chattel slavery.

options.text: Indenture and slavery were both unfree labour, but slavery was permanent, inherited and racial
Indenture and slavery were exactly the same thing
Neither involved any loss of freedom
An indentured servant was freed after a fixed term and their children were born free, while an enslaved African was held for life and the status passed to their children
Both groups crossed the Atlantic
Both worked outdoors
Because slavery was for life, inherited and fixed by race, it trapped whole families permanently in a way indenture did not
Because indenture was actually worse than slavery
Because there was no real difference between the two

questions.memo: Claim (both unfree, but slavery permanent/inherited/racial) + evidence (fixed term vs lifelong and inherited) + explanation (traps whole families forever) draws the distinction clearly.

questions.question: Compare these two sources describing the Middle Passage.

source_a.text: The shrieks of the women and the groans of the dying rendered the whole a scene of horror almost inconceivable.

source_b.text: The vessels were well ordered, and the cargo conveyed with no more loss than is usual in any long trade.

statements.text: The crossing is described as a scene of horror
The crossing is described in cold business terms as 'cargo'
The writer experienced the crossing as an enslaved person
The writer profited from the trade and downplays the suffering
Both sources describe the voyage as comfortable

questions.memo: Equiano (A), who lived it, records horror; the owner (B), who profited, calls people 'cargo' and 'loss'. Who is speaking, and what they gained, shapes the account.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Chattel slavery was a far harsher and more permanent condition than indentured servitude.'
questions.thesis: Chattel slavery was a far harsher and more permanent condition than indentured servitude.

pool.text: Enslaved people were held for life, with no end date to their bondage
Enslaved status was inherited, so children were born enslaved
Enslaved people were treated as property to be bought and sold, and the system was fixed by race
Indentured servants signed a contract written on paper
Both groups travelled by ship
Indentured servants could also be treated very harshly during their term

questions.memo: Lifelong (e1), inherited (e2), property fixed by race (e3) make slavery categorically worse. e6 is a fair counter — indenture was hard too — but it ended, and freedom followed.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why the slave ship is placed 'at the centre of Atlantic history'.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why the slave ship is placed at the centre of Atlantic history.

options.text: The slave ship connected every part of the Atlantic World system
The slave ship had nothing to do with the wider economy
The slave ship carried only goods, never people
It linked capture in Africa, the Middle Passage, and forced labour on American plantations into one chain
Ships were painted different colours
Sailors ate biscuits
Because the wealth of the whole Atlantic World flowed through that crossing, the ship symbolises the system that produced it
Because ships are interesting to look at
Because the ship had no effect on anyone

questions.memo: Claim (connected the system) + evidence (linked Africa, the Passage and the plantations) + explanation (the system's wealth flowed through it) explains the ship's central place.

questions.question: Compare these two views on why planters turned to enslaved African labour.

source_a.text: Africans were simply better suited by nature to hard labour in hot climates.

source_b.text: Planters chose enslaved Africans because they could be held for life, their children inherited the status, and they could not easily escape into the local population.

statements.text: The choice is explained by a false claim about race and nature
The choice is explained by permanence, inheritance and control
The source repeats a racist justification for slavery
The source gives economic and practical reasons
Both sources give the same explanation

questions.memo: The pamphlet (A) uses a racist myth to justify slavery; the historian (B) gives the real reasons — lifelong, inherited, hard to escape. The myth hid a cold calculation.

HIS.G11.T1.DUTCHENG.A3.title: Genocide and the slave experience — the Cape and the Americas
HIS.G11.T1.DUTCHENG.A3.description: How war, dispossession and disease decimated Native Americans and the Khoisan; the enslaved journey from capture to plantation; gendered experiences; sugar linking four continents.
HIS.G11.T1.DUTCHENG.A3.strand: T1 — The Atlantic World (Spanish & Portuguese; Dutch & English)
HIS.G11.T1.DUTCHENG.A3.caps_topic: The Atlantic World: Europe comes into contact with the wider world during the 16th to 19th centuries (Dutch and English)
HIS.G11.T1.DUTCHENG.A3.recovery_strategy: The decline of the Khoisan and Native Americans was NOT natural — it was caused by war, land seizure and imported disease. Trace the enslaved journey as stages: capture in Africa → the Middle Passage → plantation/town. And the experience was GENDERED — enslaved women faced field labour plus distinct forms of abuse. Sugar was the thread linking all four continents.

questions.question: At the Cape, which people were decimated by war, land dispossession and new diseases brought by European settlers?
questions.memo: The Khoisan of the Cape lost their land and were devastated by violence and by diseases like smallpox brought by the Dutch — a pattern parallel to the Americas.

questions.question: True or false: The collapse of the Khoisan population was a natural event with no connection to colonisation.
questions.memo: It was not natural. War, land seizure and imported disease — all results of colonisation — caused the Khoisan collapse.

questions.question: The enslaved journey began with _________ in west and central Africa.
questions.memo: The journey began with capture in Africa, then the Middle Passage across the ocean, then forced labour on plantations and in towns.

questions.question: Which single crop is described as 'linking Africa, Europe, Asia and the Americas' in one brutal system?
questions.memo: Sugar tied the continents together: African labour, American plantations, European markets and capital, and demand across the world.

questions.question: True or false: Enslaved men and women had exactly the same experiences on the plantations.
questions.memo: The experience was gendered. Enslaved women did field labour but also faced distinct burdens and forms of abuse, including sexual violence — their experience was not the same as men's.

questions.question: Both the Native Americans and the Khoisan were devastated partly by _________ brought from the Old World.
questions.memo: In both the Americas and at the Cape, imported diseases (like smallpox) killed people who had no immunity — a shared pattern of the Atlantic World.

questions.question: Sort each cause by how it contributed to the destruction of Indigenous populations.

items.text: Settlers seizing grazing and hunting grounds
Smallpox epidemics among people with no immunity
Armed raids and killings by colonial forces
Communities pushed off the land that fed them
Measles and influenza spreading through villages
Wars of conquest against resisting peoples

questions.memo: Three forces destroyed Indigenous populations: war, the loss of land, and disease. Together they amounted to genocide.

questions.question: Why does comparing the Cape and the Americas help us understand colonisation?
options: It shows the same pattern of war, dispossession and disease repeated in different places
It proves colonisation only happened in one place
It shows colonisation was always peaceful
It proves the two regions had nothing in common
questions.expected: It shows the same pattern of war, dispossession and disease repeated in different places
questions.memo: The Khoisan at the Cape and Native Americans suffered the same combination — war, land loss, disease. The repeated pattern reveals how colonisation worked in general.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to trace the enslaved journey.
questions.cloze_template: The enslaved journey began with [1] in west and central Africa. Captives then endured the [2] across the Atlantic. On arrival they were forced to labour on [3] and in towns. The experience was also [4]: enslaved women faced field work plus distinct forms of [5].
questions.memo: Capture → Middle Passage → plantation, and a gendered experience in which women faced added abuse.

questions.question: Place the stages of the enslaved journey in order — earliest first.

items.text: Capture and sale in west or central Africa
The Middle Passage across the Atlantic
Sale at a New World slave market
Forced labour on a plantation or in a town

questions.memo: Capture in Africa → the ocean crossing → sale in the Americas → forced labour. Each stage was brutal in its own way.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show this writer is wrongly treating the Khoisan's decline as natural and blameless.
questions.source_text: Sadly the Khoisan, a frail and primitive people, simply faded away of their own accord as the industrious settlers prospered, through no fault of anyone.
questions.task: Tap the phrases that hide the real causes of the Khoisan's destruction.

targets.phrase: frail and primitive people
targets.reason: Racist framing blaming the victims' supposed weakness

targets.phrase: faded away of their own accord
targets.reason: Pretends the collapse was natural, not caused by colonisation

targets.phrase: through no fault of anyone
targets.reason: Denies the violence and dispossession that caused it

questions.memo: Calling people 'frail' who 'faded away' through 'no fault of anyone' erases the war, land seizure and disease that actually destroyed them.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on the fate of the Khoisan.

source_a.text: The natives dwindled naturally, being unfit to survive alongside a more advanced people.

source_b.text: Dutch commandos seized Khoisan cattle and grazing land, and smallpox brought by ships killed thousands within months.

statements.text: The Khoisan are said to have 'dwindled naturally'
The decline is explained by cattle seizure, land loss and smallpox
The source blames the Khoisan for being 'unfit'
The source names specific actions by Dutch settlers
Both sources agree on why the Khoisan declined

questions.memo: The colonial source (A) blames the victims and calls it natural; the modern source (B) names the real causes. Specific evidence beats vague blame.

questions.question: Why is sugar a useful example for understanding the whole Atlantic World?
options: Its production tied together African labour, American land, and European capital and markets
It was grown only in Europe
It had no connection to slavery
It was never traded across the ocean
questions.expected: Its production tied together African labour, American land, and European capital and markets
questions.memo: Following sugar links the continents: enslaved Africans grew it on American plantations, European money financed it and European markets consumed it. One commodity reveals the whole system.

questions.question: What distinct hardship did many enslaved WOMEN face in addition to field labour?
options: Sexual violence and the loss of children sold away from them
questions.expected: Sexual violence and the loss of children sold away from them
questions.memo: Enslaved women endured field labour AND gender-specific abuse: sexual violence, and the anguish of children being sold away. This is why the experience is called gendered.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The destruction of the Khoisan and Native Americans was caused by colonisation, not natural decline.'
questions.thesis: The destruction of the Khoisan and Native Americans was caused by colonisation, not natural decline.

pool.text: Settlers seized the land and cattle these peoples depended on to live
Imported diseases like smallpox killed thousands who had no immunity
Colonial forces waged war and raids against communities that resisted
The Cape has a Mediterranean climate
Native Americans lived across a large continent
Some deaths came from diseases that spread unintentionally

questions.memo: Land seizure (e1), disease (e2) and war (e3) were all consequences of colonisation. e6 is a fair counter — some disease spread was unintended — but it still arrived with the colonisers.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why the enslaved experience is described as 'gendered'.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why the enslaved experience is described as 'gendered'.

options.text: Enslaved women and men did not have identical experiences
Every enslaved person had exactly the same experience
Only men were ever enslaved
Enslaved women did field labour but also faced sexual violence and the loss of children sold away from them
Women and men both crossed the Atlantic
Plantations grew sugar
Because their suffering took distinct forms, we cannot understand slavery by looking at men's experience alone
Because gender made no difference under slavery
Because women were exempt from hard labour

questions.memo: Claim (not identical) + evidence (field labour plus sexual violence and lost children) + explanation (men's experience alone is incomplete) explains 'gendered'.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on the story of sugar.

source_a.text: Sugar was a sweet luxury that brought pleasure to European tables and harmed no one.
source_a.provenance: Advertisement for a sugar merchant, 18th century

source_b.text: Every spoonful rested on a chain of suffering: African capture, the Middle Passage, and lives worked to death on Caribbean plantations.

statements.text: Sugar is presented as a harmless luxury
Sugar is linked to a chain of suffering across the Atlantic
African capture and the Middle Passage are named as part of the cost
Sugar is said to have 'harmed no one'
Both sources tell the same story about sugar

questions.memo: The advertisement (A) sells sugar as innocent pleasure; the historian (B) follows the chain of suffering behind it. The sweet product hid a brutal system.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Following sugar reveals how the whole Atlantic World was connected.'
questions.thesis: Following sugar reveals how the whole Atlantic World was connected.

pool.text: Sugar was grown by enslaved Africans on plantations in the Americas
European capital financed the plantations and European markets consumed the sugar
The demand for sugar drove the trade that carried millions of Africans across the ocean
Sugar dissolves in water
Sugar can be white or brown
Other crops like tobacco and cotton were also part of the system

questions.memo: Grown by enslaved Africans (e1), financed and consumed in Europe (e2), driving the slave trade (e3) — sugar ties the regions together. e6 is true but widens the point rather than supporting this specific thesis.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why historians call the destruction of Indigenous peoples in this period 'genocide'.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why historians call the destruction of Indigenous peoples 'genocide'.

options.text: The deliberate and large-scale destruction of whole peoples is what 'genocide' names
Genocide just means people moving to new towns
Nothing serious happened to Indigenous peoples
War, land dispossession and imported disease destroyed Native American and Khoisan societies on a vast scale
The colonies grew sugar
Ships sailed the Atlantic
Because colonisation caused destruction of this scale and kind, the word genocide fits even where killing was not the only method
Because the destruction was small and accidental
Because Indigenous peoples were unharmed

questions.memo: Claim (large-scale destruction of peoples = genocide) + evidence (war, dispossession, disease on a vast scale) + explanation (the word fits the scale and cause) makes the case.

questions.question: Compare these two views on the human cost of the Atlantic World.

source_a.text: The growth of Atlantic trade was a triumph of commerce that lifted nations to prosperity.

source_b.text: That prosperity was built on the genocide of Indigenous peoples and the enslavement of millions of Africans.

statements.text: Atlantic trade is celebrated purely as a commercial triumph
The prosperity is tied to genocide and enslavement
The human cost is named directly
The trade is described only as lifting nations to prosperity
Both sources weigh the human cost the same way

questions.memo: Source A counts only the profit; Source B counts the human cost behind it. A full history must hold both — the wealth AND the suffering that produced it.

HIS.G11.T2.HAITI.A1.title: Saint-Domingue: the richest slave colony, and everyday resistance
HIS.G11.T2.HAITI.A1.description: Haiti as French Saint-Domingue, the pinnacle of the Atlantic slave system; the crushing mortality rate; everyday resistance; enslaved people carving out spaces of autonomy.
HIS.G11.T2.HAITI.A1.strand: T2 — Slavery, Slave Resistance and the Haitian Revolution
HIS.G11.T2.HAITI.A1.caps_topic: Slavery, Slave Resistance and the Haitian Revolution
HIS.G11.T2.HAITI.A1.recovery_strategy: Saint-Domingue was the RICHEST plantation colony in the Americas — the top of the whole Atlantic slave system. And resistance did not start with the revolution: enslaved people resisted EVERY DAY by escaping, burning crops, feigning illness, working slowly, and farming their own plots. Those small spaces of autonomy are where the idea of freedom grew.

questions.question: Before the revolution, Haiti was a colony of which European country, under the name Saint-Domingue?
questions.memo: Haiti was the French colony of Saint-Domingue. Its wealth and its slave system were French.

questions.question: True or false: Saint-Domingue was the richest plantation colony in the Americas.
questions.memo: Saint-Domingue was the wealthiest plantation colony of all — the pinnacle of the Atlantic slave system, producing huge quantities of sugar and coffee.

questions.question: The wealth of Saint-Domingue rested on the brutal enslavement of the _________ majority of its population.
questions.memo: The colony's riches came from the labour of the enslaved majority, who were denied all freedom — a system built on a radical refusal of rights to most people.

questions.question: Which of these was a form of EVERYDAY resistance by enslaved people, even before open revolt?
options: Working slowly, breaking tools and feigning illness
questions.expected: Working slowly, breaking tools and feigning illness
questions.memo: Everyday resistance included working slowly, feigning sickness, breaking tools, and escaping. These quiet acts of defiance went on long before the revolution.

questions.question: True or false: Enslaved people did nothing to resist until the revolution suddenly broke out.
questions.memo: Resistance was constant beforehand — escaping, sabotage, feigning illness, and farming their own plots. The revolution grew out of this long history of resistance.

questions.question: Many enslaved people cultivated small _________ of land and sold produce at local markets, creating spaces of autonomy.
questions.memo: By farming small plots and selling at market, enslaved people carved out spaces of economic, cultural and intellectual freedom — the seedbed of the revolution.

questions.question: Sort each act by whether it is EVERYDAY resistance or OPEN/ARMED revolt.

items.text: Working slowly on purpose
Feigning sickness to avoid labour
Taking up arms against the plantation owners
Breaking tools so work cannot continue
A mass uprising of thousands of enslaved people
Escaping to live in the hills

questions.memo: Everyday resistance = quiet, individual defiance (slow work, feigned illness, sabotage, escape). Open revolt = collective armed action. Both are resistance.

questions.question: Why does the high death rate on Saint-Domingue's plantations matter for understanding the colony?
options: It shows the colony worked enslaved people to death and constantly imported more from Africa
It shows the colony was a healthy place to live
It shows few people lived there
It shows enslaved people were well cared for
questions.expected: It shows the colony worked enslaved people to death and constantly imported more from Africa
questions.memo: The mortality rate was so high that the colony depended on a constant flow of new captives from Africa — which is why so many enslaved people were African-born, shaping the revolution.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to describe resistance before the revolution.
questions.cloze_template: Enslaved people resisted [1], long before any uprising: they [2] crops, feigned [3], and worked slowly. By farming their own [4], they built small spaces of [5] where a vision of freedom could grow.
questions.memo: Daily resistance (burning crops, feigning sickness, slow work) and small plots created the autonomy in which the idea of freedom took root.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show enslaved people creating their own spaces of freedom within slavery.
questions.source_text: On their day of rest the enslaved tended their own garden plots, carried surplus yams and fruit to the Sunday market, and gathered after dark to share songs, news and the memory of Africa.
questions.task: Tap the phrases that show autonomy and self-organised life.

targets.phrase: tended their own garden plots
targets.reason: Growing their own food gave a measure of independence

targets.phrase: carried surplus yams and fruit to the Sunday market
targets.reason: Trading on their own account created economic autonomy

targets.phrase: gathered after dark to share songs, news and the memory of Africa
targets.reason: Cultural and intellectual life kept alive away from the masters

questions.memo: Garden plots, the Sunday market and night-time gatherings were spaces enslaved people made for themselves — economic, cultural and intellectual freedom inside a brutal system.

questions.question: Compare these two sources about Saint-Domingue.

source_a.text: Saint-Domingue is the jewel of the French empire, its plantations yielding more wealth than any colony on earth.

source_b.text: Behind that wealth lay sugar fields where the enslaved were worked to death and replaced by fresh shipments from Africa.

statements.text: Saint-Domingue is praised as the richest colony on earth
The wealth is linked to enslaved people being worked to death
Fresh captives were constantly shipped from Africa to replace the dead
The colony is called the 'jewel of the French empire'
Both sources describe the colony in the same way

questions.memo: The official (A) sees only the wealth; the historian (B) shows the human cost behind it. The 'jewel' was built on lives worked to death.

questions.question: What does it tell us that a large share of Saint-Domingue's enslaved people were born in Africa?
options: They brought African political ideas and experience that shaped the coming revolution
They had no memory of any other way of life
They had always lived on the plantation
questions.expected: They brought African political ideas and experience that shaped the coming revolution
questions.memo: Because so many were African-born (due to the high death rate and constant imports), African political thought and the memory of freedom fed directly into the revolution.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or a MYTH about Saint-Domingue before the revolution.

items.text: It was the richest plantation colony in the Americas
Enslaved people accepted their condition quietly
Enslaved people resisted daily through sabotage and escape
It was a poor, unimportant colony
Many of the enslaved were African-born
The plantations were healthy places with low death rates

questions.memo: True: richest colony, daily resistance, many African-born. Myths: quiet acceptance, an unimportant colony, healthy plantations.

questions.question: Why is everyday resistance important for understanding how the revolution became possible?
options: It kept the spirit of defiance and the idea of freedom alive until open revolt could succeed
It proves enslaved people were content
It shows resistance only began in 1791
It had no effect on later events
questions.expected: It kept the spirit of defiance and the idea of freedom alive until open revolt could succeed
questions.memo: Everyday resistance sustained a culture of defiance and a vision of freedom over many years, so that when the moment came, a mass revolution could erupt.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Resistance to slavery in Saint-Domingue began long before the revolution.'
questions.thesis: Resistance to slavery in Saint-Domingue began long before the revolution.

pool.text: Enslaved people routinely worked slowly, broke tools and feigned illness
Many escaped to form free communities in the hills
By farming their own plots and trading, they built spaces of autonomy and a vision of freedom
Saint-Domingue had a warm climate
Sugar was the main crop
The largest armed uprising only came in 1791

questions.memo: Sabotage (e1), escape (e2) and self-made autonomy (e3) all predate 1791. e6 is a fair counter — the big revolt came later — but resistance itself had long been continuous.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why Saint-Domingue is called the 'pinnacle' of the Atlantic slave system.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why Saint-Domingue is called the 'pinnacle' of the Atlantic slave system.

options.text: Saint-Domingue was the richest and most extreme slave colony of all
Saint-Domingue was a minor, poor colony
Saint-Domingue had no enslaved people
It produced more wealth than any other colony, worked by an enslaved majority driven at the highest death rates
It was an island
It belonged to France
Because it pushed the slave system to its richest and cruellest extreme, it stands as the system's high point — and its breaking point
Because the colony was peaceful and fair
Because slavery there was mild

questions.memo: Claim (richest, most extreme) + evidence (greatest wealth, highest death rates) + explanation (the system's high point and breaking point) explains 'pinnacle'.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on resistance in Saint-Domingue.

source_a.text: The slaves of this colony are docile and content, giving their masters no trouble.

source_b.text: Overseers' records complain endlessly of broken tools, burned cane, feigned illness and runaways.

statements.text: The enslaved are described as docile and content
The records show constant sabotage and escape
The source is written by a plantation owner reassuring himself
The evidence comes from overseers' own complaints
Both sources agree the enslaved resisted constantly

questions.memo: The owner (A) imagines contented slaves; the overseers' own records (B) reveal endless resistance. The masters' comfortable belief was contradicted by their own paperwork.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The spaces of autonomy enslaved people built were essential to the revolution that followed.'
questions.thesis: The spaces of autonomy enslaved people built were essential to the revolution that followed.

pool.text: Garden plots and markets gave enslaved people economic independence and networks
Night-time gatherings kept alive African culture, news and political ideas
These spaces nurtured a shared vision of freedom that could be mobilised
Saint-Domingue grew coffee as well as sugar
The island has mountains
The revolution also needed events in France to weaken colonial control

questions.memo: Economic independence (e1), cultural and political life (e2), and a shared vision of freedom (e3) grew in these spaces. e6 is a fair counter — French events mattered too — but the inner foundations were laid first.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why everyday resistance should count as real resistance, not just 'giving up'.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why everyday resistance counts as real resistance.

options.text: Everyday acts like sabotage and slow work were deliberate, risky defiance
Everyday acts were just laziness with no meaning
Only armed revolt counts as resistance
Breaking tools, feigning illness and escaping all carried severe punishment if discovered, yet enslaved people did them anyway
The weather was hot
Sugar was valuable
Choosing to defy at great personal risk shows a will to resist, even when open revolt was impossible
It shows the enslaved did not care about freedom
It shows resistance was pointless

questions.memo: Claim (deliberate, risky defiance) + evidence (severe punishment risked anyway) + explanation (a will to resist when revolt was impossible) shows everyday resistance was real.

questions.question: Compare these two views of Saint-Domingue's place in the Atlantic World.

source_a.text: It was simply one French sugar island among many, of no special importance.

source_b.text: It was the single most profitable colony on earth and the pinnacle of the whole Atlantic slave system.

statements.text: The colony is treated as ordinary and unimportant
The colony is treated as the pinnacle of the slave system
The colony is called the most profitable on earth
The colony is described as 'one among many'
Both sources rank the colony the same way

questions.memo: Source A underrates the colony; Source B places it at the very top of the slave system. Getting its importance right is the key to understanding why its revolution shook the world.

HIS.G11.T2.HAITI.A2.title: The Revolution (1791–1804): Toussaint L'Ouverture and the French link
HIS.G11.T2.HAITI.A2.description: Causes and course of the revolution; entanglement with the French Revolution, which excluded Africans; Toussaint L'Ouverture; African-born influence and women's participation; the first nation led by former slaves.
HIS.G11.T2.HAITI.A2.strand: T2 — Slavery, Slave Resistance and the Haitian Revolution
HIS.G11.T2.HAITI.A2.caps_topic: Slavery, Slave Resistance and the Haitian Revolution
HIS.G11.T2.HAITI.A2.recovery_strategy: The French Revolution's 'liberty, equality, fraternity' EXCLUDED enslaved Africans — they were not counted as fully human — so Haitians had to win freedom themselves. Anchor the facts: 1791–1804, led by Toussaint L'Ouverture, powered by African-born enslaved people (and women in combat and debate), ending with the first nation in history led by formerly enslaved people.

questions.question: In which years did the Haitian Revolution take place?
questions.memo: The Haitian Revolution ran from 1791 (the great uprising) to 1804 (independence). Anchor these dates.

questions.question: Who was the most famous leader of the Haitian Revolution?
questions.memo: Toussaint L'Ouverture was the revolution's most famous leader — a formerly enslaved man who became a brilliant general and statesman.

questions.question: The French Revolution of 1789 proclaimed liberty, equality and _________.
questions.memo: 'Liberty, equality, fraternity' was the slogan of the French Revolution — but at first it excluded enslaved Africans.

questions.question: True or false: The French Revolution's ideals of liberty and equality at first EXCLUDED enslaved Africans.
questions.memo: France's revolutionaries excluded the enslaved on the grounds that they were 'not fully human'. Haitians had to seize freedom for themselves — France did not give it.

questions.question: What was the outcome of the revolution for Haiti in 1804?
options: It became the first nation led by formerly enslaved people
It became a colony of Britain
questions.expected: It became the first nation led by formerly enslaved people
questions.memo: In 1804 Haiti became independent — the first nation in the world led by people who had themselves been enslaved.

questions.question: Many of the revolution's fighters were _________-born, bringing African political experience to the struggle.
questions.memo: A large share of the enslaved were African-born and brought African political and military experience — a powerful force in the revolution.

questions.question: Sort each statement as describing the FRENCH Revolution or the HAITIAN Revolution.

items.text: Began in 1789 in Europe
Led by formerly enslaved people like Toussaint L'Ouverture
Proclaimed liberty and equality but excluded enslaved Africans
Ended with the first nation led by former slaves (1804)
Took place on a Caribbean island
Took place in a major European country

questions.memo: French Revolution: 1789, Europe, excluded the enslaved. Haitian Revolution: Caribbean, led by former slaves, ended in 1804 independence.

questions.question: Why did enslaved Haitians have to fight for their own freedom rather than simply receiving it from revolutionary France?
options: France's promises of liberty and equality did not include enslaved Africans
France had already freed them in 1789
France had no slaves in its colonies
Haiti was never a French colony
questions.expected: France's promises of liberty and equality did not include enslaved Africans
questions.memo: France's 'rights of man' excluded the enslaved. Only by rising up could Haitians force the issue — they took freedom, they were not handed it.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to outline the revolution.
questions.cloze_template: The Haitian Revolution lasted from [1] to [2]. Its most famous leader was [3]. Although it was linked to the French Revolution, France's ideals had [4] enslaved Africans. In the end, Haiti became the first nation led by formerly [5] people.
questions.memo: 1791–1804, led by Toussaint L'Ouverture, against a France that had excluded the enslaved, ending with the first nation led by former slaves.

questions.question: Place these events in chronological order — earliest first.

items.text: The French Revolution proclaims liberty, equality, fraternity (1789)
The great enslaved uprising begins in Saint-Domingue (1791)
Toussaint L'Ouverture rises to lead the revolution
Haiti declares independence (1804)

questions.memo: 1789 in France → 1791 uprising → Toussaint's leadership → 1804 independence. The two revolutions were intertwined but Haiti went further.

questions.question: Tap the phrases showing that France's 'rights of man' were not meant to apply to enslaved Africans.
questions.source_text: All men are born free and equal in rights, declared the Assembly; yet the same deputies insisted that the colonies and their valuable slave property must remain untouched.
questions.task: Tap the phrases that reveal the exclusion of the enslaved.

targets.phrase: All men are born free and equal in rights
targets.reason: The grand promise that was not extended to the enslaved

targets.phrase: the colonies and their valuable slave property must remain untouched

questions.memo: The same Assembly that proclaimed universal rights protected 'slave property'. The promise and the exclusion sat side by side — which is why Haitians had to act.

questions.question: What role did women play in the Haitian Revolution?
options: They took part in both military combat and political debate
They were not involved at all
They only watched from a distance
questions.expected: They took part in both military combat and political debate
questions.memo: African and Haitian women participated in military combat and in political debate — they were active makers of the revolution, not bystanders.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on the French Revolution and slavery.

source_a.text: The Revolution of 1789 gave freedom to all people under French rule, slave and free alike.

source_b.text: The 1789 Declaration proclaimed equality but the National Assembly refused to abolish colonial slavery, which continued for years.

statements.text: 1789 is said to have freed everyone, enslaved and free
The Assembly refused to abolish colonial slavery in 1789
Slavery continued in the colonies for years after 1789
The source claims freedom was given to 'slave and free alike'
Both sources agree on what 1789 did for the enslaved

questions.memo: The simplified story (A) says France freed everyone; the accurate account (B) shows the Assembly protected slavery. The myth hides why Haitians had to fight.

questions.question: Why is it significant that so many fighters were African-born?
options: They brought military experience and African political ideas, strengthening the revolution
They wanted to return to slavery
questions.expected: They brought military experience and African political ideas, strengthening the revolution
questions.memo: African-born fighters carried memories of freedom, military skills and political traditions from Africa, which shaped the revolution's strength and ideas.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Haitians won their freedom themselves — France did not grant it.'
questions.thesis: Haitians won their freedom themselves; France did not grant it.

pool.text: France's 1789 Declaration excluded the enslaved and the Assembly protected colonial slavery
Freedom came only after a thirteen-year armed struggle led by the enslaved themselves
France under Napoleon even tried to restore slavery, and was defeated
Haiti is a Caribbean island
The French Revolution had a famous slogan
France did briefly abolish colonial slavery in 1794 under pressure

questions.memo: Exclusion (e1), a long self-led war (e2), and defeating Napoleon's attempt to re-enslave them (e3) show Haitians won freedom themselves. e6 is a real counter — the 1794 abolition under pressure — but it was forced by the revolt and later reversed.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining the relationship between the French and Haitian revolutions.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining the relationship between the French and Haitian revolutions.

options.text: The Haitian Revolution was inspired by the French but went further than it
The two revolutions had nothing to do with each other
The French Revolution freed Haiti directly
France proclaimed liberty and equality but excluded the enslaved, so Haitians fought to extend those ideals to themselves
Both events happened in the same decade
Both involved a lot of people
By demanding freedom for the enslaved, Haiti realised the promise of liberty more fully than France itself had
Haiti simply copied France exactly
The French Revolution had no ideals

questions.memo: Claim (inspired by but went further) + evidence (France excluded the enslaved, Haitians fought to be included) + explanation (Haiti realised liberty more fully) captures the relationship.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on Toussaint L'Ouverture.

source_a.text: A dangerous brigand who led the slaves into bloody rebellion against their lawful masters.

source_b.text: A formerly enslaved man of remarkable military and political genius who led his people toward freedom.

statements.text: Toussaint is condemned as a dangerous brigand
Toussaint is praised as a man of genius leading his people to freedom
The source is written by a planter who lost his slaves
The source recognises Toussaint's former enslavement and his leadership
Both sources judge Toussaint the same way

questions.memo: The planter (A), who lost his property, calls Toussaint a brigand; the biographer (B) recognises his genius. The viewpoint of the writer shapes the judgement.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Enslaved people themselves, including African-born fighters and women, were the makers of the Haitian Revolution.'
questions.thesis: Enslaved people themselves, including African-born fighters and women, were the makers of the Haitian Revolution.

pool.text: The revolution was led by formerly enslaved people such as Toussaint L'Ouverture
African-born fighters brought military experience and political ideas to the struggle
Women took part in both combat and political debate
The island produced a great deal of sugar
France is in Europe
Events in France also helped by weakening colonial authority

questions.memo: Led by former slaves (e1), powered by African-born fighters (e2) and women (e3). e6 is a fair counter — French events helped — but the enslaved were the agents.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why 1804 was a turning point in world history.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why 1804 was a turning point in world history.

options.text: 1804 produced the first nation in the world led by formerly enslaved people
1804 was the year France was founded
1804 had no lasting importance
After thirteen years of struggle, enslaved Haitians defeated their masters and a European army to win independence
Haiti grew coffee
The island is mountainous
For the first time, people who had been enslaved governed their own free nation, proving the slave system could be overthrown
It made no difference to enslaved people elsewhere
It restored slavery across the Americas

questions.memo: Claim (first nation led by former slaves) + evidence (defeated masters and a European army after 13 years) + explanation (proved slavery could be overthrown) shows why 1804 was a turning point.

questions.question: Compare these two views of who deserves credit for the end of slavery in Haiti.

source_a.text: It was the enlightened generosity of the French nation that lifted the chains of slavery.

source_b.text: The enslaved of Saint-Domingue won their own freedom by force of arms, against France's repeated attempts to keep or restore slavery.

statements.text: Credit is given to French generosity
Credit is given to the enslaved who fought for themselves
France is said to have tried to keep or restore slavery
France is praised for 'lifting the chains of slavery'
Both sources give the same credit

questions.memo: Source A flatters France; Source B records that the enslaved freed themselves against French resistance. The 'generous France' story erases the people who actually won the freedom.

HIS.G11.T2.HAITI.A3.title: A universal freedom — and the price Haiti paid
HIS.G11.T2.HAITI.A3.description: Haiti's universal idea of freedom going beyond the American and French revolutions; the fear it caused; France and the US's hostile response and the crippling indemnity; influence on anti-slavery and anti-colonial struggles.
HIS.G11.T2.HAITI.A3.strand: T2 — Slavery, Slave Resistance and the Haitian Revolution
HIS.G11.T2.HAITI.A3.caps_topic: Slavery, Slave Resistance and the Haitian Revolution
HIS.G11.T2.HAITI.A3.recovery_strategy: Haiti went FURTHER than France or America: it said freedom must include EVERYONE, including Black slaves. For that it was PUNISHED, not rewarded — France forced a crushing indemnity and the US feared the example it set. But the idea spread: Haiti inspired anti-slavery and anti-colonial struggles across the Caribbean and Africa for generations.

questions.question: What made Haiti's idea of freedom more radical than the American and French revolutions?
options: It insisted that freedom and equality must include enslaved Black people
It applied only to wealthy landowners
questions.expected: It insisted that freedom and equality must include enslaved Black people
questions.memo: America and France proclaimed liberty but kept slavery. Haiti advanced a UNIVERSAL freedom — it had to include the emancipation of Black slaves. That was the most radical claim of the age.

questions.question: True or false: After winning independence, Haiti was welcomed and rewarded by France and the United States.
questions.memo: Haiti was punished, not rewarded. France demanded a crippling indemnity, and the US — a slave-owning society — feared and shunned the example Haiti set.

questions.question: France forced Haiti to pay a huge sum of money, called an _________, as the price of recognising its independence.
questions.memo: France demanded a massive indemnity (in effect, payment for the 'lost property' of the freed slaves), crippling Haiti's economy for generations.

questions.question: Why did slave owners in the United States fear the Haitian Revolution?
options: It showed enslaved people could overthrow their masters and win
It had no effect on them
It strengthened slavery in the US
questions.expected: It showed enslaved people could overthrow their masters and win
questions.memo: Haiti proved that an enslaved people could defeat their masters and a European army. US slave owners feared this example would inspire their own enslaved people.

questions.question: True or false: The Haitian Revolution inspired anti-slavery and anti-colonial struggles elsewhere.
questions.memo: Haiti became a beacon: it inspired enslaved people, abolitionists and later anti-colonial movements in the Caribbean and across Africa.

questions.question: Haiti's idea that no one should be a slave was a _________ conception of freedom — it applied to everyone.
questions.memo: A universal conception of freedom means it applies to all human beings without exception — the principle Haiti advanced and the American and French revolutions had not.

questions.question: Sort each statement as a way Haiti was PUNISHED for its freedom or a way Haiti INSPIRED others.

items.text: France demanded a crippling indemnity
Enslaved people elsewhere took hope from Haiti's victory
The US refused to recognise Haiti for decades
Anti-colonial movements in Africa later looked to Haiti's example
Haiti was diplomatically isolated and trade was restricted
Abolitionists pointed to Haiti to argue slavery could end

questions.memo: Punished: the indemnity, US non-recognition, isolation. Inspired: hope for the enslaved, later anti-colonial movements, abolitionist arguments.

questions.question: Why is it a contradiction that France demanded payment from Haiti for the freed slaves?
options: It treated freed human beings as lost property to be paid for
It gave Haiti too much money
It freed even more enslaved people
It had nothing to do with slavery
questions.expected: It treated freed human beings as lost property to be paid for
questions.memo: The indemnity, in effect, made Haiti pay France for the 'property' it had lost — the people themselves. Charging the formerly enslaved for their own freedom exposed the cruelty of the slave system's logic.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to describe Haiti's place in history.
questions.cloze_template: Haiti advanced a [1] idea of freedom that included the enslaved. For this it was [2], not rewarded: France demanded a crippling [3] and the United States refused [4] for decades. Yet Haiti [5] anti-slavery and anti-colonial struggles around the world.
questions.memo: Universal freedom → punished by indemnity and non-recognition → yet inspired struggles worldwide. That is Haiti's paradox.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show the fear Haiti's revolution caused among slave-owning powers.
questions.source_text: News of the black republic spread terror through the plantations of the South; planters spoke of a contagion of revolt, and governments resolved to starve the new nation of trade and recognition.
questions.task: Tap the phrases that reveal fear and the wish to isolate Haiti.

targets.phrase: spread terror through the plantations of the South
targets.reason: Shows slave owners' fear of a similar revolt

targets.phrase: a contagion of revolt
targets.reason: Treats Haiti's example as a dangerous, spreading threat

targets.phrase: starve the new nation of trade and recognition
targets.reason: The decision to isolate and punish Haiti

questions.memo: 'Terror', 'contagion of revolt', and the plan to 'starve' Haiti of trade and recognition all show how the example of a free black republic frightened slave-owning powers.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on how the world responded to Haiti's independence.

source_a.text: The free nations rejoiced and welcomed Haiti warmly into the family of independent states.

source_b.text: France imposed a ruinous indemnity and the United States withheld recognition for nearly sixty years.

statements.text: Haiti was warmly welcomed by other nations
France imposed a ruinous indemnity on Haiti
The US withheld recognition for decades
The nations are said to have 'rejoiced' at Haiti's freedom
Both sources describe the same response

questions.memo: The romantic version (A) imagines a warm welcome; the record (B) shows indemnity and decades of non-recognition. Haiti was punished, not embraced.

questions.question: How did the crippling indemnity affect Haiti over the long term?
options: It drained the economy for generations, keeping the new nation poor
It made Haiti the richest country in the Americas
It was quickly cancelled by France
questions.expected: It drained the economy for generations, keeping the new nation poor
questions.memo: Repaying the indemnity (and the loans taken to pay it) drained Haiti's resources for over a century — a major reason for its long-term poverty.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or a MYTH about Haiti after independence.

items.text: France forced Haiti to pay an indemnity
Haiti was warmly welcomed by all nations
The US refused recognition for decades
Haiti's example had no influence anywhere
Haiti inspired enslaved and colonised people elsewhere
Independence made Haiti instantly rich

questions.memo: True: the indemnity, US non-recognition, Haiti's inspiring example. Myths: a warm welcome, no influence, instant wealth.

questions.question: In what way did Haiti's revolution challenge the whole Atlantic slave system?
options: It turned the most profitable slave colony into a free nation that rejected slavery
It had no effect on other colonies
questions.expected: It turned the most profitable slave colony into a free nation that rejected slavery
questions.memo: By overthrowing slavery in the system's most valuable colony and founding a nation on its rejection, Haiti struck at the heart of the Atlantic slave system itself.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Haiti advanced a more universal idea of freedom than the American or French revolutions.'
questions.thesis: Haiti advanced a more universal idea of freedom than the American or French revolutions.

The American and French revolutions did spread important ideas of rights

Because Haiti had done nothing of importance

questions.memo: Claim (punished because it threatened slavery) + evidence (indemnity, non-recognition) + explanation (isolate and bankrupt the threat) explains the punishment.

questions.thesis: Haiti's revolution had a global impact, despite efforts to isolate it.

questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why the indemnity was deeply unjust.

source_a.text: The true birth of human rights lies in the American and French declarations alone.
