questions.memo: Source A leaves Haiti out of the human-rights story; Source B places it at the centre as the revolution that demanded rights for everyone. Including Haiti changes how we understand where universal rights began.

HIS.G11.T3.CENTRAL.A1.title: Why larger, centralised states emerged
HIS.G11.T3.CENTRAL.A1.description: The shift from small chiefdoms to larger centralised kingdoms in the late 1700s and early 1800s; the combination of population growth, drought, trade and European pressure; the historiographical debate; the trade-off with democratic features.
HIS.G11.T3.CENTRAL.A1.strand: T3 — Political Centralisation & African Kingdoms in Southern Africa
HIS.G11.T3.CENTRAL.A1.caps_topic: Political Centralisation and African kingdoms in southern Africa before the nineteenth century
HIS.G11.T3.CENTRAL.A1.recovery_strategy: MANY factors stacked up — population growth, drought, long-distance trade, and pressure from European settlement to the south. No single cause, and no single great man. And centralisation had a COST: bigger, stronger kingdoms also became more hierarchical and coercive, losing some of the consultative, democratic features (like the imbizo) of the smaller societies they replaced.

questions.question: In which period did larger, more centralised kingdoms emerge in southern Africa?
questions.memo: The shift from small chiefdoms to large centralised kingdoms happened in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.

questions.question: True or false: Centralisation in southern Africa had several causes, not just one.
questions.memo: Population growth, drought, long-distance trade and pressure from European settlement all combined. No single cause explains it.

questions.question: A period of severe _________ put pressure on land and cattle, helping drive the formation of larger kingdoms.
questions.memo: Climatic change, especially drought, strained resources and pushed societies toward larger, more organised states that could control land and cattle.

questions.question: Which of these was NOT one of the main causes of centralisation in southern Africa?
options: The arrival of railways and electricity
Pressure from European settlement to the south
questions.expected: The arrival of railways and electricity
questions.memo: Railways and electricity came much later. The real causes were population growth, drought, trade, and pressure from European settlement.

questions.question: True or false: Becoming a larger, centralised kingdom improved every aspect of these societies and had no downsides.
questions.memo: Centralisation brought military strength but also made rule more hierarchical and coercive, eroding consultative, democratic features like the imbizo.

questions.question: As kingdoms centralised, power became more _________ — concentrated at the top, under the king.
questions.memo: Centralisation made political structures more hierarchical: power moved up to the king, away from the wider community.

questions.question: Sort each item as a CAUSE of centralisation or a CONSEQUENCE of it.

items.text: Growing population competing for land
Drought straining grazing and crops
More hierarchical, top-down rule
Long-distance trade bringing new wealth
The weakening of consultative bodies like the imbizo
Larger standing armies under the king

questions.memo: Causes: population, drought, trade, European pressure. Consequences: hierarchy, weaker consultation, standing armies.

questions.question: Why do historians warn against explaining centralisation by 'one great leader' alone?
options: Broad forces like population, drought and trade were already pushing societies toward larger states
Because no leaders existed at the time
Because leaders had no influence whatsoever
questions.expected: Broad forces like population, drought and trade were already pushing societies toward larger states
questions.memo: Leaders like Shaka mattered, but they acted within deeper forces — population pressure, drought, trade — that were reshaping society. Crediting one man alone misses the bigger picture.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to explain the rise of centralised kingdoms.
questions.cloze_template: In the late [1] and early [2], several forces combined: a growing [3], severe drought, long-distance [4], and pressure from European settlement. The result was larger, more centralised kingdoms in which power became more [5].
questions.memo: Late 1700s–early 1800s; population, drought, trade and European pressure; the outcome was more hierarchical, centralised rule.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show this writer crediting centralisation to a SINGLE cause, ignoring the others.
questions.source_text: The mighty kingdoms of the region arose for one reason and one reason only: the sheer genius of a single great warrior-king, without whom nothing would have changed.
questions.task: Tap the phrases that wrongly reduce a complex change to one cause.

targets.phrase: for one reason and one reason only
targets.reason: Claims a single cause where many existed

targets.phrase: the sheer genius of a single great warrior-king
targets.reason: Credits one individual for a broad social change

targets.phrase: without whom nothing would have changed
targets.reason: Denies the role of population, drought and trade

questions.memo: 'One reason only', 'a single great king', 'without whom nothing would have changed' — all signs of single-cause thinking that ignores population, drought and trade.

questions.question: Compare these two explanations of why centralised kingdoms arose.

source_a.text: These great states were the work of one extraordinary king whose will reshaped the land.

source_b.text: Population growth, drought, expanding trade and pressure from the colonial frontier together pushed many societies toward centralisation.

statements.text: Centralisation is explained by one extraordinary king
Centralisation is explained by several combined forces
Drought and trade are named as causes
The change is credited to a single will reshaping the land
Both sources give the same explanation

questions.memo: Source A is single-cause 'great man' history; Source B identifies the combination of forces. Historians favour B — many causes, not one hero.

questions.question: How did long-distance trade help drive the formation of larger kingdoms?
options: Control of trade brought wealth that rulers used to build and reward larger states
Trade had no effect on politics
questions.expected: Control of trade brought wealth that rulers used to build and reward larger states
questions.memo: Rulers who controlled long-distance trade gained wealth (in goods and cattle) to attract followers, reward warriors and build power — feeding centralisation.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or a MYTH about centralisation in southern Africa.

items.text: Several forces combined to drive centralisation
Centralisation was caused by one great leader alone
Centralisation made rule more hierarchical
Centralisation improved every part of society with no cost
Drought and population growth were among the causes
There were no organised societies before centralisation

questions.memo: True: many causes, more hierarchy, drought and population among the causes. Myths: one great leader, no costs, no prior societies.

questions.question: What does the word 'imbizo' refer to in these societies?
options: A public gathering where the community could be consulted
questions.expected: A public gathering where the community could be consulted
questions.memo: The imbizo was a public gathering for consultation — a democratic feature of smaller societies that centralisation tended to weaken.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Centralisation in southern Africa had many causes, not a single one.'
questions.thesis: Centralisation in southern Africa had many causes, not a single one.

pool.text: Growing population increased competition for land and cattle
Drought strained resources and pushed societies to organise
Long-distance trade and pressure from European settlement reshaped the region
Southern Africa has a varied landscape
Cattle are large animals
Strong individual leaders did play an important role

questions.memo: Population (e1), drought (e2), trade and European pressure (e3) all contributed. e6 is a fair counter — leaders mattered — but they worked within these broader forces.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining the trade-off that came with centralisation.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining the trade-off that came with centralisation.

options.text: Centralisation brought strength but cost some of the older democratic features
Centralisation had only benefits
Centralisation made societies weaker in every way
Larger kingdoms gained powerful armies but rule became more hierarchical and consultative bodies like the imbizo lost influence
The kingdoms kept cattle
Southern Africa is large
Power concentrated in the king brought military strength but reduced the say ordinary people had once held
There was no cost to becoming centralised
Centralisation gave everyone more power

questions.memo: Claim (strength at a cost) + evidence (armies up, imbizo down) + explanation (power to the king, less say for the people) captures the trade-off.

questions.question: Compare these two views on the consequences of centralisation.

source_a.text: The rise of the great kingdoms was pure progress, lifting scattered tribes into mighty, ordered nations.

source_b.text: As power gathered around the king, the old consultative gatherings lost their voice and rule grew more coercive.

statements.text: Centralisation is described as pure progress
Centralisation is shown to weaken consultation and increase coercion
The old consultative gatherings are said to lose their voice
Scattered tribes are said to be 'lifted' into mighty nations
Both sources weigh centralisation the same way

questions.memo: Source A sees only progress; Source B records the democratic cost. A balanced view holds both the new strength and the lost consultation.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Centralisation strengthened these kingdoms but weakened their democratic features.'
questions.thesis: Centralisation strengthened these kingdoms but weakened their democratic features.

pool.text: Centralised kingdoms could raise large standing armies and resist their rivals
Power concentrated in the king rather than being shared with the community
Consultative gatherings such as the imbizo lost their former influence
The kingdoms were located in southern Africa
Kings wore distinctive dress
Some kings still consulted advisers and councils

questions.memo: Military strength (e1), power concentrated in the king (e2), weakened imbizo (e3). e6 is a fair counter — some consultation survived — but its influence shrank.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why 'great man' history gives an incomplete picture of centralisation.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why 'great man' history is incomplete here.

options.text: Crediting one leader alone hides the deeper forces driving centralisation
One leader explains everything that happened
Leaders had no role at all
Population growth, drought, trade and colonial pressure were reshaping many societies at once, not just one kingdom
Kings were tall
The region has rivers
Because the same broad forces produced centralisation in several places, a full explanation must include them alongside individual leaders
Because individual leaders are the only thing that ever matters
Because nothing caused centralisation

questions.memo: Claim (one leader hides deeper forces) + evidence (broad forces reshaping many societies) + explanation (a full account needs both) shows why 'great man' history is incomplete.

questions.question: Compare these two interpretations historians offer for centralisation.

source_a.text: Everything flowed from the disruption caused by one expanding kingdom and its wars.

source_b.text: Environmental, economic and external pressures across the whole region created the conditions for many kingdoms to centralise.

statements.text: The cause is traced to one kingdom's wars
The cause is traced to region-wide environmental, economic and external pressures
The explanation covers many kingdoms, not one
Everything is said to 'flow from' a single expanding kingdom
Both interpretations are identical

questions.memo: The older view (A) centres one kingdom's wars; the modern view (B) sees region-wide forces. This is a live historiographical debate — and B reflects current thinking.

HIS.G11.T3.CENTRAL.A2.title: Two models of power: the Bapedi and the amaZulu
HIS.G11.T3.CENTRAL.A2.description: Bapedi/Maroteng consolidation through royal marriage, ilobolo, the Batseta system and local mephato regiments; amaZulu consolidation through military innovation and the permanent amabutho in amakhanda military towns.
HIS.G11.T3.CENTRAL.A2.strand: T3 — Political Centralisation & African Kingdoms in Southern Africa
HIS.G11.T3.CENTRAL.A2.caps_topic: Political Centralisation and African kingdoms in southern Africa before the nineteenth century
HIS.G11.T3.CENTRAL.A2.recovery_strategy: Two routes to power. BAPEDI/Maroteng = consolidation by MARRIAGE and DIPLOMACY (principal wives from the Maroteng, ilobolo, the Batseta monitors); their mephato stayed local and gathered only when called. ZULU = consolidation by MILITARY system (the amabutho lived for years in amakhanda barracks under the king, marrying only in their forties). The Pedi regiments were local and temporary; the Zulu regiments were permanent and centralised.

questions.question: The Bapedi Kingdom was built up by the ruling group known as the:
questions.memo: The Maroteng were the ruling lineage of the Bapedi Kingdom in today's Limpopo, consolidating power from the 1600s onward.

questions.question: The amaZulu Kingdom was centralised under the leadership of:
questions.memo: Shaka kaSenzangakhona built the amaZulu into a powerful centralised kingdom through military and political innovation.

questions.question: The Zulu permanent age-regiments, housed in military towns, were called _________.
questions.memo: The amabutho were Shaka's standing age-regiments. (The amakhanda were the military towns where they lived.)

questions.question: True or false: The Bapedi consolidated power partly through royal marriages, requiring subordinate chiefdoms to take a principal wife from the Maroteng.
questions.memo: By insisting subordinate chiefdoms take their principal (heir-bearing) wife from the Maroteng, the Bapedi tied other chiefdoms to the ruling line through marriage and bridewealth.

questions.question: Bridewealth, used by the Maroteng to build alliances, is known as magadi or _________.
questions.memo: Magadi/ilobolo (bridewealth) flowed to the Maroteng through royal marriages, building wealth and binding chiefdoms to the ruling lineage.

questions.question: True or false: The Zulu amabutho lived for years in military towns directly under the king's authority.
questions.memo: Young men left their villages to live for years in the amakhanda (military towns), under the king rather than their local chiefs, and could marry only in their forties.

questions.question: Sort each feature as belonging to the BAPEDI (Maroteng) or the AMAZULU way of building power.

items.text: Royal marriages tying chiefdoms to the ruling line
Permanent age-regiments (amabutho) living in military towns
The Batseta system monitoring subordinate chiefdoms
Men leaving their villages for years under the king
Mephato regiments that gathered only when summoned
Military innovations like the stabbing spear and drilling

questions.memo: Bapedi: marriage, ilobolo, Batseta, local mephato. Zulu: military innovation, permanent amabutho in amakhanda under the king.

questions.question: What was the key difference between the Pedi mephato and the Zulu amabutho?
options: Mephato were local and gathered only when called; amabutho were permanent and lived under the king
Mephato were larger than the whole Zulu army
questions.expected: Mephato were local and gathered only when called; amabutho were permanent and lived under the king
questions.memo: The crucial difference: Pedi mephato stayed in their chiefdoms and assembled only when summoned; Zulu amabutho were permanent, living for years in military towns directly under the king's control.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to compare the two kingdoms.
questions.cloze_template: The Bapedi built power through royal [1] and the [2] system that watched over subordinate chiefdoms; their [3] regiments gathered only when called. The amaZulu built power through military innovation and the permanent [4], who lived for years in military towns under the [5].
questions.memo: Bapedi: marriages, Batseta, local mephato. Zulu: permanent amabutho under the king. Two different routes to centralised power.

questions.question: The Batseta system allowed the Maroteng to:
options: Monitor and stay informed about the affairs of subordinate chiefdoms
questions.expected: Monitor and stay informed about the affairs of subordinate chiefdoms
questions.memo: The Batseta were like ambassadors or monitors stationed to keep the Maroteng informed about each subordinate chiefdom — a tool of political control.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that describe how the Zulu amabutho system concentrated power in the KING.
questions.source_text: Young men of like age were gathered from every chiefdom into regiments housed in the king's military towns, where they served him directly for years, far from their fathers and local chiefs, and could not marry until released.
questions.task: Tap the phrases showing the king's direct control over the regiments.

targets.reason: Cuts across local loyalties to unify under the king

targets.phrase: served him directly for years
targets.reason: Loyalty owed to the king, not local chiefs

targets.phrase: far from their fathers and local chiefs
targets.reason: Removes the influence of local authority

targets.phrase: could not marry until released
targets.reason: The king controlled even their personal lives

questions.memo: Drawn from all chiefdoms, serving the king directly, removed from local chiefs, unable to marry — every detail shifts loyalty and control to the king.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on how the Bapedi and amaZulu built power.

source_a.text: The Maroteng wove subordinate chiefdoms into the kingdom through marriage alliances and bridewealth, monitored by their Batseta.

source_b.text: Shaka drew young men from every chiefdom into permanent regiments in his military towns, owing loyalty to him alone.

statements.text: Power is built through marriage alliances and monitoring
Power is built through permanent regiments loyal to the king
The Batseta are used to monitor subordinate chiefdoms
Young men serve the king in military towns
Both kingdoms used identical methods

questions.memo: Bapedi (A): marriage, bridewealth, Batseta. Zulu (B): permanent regiments under the king. Different tools, same goal of centralised power.

questions.question: Why is it wrong to say Shaka 'invented' organised statehood in southern Africa?
options: Organised chiefdoms and kingdoms, like the Bapedi, already existed before and alongside the Zulu
Because the Zulu had no state at all
Because no states existed anywhere in Africa
questions.expected: Organised chiefdoms and kingdoms, like the Bapedi, already existed before and alongside the Zulu
questions.memo: The Bapedi and others were organised states before and during Shaka's rise. Shaka innovated powerfully, but he built on a region already full of organised polities.

questions.question: Which military innovations are associated with Shaka's amaZulu?
options: The short stabbing spear, large shields and disciplined drilling
questions.expected: The short stabbing spear, large shields and disciplined drilling
questions.memo: Shaka's reforms included the short stabbing spear (for close combat), large shields, and disciplined drilling of the amabutho — a more effective way of war.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The Bapedi and amaZulu built power in fundamentally different ways.'
questions.thesis: The Bapedi and amaZulu built power in fundamentally different ways.

pool.text: The Bapedi tied chiefdoms to the ruling line through marriage and bridewealth
The Bapedi mephato stayed local and gathered only when summoned
The amaZulu kept permanent regiments in military towns under the king's direct control
Both kingdoms were in southern Africa
Both used cattle
Both kingdoms aimed at the same goal of centralised power

questions.memo: Marriage/diplomacy and local mephato (e1, e2) vs permanent royal regiments (e3) show the methods differed. e6 is a fair counter — the goal was the same — but the methods were not.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph comparing the Pedi mephato and the Zulu amabutho.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph comparing the mephato and the amabutho.

options.text: Both were regiments, but the amabutho were far more centralised than the mephato
The mephato and amabutho were identical
Neither had anything to do with the army
Mephato gathered locally only when called, while amabutho lived for years in the king's military towns
Both involved young men
Both existed in southern Africa
Because the amabutho served the king directly and permanently, they concentrated power in the king far more than the local mephato did
Because there was no real difference between them
Because the mephato were more centralised than the amabutho

questions.memo: Claim (both regiments, amabutho more centralised) + evidence (local-when-called vs permanent royal towns) + explanation (amabutho concentrated power in the king) makes the comparison.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on the regiment systems.

source_a.text: Among the Bapedi, the young men trained near home and returned to their families, assembling only at the chief's call.

source_b.text: In Shaka's kingdom the regiments were permanent, the young men living in royal barracks for years and marrying only late in life.

statements.text: The regiments trained near home and returned to their families
The regiments were permanent and lived in royal barracks
Young men married only late in life
The regiments assembled only at the chief's call
Both systems organised their regiments identically

questions.memo: The Bapedi system (A) was local and temporary; the Zulu system (B) was permanent and centralised. The contrast is the heart of this comparison.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The Zulu amabutho system concentrated power in the king more than the Bapedi system did.'
questions.thesis: The Zulu amabutho system concentrated power in the king more than the Bapedi system did.

pool.text: Amabutho were drawn from every chiefdom and owed loyalty to the king, not to local chiefs
They lived permanently in the king's military towns for years
The king even controlled when they could marry
The Bapedi lived in today's Limpopo
Both kingdoms kept cattle
The Bapedi Batseta system also gave the ruler real control over chiefdoms

questions.memo: Loyalty to the king (e1), permanent royal service (e2), control of marriage (e3) show greater concentration. e6 is a fair counter — the Bapedi had real control too — but it worked through chiefdoms, not direct royal command.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why both the Bapedi and amaZulu count as 'centralised' kingdoms despite their different methods.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why both count as centralised kingdoms.

options.text: Both used their methods to bring many chiefdoms under one ruling authority
Neither kingdom was actually centralised
Only the amaZulu ever had a ruler
The Bapedi bound chiefdoms through marriage and monitoring, while the amaZulu bound men directly to the king through permanent regiments
Both kingdoms had names
Both lay south of the equator
Different tools served the same end: pulling formerly separate chiefdoms under a single central authority
Centralisation means staying completely separate
The two had nothing in common at all

questions.memo: Claim (both brought chiefdoms under one authority) + evidence (marriage/monitoring vs permanent regiments) + explanation (different tools, same centralising end) explains why both count.

questions.question: Compare these two views on Shaka's place in southern African history.

source_a.text: Shaka conjured a nation out of nothing, the sole creator of statehood in a land of scattered savages.

source_b.text: Shaka was a gifted innovator who reorganised an already complex region of established chiefdoms and kingdoms.

statements.text: Shaka is said to have created statehood from nothing
Shaka is shown reorganising an already complex region
The region is recognised as having established chiefdoms before Shaka
The land is described as full of 'scattered savages'
Both sources judge Shaka's role the same way

questions.memo: The colonial account (A) erases existing societies to glorify (and 'other') Shaka; the modern view (B) recognises the complex region he reshaped. Shaka innovated, but he did not start from nothing.

HIS.G11.T3.CENTRAL.A3.title: The cost of centralisation and the clash with Britain
HIS.G11.T3.CENTRAL.A3.description: Erosion of the imbizo and rise of authoritarian rule; encounters with British imperialism — Isandlwana, Ulundi, the Anglo-Pedi War; loss of land and sovereignty; the migrant labour system built on the old regiments.
HIS.G11.T3.CENTRAL.A3.strand: T3 — Political Centralisation & African Kingdoms in Southern Africa
HIS.G11.T3.CENTRAL.A3.caps_topic: Political Centralisation and African kingdoms in southern Africa before the nineteenth century
HIS.G11.T3.CENTRAL.A3.recovery_strategy: Centralisation came at the price of the imbizo and consultative rule — power moved up to the king. But these kingdoms RESISTED hard: the Zulu CRUSHED the British at Isandlwana (22 Jan 1879) before losing at Ulundi, and the Pedi held out until Britain brought in Swazi mercenaries. The cruel twist: the migrant labour system was later built on the same regiments these kingdoms had created.

questions.question: At which 1879 battle did the amaZulu inflict a major defeat on the British army?
questions.memo: At Isandlwana on 22 January 1879, the Zulu crushed a British force — a shocking defeat for the British Empire.

questions.question: True or false: As kingdoms centralised, consultative gatherings like the imbizo lost influence and rule became more authoritarian.
questions.memo: Centralisation concentrated power in the king. The imbizo and other consultative features weakened, and rule grew more authoritarian.

questions.question: After their victory at Isandlwana, the amaZulu were finally defeated by the British at the battle of _________.
questions.memo: The Zulu won at Isandlwana but were defeated later in 1879 at Ulundi, after which they lost their independence.

questions.question: In the Anglo-Pedi War, the British finally defeated the Bapedi only with the help of _________ mercenaries.
questions.memo: The Bapedi under Sekhukhune resisted fiercely; Britain defeated them in 1879 only by using Swazi mercenaries.

questions.question: True or false: African kingdoms offered no real resistance to British invasion.
questions.memo: They resisted fiercely. The Zulu won at Isandlwana, and the Pedi held out until Britain brought in Swazi mercenaries. Resistance was real and at times victorious.

questions.question: After their defeat, African kingdoms lost their land and their _________ — their right to govern themselves.
questions.memo: Defeat meant the loss of land and of sovereignty — the right to rule themselves — as the British dismantled independent African political power.

questions.question: Sort each statement as a COST of centralisation or an example of RESISTANCE to Britain.

items.text: The imbizo lost its influence
The Zulu victory at Isandlwana
Rule became more authoritarian
The Pedi holding out until Swazi mercenaries were used
Power concentrated in the king at the community's expense
Kingdoms fighting British invasion in 1879

questions.memo: Costs: weaker imbizo, authoritarian rule, power to the king. Resistance: Isandlwana, the Pedi stand, the wars of 1879.

questions.question: What was the 'cruel twist' in how the colonial migrant labour system began?
options: It was built on the same regiments that African kingdoms had created
It started before any African kingdoms existed
It had no connection to the defeated kingdoms
It was run by the African kings themselves
questions.expected: It was built on the same regiments that African kingdoms had created
questions.memo: After conquest, the regimental systems that had organised young men for African kings were redirected to supply migrant labour to colonial mines — turning a tool of African power into a tool of colonial exploitation.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to describe the clash with British imperialism.
questions.cloze_template: In [1] the amaZulu defeated the British at [2], but were later beaten at Ulundi. The Bapedi under Sekhukhune resisted until Britain used [3] mercenaries. In the end the kingdoms lost their land and their [4], and the regiments were redirected to supply [5] labour to the mines.
questions.memo: 1879: Isandlwana then Ulundi; Pedi beaten with Swazi mercenaries; loss of land and sovereignty; regiments redirected to migrant labour.

questions.question: Place these events in chronological order — earliest first.

items.text: The amaZulu defeat the British at Isandlwana (Jan 1879)
The British defeat the amaZulu at Ulundi (1879)
The Bapedi are defeated with the help of Swazi mercenaries (1879)
Defeated kingdoms lose land and sovereignty; migrant labour to the mines grows

questions.memo: Isandlwana (Jan 1879) → Ulundi (mid-1879) → Pedi defeat (1879) → loss of sovereignty and the rise of migrant labour.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show centralisation had eroded the community's say in government.
questions.source_text: Where once the people had gathered in open imbizo to debate the chief's decisions, now the king's word alone was law, and to question it openly was to risk death.

the king's word alone was law

targets.reason: Shows rule had become coercive and authoritarian

questions.memo: The imbizo gave way to the king's sole word, backed by fear. That shift from consultation to coercion was the democratic cost of centralisation.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on the wars of 1879.

source_a.text: The savage tribes were swiftly and easily subdued by British arms, offering little real resistance.

source_b.text: At Isandlwana a British army was annihilated, and the Pedi were broken only after months of fighting and the use of Swazi allies.

questions.memo: The imperial story (A) belittles the resistance; the evidence (B) shows fierce, sometimes victorious resistance. The 'easily subdued' claim is propaganda, not history.

questions.question: Why did Britain want to break up the centralised African kingdoms?
options: Their strength blocked British plans for a single federation of white-controlled territories
Britain admired them and wanted to protect them
The kingdoms had no land Britain wanted
Britain had no interest in southern Africa
questions.expected: Their strength blocked British plans for a single federation of white-controlled territories
questions.memo: The very centralisation that made the Zulu and Pedi strong also made them obstacles to Britain's plan for a federation of white settler territories — so Britain set out to destroy their power.

questions.question: How did the conquest of these kingdoms feed the colonial economy?
options: Defeated men, organised by the old regiment system, were funnelled into migrant labour in the mines
The kingdoms were left completely untouched
The mines closed after the wars
Africans were given ownership of the mines
questions.expected: Defeated men, organised by the old regiment system, were funnelled into migrant labour in the mines
questions.memo: With land and sovereignty gone, men who had served in regiments were pushed into migrant labour on the mines — the regimental tradition repurposed for colonial profit.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'African kingdoms mounted serious resistance to British imperialism.'
questions.thesis: African kingdoms mounted serious resistance to British imperialism.

pool.text: The amaZulu destroyed a British army at Isandlwana in January 1879
The Bapedi held out until Britain resorted to Swazi mercenaries
The centralised kingdoms' armies forced Britain into hard, costly campaigns
Southern Africa has gold and diamonds
The British wore red coats
In the end both kingdoms were defeated and lost their sovereignty

questions.memo: Isandlwana (e1), the Pedi stand (e2), costly campaigns (e3) prove serious resistance. e6 is a fair counter — they were defeated in the end — but defeat does not mean they did not resist.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining the democratic cost of centralisation.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining the democratic cost of centralisation.

options.text: Centralisation reduced the say ordinary people had in government
Centralisation gave ordinary people more power
Centralisation had no effect on government
Consultative gatherings like the imbizo lost their influence as the king's word became law

The region had good grazing
As power concentrated in the king, the older traditions of consultation and debate were pushed aside, making rule more coercive
Because everyone gained an equal vote
Because the king consulted the people more than before

questions.memo: Claim (less say for the people) + evidence (imbizo weakened, king's word law) + explanation (power to the king made rule coercive) explains the democratic cost.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on the fate of African sovereignty.

source_a.text: By bringing these lands under the Crown, Britain delivered the blessings of order and civilisation.

source_b.text: Conquest stripped African kingdoms of their land and sovereignty and drove their men into the mines as migrant labourers.

Conquest is shown stripping land and sovereignty and forcing men into the mines
Migrant labour in the mines is named as a consequence
Britain is said to deliver 'the blessings of order and civilisation'
Both sources judge the conquest the same way

questions.memo: The colonial dispatch (A) calls conquest a blessing; the historian (B) records dispossession and forced labour. The 'blessings of civilisation' framing hides the loss of land, freedom and self-rule.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The migrant labour system grew directly out of the conquest of the centralised kingdoms.'
questions.thesis: The migrant labour system grew directly out of the conquest of the centralised kingdoms.

pool.text: Conquest stripped kingdoms of the land that had supported their people
Men who had served in regiments were now directed into the mines
The regimental organisation of young men was repurposed to supply colonial labour
Gold was discovered in the region
The mines were deep underground
Some men also migrated to the mines seeking cash wages of their own accord

questions.memo: Loss of land (e1), redirection of regiment men (e2), repurposed organisation (e3) link conquest to migrant labour. e6 is a fair counter — some migration was voluntary — but conquest created the conditions for it.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why the Zulu victory at Isandlwana mattered, even though they were later defeated.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why Isandlwana mattered despite the later defeat.

options.text: Isandlwana proved a centralised African kingdom could defeat a modern European army
Isandlwana proved Africans could not fight
Isandlwana had no significance

The Zulu kept cattle
Even though Ulundi followed, Isandlwana showed the strength of centralised African states and is remembered as a major victory
The victory meant nothing because they lost later
The victory proved African armies were weak

questions.memo: Claim (a kingdom beat a modern army) + evidence (a British force annihilated, the Empire shocked) + explanation (it showed African strength and is remembered despite Ulundi) makes the case.

questions.question: Compare these two views on the legacy of the conquered kingdoms' regiments.

source_a.text: Once the tribes were pacified, their warlike ways were happily forgotten and they settled into peaceful labour.

source_b.text: The discipline of the old regiments was redirected by colonial authorities to channel young men into migrant labour on the mines.

statements.text: The men are said to have 'happily' settled into peaceful labour
The old regimental discipline was redirected into migrant labour
Colonial authorities are named as channelling men into the mines
The men's 'warlike ways' are said to be 'happily forgotten'
Both sources describe the same process the same way

questions.memo: The colonial account (A) pretends men chose peaceful labour freely; the historian (B) shows the regimental system was repurposed to force them into the mines. The comfortable story hides the coercion.

HIS.G11.T4.SCRAMBLE.A1.title: The Scramble and the Berlin Conference
HIS.G11.T4.SCRAMBLE.A1.description: The post-1880 partition of Africa; the meaning of imperialism and 'scramble'; the Berlin Conference of 1884–85 formalising conquest and drawing boundaries; the speed and coordination, with no African representation.
HIS.G11.T4.SCRAMBLE.A1.recovery_strategy: The Berlin Conference (1884–85) is where Europeans drew Africa's borders — and NO Africans were there. It is called a 'scramble' because European nations RACED and competed to grab territory after 1880, carving up the whole continent with shocking speed and coordination. This was fast and deliberate, not slow and accidental.

questions.question: In which decade did the Scramble for Africa rapidly accelerate?
questions.memo: The generation after 1880 saw the bulk of Africa partitioned and conquered by European powers at remarkable speed.

questions.question: The conference that formalised the European conquest of Africa and helped draw its borders was held in:
questions.memo: The Berlin Conference of 1884–85 set the rules for the partition of Africa and shaped its colonial boundaries.

questions.question: True or false: African leaders were invited to the Berlin Conference to help decide the continent's borders.
questions.memo: No Africans were present at Berlin. Europeans drew the borders of African lands without consulting the people who lived there.

questions.question: The violent expansion of European empires into Africa during this period is called _________.
questions.memo: Imperialism is the policy of extending a nation's power by colonising and dominating other lands — exactly what Europe did to Africa after 1880.

questions.question: Why is the period called a 'scramble'?
options: European nations competed in a rapid race to seize African territory
It happened slowly over many centuries
No country wanted any African land
questions.expected: European nations competed in a rapid race to seize African territory
questions.memo: 'Scramble' captures the rushed, competitive race between European powers to grab as much territory as possible before their rivals did.

questions.question: What was most remarkable about how Europe carved up Africa after 1880?
options: The speed, coordination and (from the European view) ease of the conquest
That it took over five hundred years
questions.expected: The speed, coordination and (from the European view) ease of the conquest
questions.memo: Within roughly a generation, almost the whole continent was partitioned — the speed and coordination were what set this period apart.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or a MYTH about the Scramble and the Berlin Conference.

items.text: The Berlin Conference was held in 1884–85
African leaders attended and agreed to the borders
The partition happened mainly after 1880, very quickly
Europe took over Africa slowly over many centuries with no rush
European powers competed to claim territory
The borders carefully followed African ethnic lines

questions.memo: True: Berlin 1884–85, rapid post-1880 partition, European competition. Myths: African attendance, slow takeover, borders following ethnic lines.

questions.question: What was the main purpose of the Berlin Conference for the European powers?
options: To set rules so they could divide Africa among themselves without going to war with each other
To end all trade with Africa
To return land to African kingdoms
questions.expected: To set rules so they could divide Africa among themselves without going to war with each other
questions.memo: Berlin was about managing European rivalry: agreeing rules for claiming African territory so the powers would not fight one another over it.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to describe the Scramble for Africa.
questions.cloze_template: After [1], European powers raced to seize African territory — a process called the [2] for Africa. At the [3] Conference of 1884–85 they set rules for partition and drew [4], with no [5] present.
questions.memo: After 1880, the Scramble; at the Berlin Conference (1884–85) Europeans drew Africa's borders with no Africans present.

questions.question: Place these events in chronological order — earliest first.

items.text: European powers begin competing for African territory (1870s)
The Berlin Conference sets the rules for partition (1884–85)
Most of Africa is conquered and occupied (by the early 1900s)

questions.memo: Competition in the 1870s → Berlin Conference 1884–85 → most of Africa occupied by the early 1900s. A single generation transformed the continent.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that reveal Africans were treated as absent or irrelevant at the Berlin Conference.
questions.source_text: Around the great map the ministers of Europe drew their lines, dividing rivers and peoples with the stroke of a pen, untroubled by the wishes of those who actually lived upon the land.
questions.task: Tap the phrases showing Africans were ignored.

targets.phrase: the ministers of Europe drew their lines
targets.reason: Only Europeans are making the decisions

targets.phrase: dividing rivers and peoples with the stroke of a pen
targets.reason: Borders imposed with no regard for what was on the ground

targets.phrase: untroubled by the wishes of those who actually lived upon the land

questions.memo: Europeans 'drew their lines', divided 'peoples with the stroke of a pen', and were 'untroubled' by Africans' wishes — Africa was carved up without its people's consent.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on the Berlin Conference.

source_a.text: The powers met in a spirit of cooperation to bring order and civilisation to a dark continent.

source_b.text: At Berlin, Europeans divided a continent they did not own, drawing borders across peoples without consulting a single African.

statements.text: The conference is praised as bringing 'order and civilisation'
The conference is shown dividing a continent without African consent
Not a single African was consulted
Africa is called a 'dark continent'
Both sources describe the conference the same way

questions.memo: The European account (A) dresses partition as a civilising mission; the modern history (B) names it as dividing a continent without consent. The 'order and civilisation' framing hides the conquest.

questions.question: What does it mean that European powers had 'coordinated' the partition?
options: They agreed rules among themselves to claim land without fighting each other
Each acted in total secret from the others
They asked Africans to coordinate it
They refused to claim any land
questions.expected: They agreed rules among themselves to claim land without fighting each other
questions.memo: Coordination meant the European powers set shared rules (as at Berlin) so they could divide Africa among themselves while avoiding war with one another.

questions.question: Before 1880, how much of Africa had Europeans already colonised?
options: Only parts, such as some coastal areas and the Cape
questions.expected: Only parts, such as some coastal areas and the Cape
questions.memo: Before 1880 Europe held only scattered parts of Africa (coastal trading areas, the Cape). The Scramble after 1880 is what rapidly seized the rest.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The Scramble for Africa was rapid and coordinated, not slow and accidental.'
questions.thesis: The Scramble for Africa was rapid and coordinated, not slow and accidental.

pool.text: Most of the continent was partitioned within roughly one generation after 1880
At the Berlin Conference the powers agreed shared rules for claiming territory
European nations competed in a deliberate race to grab land before their rivals
Africa is a very large continent
Berlin is a city in Europe
A few coastal areas had been colonised gradually before 1880

questions.memo: One generation (e1), agreed rules (e2), a deliberate race (e3) show speed and coordination. e6 is a fair counter — some earlier gradual colonisation existed — but the post-1880 scramble was fast and planned.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why it matters that no Africans were at the Berlin Conference.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why it matters that no Africans were at Berlin.

options.text: Africa's borders were imposed by outsiders without the consent of its people
Africans designed their own borders at Berlin
The borders did not matter to anyone
European ministers drew the boundaries across rivers and peoples while no African was present to object
Berlin is a large city
The conference lasted several months
Because outsiders drew the lines, the borders ignored African realities and left problems that still affect the continent
Because Africans agreed to every line
Because the borders perfectly matched African nations

questions.memo: Claim (borders imposed without consent) + evidence (Europeans drew them, no African present) + explanation (ignored African realities, lasting problems) explains why it matters.

questions.question: Compare these two views on what the Scramble was driven by.

source_a.text: Europe acted from a noble duty to civilise and uplift the peoples of Africa.

source_b.text: The powers were locked in a competitive race for territory, resources and prestige, dressed up in the language of civilisation.

statements.text: The Scramble is explained as a noble civilising duty
The Scramble is explained as a competitive race dressed up in fine language
Territory, resources and prestige are named as the real drivers
Europe is said to act from a duty to 'civilise and uplift'
Both sources give the same explanation

questions.memo: The imperial speech (A) claims a civilising duty; the historian (B) points to the real race for land and resources. The 'civilising' language was a cover for competition.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The Berlin Conference imposed European control on Africa without African consent.'
questions.thesis: The Berlin Conference imposed European control on Africa without African consent.

pool.text: No African representatives were present at the conference
European powers set rules for claiming African land among themselves
Borders were drawn across African peoples without consulting them
The conference was held in winter
Maps were used at the conference
Some European powers already had footholds in Africa before Berlin

questions.memo: No Africans present (e1), Europeans setting the rules (e2), borders drawn without consent (e3). e6 is a fair counter — earlier footholds existed — but Berlin still imposed control without African consent.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why the Scramble for Africa is described as a turning point in modern history.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why the Scramble is described as a turning point in modern history.

options.text: In about a generation, almost an entire continent was conquered and reshaped
The Scramble changed nothing of importance
The Scramble affected only Europe
After 1880, European powers partitioned and occupied most of Africa with extraordinary speed
Africa has many rivers
Europe has many countries
The borders and colonial structures created then still shape Africa today, which is why it is a turning point
Because nothing from that period survived
Because Africa was unaffected by it

questions.memo: Claim (a continent reshaped in a generation) + evidence (rapid post-1880 partition) + explanation (its borders and structures still shape Africa) explains the turning point.

questions.question: Compare these two views on the speed of the Scramble.

source_a.text: Europe's presence in Africa grew gently and gradually over many quiet centuries.

source_b.text: Although a few coastal footholds were older, the conquest of the interior happened with astonishing speed after 1880.

statements.text: European control is said to have grown gently over many centuries
The conquest of the interior is said to have happened with astonishing speed after 1880
A few older coastal footholds are acknowledged
The whole process is described as gradual and quiet
Both sources describe the same pace of change

questions.memo: Source A blurs the timeline into a gentle gradual story; Source B captures the real picture — old coastal footholds, but a sudden, rapid conquest of the interior after 1880.

HIS.G11.T4.SCRAMBLE.A2.title: Why did it happen? The competing explanations
HIS.G11.T4.SCRAMBLE.A2.description: The historiographical debate: economic, Scientific Racism/Eugenics, diplomatic, and African-dimension theories; how Europeans justified colonisation; the recognition that there is no single agreed cause.
HIS.G11.T4.SCRAMBLE.A2.recovery_strategy: Historians DISAGREE about the cause — economic, scientific racism/eugenics, diplomatic rivalry, and the African dimension are four competing explanations, not one answer. And 'scientific racism' was NOT real science: it was a pseudo-scientific ideology invented to make conquest look justified. Weighing these theories against each other is exactly what the topic asks you to do.

questions.question: How many main explanations do historians offer for why Europe partitioned Africa?
options: Several competing ones, including economic, racial, diplomatic and African-dimension theories
questions.expected: Several competing ones, including economic, racial, diplomatic and African-dimension theories
questions.memo: There is no single agreed cause. Historians weigh several explanations: economic, Scientific Racism/Eugenics, diplomatic, and the African dimension.

questions.question: The 'economic' explanation says Europe took Africa mainly for:
options: Markets, raw materials and places to invest
questions.expected: Markets, raw materials and places to invest
questions.memo: The economic theory stresses Europe's hunger for raw materials, new markets for its goods, and places to invest its capital.

questions.question: True or false: 'Scientific racism' was genuine science that proved Europeans were superior.
questions.memo: Scientific racism was pseudo-science — fake science dressed up in scientific language to justify conquest. Modern science has completely refuted it.

questions.question: The belief in improving the human race by favouring 'superior' groups, used to justify conquest, is called _________.
questions.memo: Eugenics was the pseudo-scientific idea behind 'scientific racism', used to claim Europeans were a superior race entitled to rule others.

questions.question: The 'diplomatic' explanation focuses on:
options: Rivalry between European powers and the balance of power between them
questions.expected: Rivalry between European powers and the balance of power between them
questions.memo: The diplomatic theory stresses European rivalry: each power grabbed African land partly to keep up with, and not be outdone by, its rivals.

questions.question: The 'African dimension' explanation looks at:
options: Conditions within Africa itself that shaped how the Scramble unfolded
The shape of the African coastline
The size of European armies alone
questions.expected: Conditions within Africa itself that shaped how the Scramble unfolded
questions.memo: The African-dimension theory reminds us that conditions inside Africa — its politics, economies and conflicts — also shaped how and where colonisation happened.

questions.question: Match each explanation of the Scramble to its main idea.

items.text: Europe needed raw materials and new markets
A false belief that Europeans were a superior race entitled to rule
Powers grabbed land to keep up with their rivals
Places to invest surplus capital
Pseudo-science used to justify conquest
The European balance of power

questions.memo: Economic = materials, markets, investment. Racial = pseudo-scientific superiority. Diplomatic = rivalry and balance of power.

questions.question: Why is it important to know there are several competing theories of the Scramble?
options: It shows historians weigh evidence and debate, rather than there being one simple answer
It proves history can never be known
It means all explanations are equally worthless
It means the Scramble never happened
questions.expected: It shows historians weigh evidence and debate, rather than there being one simple answer
questions.memo: Big historical events usually have several causes. Knowing the competing theories teaches you to weigh evidence rather than accept one tidy story.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to summarise the debate over the Scramble.
questions.cloze_template: Historians offer competing explanations for the Scramble. The [1] theory stresses markets and raw materials. Scientific Racism, a form of [2], claimed Europeans were superior. The [3] theory stresses rivalry between powers. The [4] dimension looks at conditions within [5] itself.
questions.memo: Economic (markets/materials), Scientific Racism (pseudo-science), diplomatic (rivalry), and the African dimension (conditions in Africa) — four competing explanations.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show this is a pseudo-scientific RACIST justification, not real science.
questions.source_text: It is the plain finding of science that the European stands at the summit of the races, and that it is his natural destiny and duty to govern the lesser, childlike peoples of the tropics.
questions.task: Tap the phrases that reveal racist pseudo-science.

targets.phrase: the European stands at the summit of the races
targets.reason: A false racial ranking presented as fact

targets.phrase: natural destiny and duty to govern
targets.reason: Dresses conquest up as a natural duty

targets.phrase: lesser, childlike peoples of the tropics
targets.reason: Dehumanising racist description to justify rule

questions.memo: Ranking 'races', claiming a 'destiny to govern', and calling others 'lesser, childlike peoples' are racist claims dressed in scientific language — used to justify conquest.

questions.question: Compare these two sources explaining the Scramble.

source_a.text: The conquest of Africa flowed from a single, simple cause: Europe's hunger for raw cotton and rubber.

source_b.text: Economic motives mattered, but so did great-power rivalry, racist ideology and conditions within Africa itself.

statements.text: The Scramble is explained by a single economic cause
The Scramble is explained by several interacting causes
Racist ideology and conditions within Africa are included as causes
The cause is said to be 'single' and 'simple'
Both sources give the same explanation

questions.memo: Source A reduces the Scramble to one cause; Source B shows historians weigh several. The single-cause story is tidy but incomplete.

questions.question: How did 'scientific racism' make conquest seem acceptable to Europeans?
options: It claimed Europeans were a superior race with a duty to rule 'lesser' peoples
It proved all races were equal
It had no effect on how Europeans saw conquest
It encouraged Europeans to leave Africa alone
questions.expected: It claimed Europeans were a superior race with a duty to rule 'lesser' peoples
questions.memo: By dressing up racism as science, it let Europeans believe conquest was a natural duty rather than theft — a powerful justification for imperialism.

questions.question: True or false: Recognising the 'African dimension' means seeing Africans only as helpless victims of the Scramble.
questions.memo: The African dimension does the opposite: it recognises that African politics, economies and actions shaped how the Scramble unfolded — Africans were agents, not just victims.

questions.question: What is the danger of accepting only ONE explanation for the Scramble?
options: It oversimplifies a complex event and can hide important causes
There is no danger; one cause is always best
It makes the event easier to understand correctly
It proves the other causes never existed
questions.expected: It oversimplifies a complex event and can hide important causes
questions.memo: Sticking to one cause flattens a complex event. The economic, racial, diplomatic and African dimensions each capture part of the truth.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'The Scramble for Africa cannot be explained by a single cause.'
questions.thesis: The Scramble for Africa cannot be explained by a single cause.

pool.text: Economic motives — markets, raw materials, investment — clearly played a part
Great-power rivalry pushed nations to grab land to keep up with each other
Racist ideology and conditions within Africa also shaped the conquest
Africa is a large continent
The Berlin Conference was held indoors
For some specific colonies, one motive may have been clearly dominant

questions.memo: Economic (e1), diplomatic (e2), and racial plus African-dimension factors (e3) all contributed. e6 is a fair counter — one motive may dominate in a single case — but overall the Scramble was multi-causal.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why 'scientific racism' was not real science.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining why 'scientific racism' was not real science.

options.text: Scientific racism was pseudo-science used to justify conquest, not genuine science
Scientific racism was proven true by modern science
Scientific racism had no connection to imperialism
It started from the conclusion that Europeans were superior and dressed that racism in scientific language, and modern science has refuted it
It was written in books
It used long words
Because it worked backward from a racist belief rather than following evidence, it was ideology disguised as science — useful for justifying conquest
Because all science is unreliable
Because Europeans really were superior

questions.memo: Claim (pseudo-science to justify conquest) + evidence (started from racism, since refuted) + explanation (worked backward from belief, not evidence) explains why it was not real science.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on the role of racism in the Scramble.

source_a.text: Science had established beyond doubt the natural superiority of the European and his right to rule.

source_b.text: What was called 'race science' was a pseudo-scientific ideology built to justify the conquest already under way.

statements.text: European superiority is presented as established science
'Race science' is identified as a pseudo-scientific ideology
The racism is said to justify a conquest already under way
The 'right to rule' is presented as scientifically proven
Both sources treat race science the same way

questions.memo: The 1895 textbook (A) presents racism as proven science; the modern history (B) exposes it as ideology serving conquest. Calling it 'science' was the trick.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Economic motives were a major driver of the Scramble for Africa.'
questions.thesis: Economic motives were a major driver of the Scramble for Africa.

pool.text: Industrial Europe needed raw materials such as rubber, cotton and minerals
European producers wanted new markets to sell their manufactured goods
Investors sought new places to put surplus capital for profit
Africa has many different climates
European ships were made of metal and wood
Diplomatic rivalry and racism were also important causes

questions.memo: Raw materials (e1), markets (e2), and investment (e3) make the economic case. e6 is a fair counter — other causes mattered too — but it does not weaken the economic driver itself.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why studying competing theories makes you a better history student.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why studying competing theories makes you a better history student.

options.text: Comparing competing explanations teaches you to weigh evidence instead of accepting one story
You should always memorise just one cause
Competing theories prove history is pointless
The Scramble has economic, diplomatic, racial and African-dimension explanations, each supported by different evidence
History books are long
The Scramble happened in Africa
Weighing the strengths and limits of each theory builds the judgement real historical analysis requires
Memorising one theory is all that matters
It is better to ignore the evidence entirely

questions.memo: Claim (weigh evidence, not one story) + evidence (four theories, each with its own support) + explanation (weighing them builds historical judgement) explains the value of studying the debate.

questions.question: Compare these two ways of writing about the causes of the Scramble.

source_a.text: The cause of the Scramble was obvious and beyond dispute, requiring no further discussion.

source_b.text: Historians continue to debate the relative weight of economic, diplomatic, racial and African factors.

statements.text: The cause is treated as obvious and beyond dispute
The cause is treated as an ongoing debate among historians
Several competing factors are named
The cause is said to require 'no further discussion'
Both sources treat the causes the same way

questions.memo: Source A shuts down debate; Source B keeps it open and names the competing factors. Good history treats causes as something to weigh, not a closed case.

HIS.G11.T4.SCRAMBLE.A3.title: Consequences: artificial borders, resistance and genocide
HIS.G11.T4.SCRAMBLE.A3.description: Artificial colonial boundaries splitting peoples; African resistance including the Battle of Adwa; the genocides in the Belgian Congo and German South-West Africa (Herero and Nama); the lasting legacy.
HIS.G11.T4.SCRAMBLE.A3.recovery_strategy: Colonial borders IGNORED African peoples — they split groups like the Shangaan/Tsonga across Mozambique and South Africa. Africans DID resist and sometimes won: Ethiopia defeated Italy at Adwa (1896). And conquest brought genocide — remember the Belgian Congo and the German killing of the Herero and Nama in Namibia. Those borders and wounds still shape Africa today.

questions.question: A major lasting consequence of the Scramble was that colonial borders:
options: Split peoples who culturally belonged together and forced different groups into one colony
Followed African ethnic and cultural lines exactly
Disappeared as soon as the colonisers left
questions.expected: Split peoples who culturally belonged together and forced different groups into one colony
questions.memo: Colonial borders were artificial: they cut through peoples who belonged together and lumped different groups into single colonies, creating lasting tensions.

questions.question: At the Battle of Adwa in 1896, which African country defeated an invading European army?
questions.memo: At Adwa in 1896, Ethiopia decisively defeated Italy — a rare and famous African victory against the Scramble.

questions.question: True or false: Colonial borders carefully followed the cultural and ethnic lines of African peoples.
questions.memo: The borders did the opposite — they ignored African realities, splitting some peoples apart and forcing others together. This is what 'artificial borders' means.

questions.question: The Shangaan/Tsonga people were split by colonial borders between South Africa and _________.
questions.memo: The Shangaan/Tsonga were divided between Portuguese Mozambique and South Africa — one people cut in two by a colonial line.

questions.question: In which colony did a notorious genocide take place under King Leopold's rule?
questions.memo: The Belgian Congo under King Leopold II saw mass atrocities and death on a horrific scale — one of the most studied genocides of the colonial period.

questions.question: In German South-West Africa (today's Namibia), the Germans committed genocide against the _________ and Nama peoples.
questions.memo: The German genocide of the Herero and Nama in South-West Africa (Namibia) is often called the first genocide of the twentieth century.

questions.question: Sort each item as an example of ARTIFICIAL BORDERS, RESISTANCE, or COLONIAL GENOCIDE.

items.text: The Shangaan/Tsonga split between Mozambique and South Africa
Ethiopia's victory over Italy at Adwa
The mass atrocities in the Belgian Congo
Lesotho and Botswana cut off from South Africa
The German killing of the Herero and Nama
African armies fighting European invasion

questions.memo: Borders: split peoples. Resistance: Adwa, African armies fighting. Genocide: the Congo, the Herero and Nama.

questions.question: Why are colonial borders described as a lasting problem for Africa?
options: They still divide some peoples and group rivals together, fuelling later conflicts
They were all redrawn fairly after independence
They had no effect once colonisers left
questions.expected: They still divide some peoples and group rivals together, fuelling later conflicts
questions.memo: Most independent African states kept the colonial borders. Because those lines split peoples and forced rivals together, they have contributed to conflicts that persist today.

questions.question: Fill the blanks to summarise the consequences of the Scramble.
questions.cloze_template: The Scramble left [1] borders that split peoples such as the [2] across Mozambique and South Africa. Africans [3] the conquest — Ethiopia defeated Italy at [4] in 1896. Conquest also brought [5], as in the Belgian Congo and against the Herero and Nama.
questions.memo: Artificial borders (Shangaan/Tsonga split), resistance (Adwa 1896), and genocide (Congo; Herero and Nama) — the three great consequences.

questions.question: Why was the Battle of Adwa especially significant?
options: It showed an African nation could defeat a European power and keep its independence
It was the only battle in the whole Scramble
It led directly to the Berlin Conference
It ended colonialism across all of Africa
questions.expected: It showed an African nation could defeat a European power and keep its independence
questions.memo: Adwa proved European conquest was not inevitable: Ethiopia defeated Italy and remained independent, inspiring others and challenging the myth of European invincibility.

questions.question: Tap the phrases that show colonial borders ignored the people who lived there.
questions.source_text: The new boundary ran straight through the heart of a single people, leaving cousins in two different colonies, ruled by two different languages, divided by a line none of them had ever asked for.
questions.task: Tap the phrases showing the borders split a people unnaturally.

targets.phrase: straight through the heart of a single people
targets.reason: One people divided by the border

targets.phrase: leaving cousins in two different colonies
a line none of them had ever asked for
targets.reason: The border was imposed without African consent

questions.memo: A border 'through the heart of a single people', splitting 'cousins', that 'none of them had ever asked for' — the very definition of an artificial colonial boundary.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on African resistance to the Scramble.

source_a.text: The natives, overawed by European power, submitted everywhere without serious struggle.

source_b.text: From Ethiopia's victory at Adwa to countless local wars, Africans resisted the conquest fiercely, though most were eventually overcome.

statements.text: Africans are said to have submitted everywhere without struggle
Africans are shown resisting fiercely, including at Adwa
Most resistance was eventually overcome
Africans are described as 'overawed' and submissive
Both sources agree on the scale of resistance

questions.memo: The colonial account (A) erases resistance; the modern history (B) records it — from Adwa to countless local wars. The 'submitted without struggle' claim is false.

questions.question: The German campaign against the Herero and Nama is often described as:
options: The first genocide of the twentieth century
questions.expected: The first genocide of the twentieth century
questions.memo: Germany's deliberate destruction of the Herero and Nama in South-West Africa (1904 onwards) is widely regarded as the first genocide of the twentieth century.

questions.question: Why did most newly independent African states keep the old colonial borders?
options: Redrawing them risked even worse conflict, so the artificial lines mostly remained
Africans had drawn them in the first place
The borders had no practical importance
questions.expected: Redrawing them risked even worse conflict, so the artificial lines mostly remained
questions.memo: At independence, leaders feared that reopening borders would spark new wars, so the artificial colonial lines were largely kept — which is why their problems persist.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'Colonial borders were artificial and have had a lasting harmful legacy.'
questions.thesis: Colonial borders were artificial and have had a lasting harmful legacy.

pool.text: Borders split single peoples, such as the Shangaan/Tsonga, across different colonies
They forced rival or unrelated groups together into one colonial state
Independent states largely kept these lines, carrying their tensions into the present
Africa has many rivers and mountains
Maps are drawn on paper
A few colonial borders did happen to follow natural features like rivers

questions.memo: Splitting peoples (e1), forcing rivals together (e2), and persisting after independence (e3) show the artificial borders' harmful legacy. e6 is a fair counter — some followed rivers — but most ignored the people on the ground.

questions.question: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining the significance of the Battle of Adwa.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-sentence paragraph explaining the significance of the Battle of Adwa.

Adwa had no lasting importance
In 1896 Ethiopia decisively defeated the invading Italian army and kept its independence
Ethiopia is in East Africa
Italy is in Europe
By breaking the myth of European invincibility, Adwa inspired later resistance and became a symbol of African independence
It showed conquest was always impossible to resist
It made no difference to other Africans

questions.memo: Claim (an African nation beat a European power) + evidence (Ethiopia defeated Italy in 1896, stayed free) + explanation (broke the invincibility myth, inspired others) captures Adwa's significance.

questions.question: Compare these two sources on colonial rule in the Congo.

source_a.text: Under enlightened European guidance, the Congo was opened to commerce and the benefits of civilisation.

source_b.text: Forced labour, mutilation and mass death under Leopold's regime killed millions of Congolese people.

statements.text: Colonial rule is praised as bringing commerce and civilisation
Colonial rule is shown causing forced labour, mutilation and mass death
Millions of Congolese deaths are named
The Congo is said to have received 'the benefits of civilisation'
Both sources describe Congo's colonial experience the same way

questions.memo: The company report (A) sells a civilising story; the historian (B) records genocide. The gap between the two shows how colonial propaganda hid mass atrocity.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis: 'African resistance to the Scramble was real and significant, even though most was defeated.'
questions.thesis: African resistance to the Scramble was real and significant, even though most was defeated.

pool.text: Ethiopia defeated Italy at Adwa and kept its independence
Countless African societies fought wars against European invasion
Resistance forced the colonisers into costly, prolonged campaigns
Africa has many languages
European armies carried flags
In the end, most African societies were conquered

questions.memo: Adwa (e1), widespread wars (e2), costly campaigns (e3) prove resistance was real and significant. e6 is a fair counter — most were defeated — but defeat does not erase the resistance.

questions.question: Build a paragraph explaining why the genocides of the Scramble must be remembered.
questions.prompt: Build a paragraph explaining why the genocides of the Scramble must be remembered.

options.text: The colonial genocides reveal the true violence behind the 'civilising' rhetoric
The genocides were minor and best forgotten
No genocides occurred during the Scramble
Millions died in the Belgian Congo, and Germany destroyed most of the Herero and Nama in Namibia
Africa has a long coastline
The Scramble involved many countries
Remembering them counters the myth that colonialism was benign and honours the victims
Forgetting them makes history more accurate
They prove colonialism was harmless

questions.memo: Claim (genocides reveal the real violence) + evidence (the Congo; the Herero and Nama) + explanation (remembering counters the benign-colonialism myth and honours victims) makes the case.

questions.question: Compare these two overall judgements of the Scramble's legacy.

source_a.text: On balance, European rule brought roads, schools and order that benefited Africa greatly.

source_b.text: The Scramble left artificial borders, the wounds of genocide, and economies built to serve Europe — a legacy Africa still grapples with.

statements.text: The legacy is judged as a great benefit to Africa
The legacy is judged as artificial borders, genocide and exploitative economies
The legacy is said to be one Africa still grapples with
European rule is credited with roads, schools and order
Both sources reach the same judgement

questions.memo: The apologist (A) tallies only the supposed benefits; the historian (B) weighs the borders, genocide and exploitation. A serious judgement of the Scramble must face its lasting harm, not just list roads and schools.
